bullets: A new release in this feed, OpenGray, evaluates whether radiotherapy-planning agents make the correct decision, not merely whether they produce a favorable dose plan. Its known-answer tasks include incompatible treatment goals, where an agent should recognize that no valid plan exists, and a feasible control with a stored plan satisfying every hard goal. Why it matters: If you evaluate clinical planning agents, OpenGray lets you test whether an agent appropriately requests review or stops, rather than rewarding it for optimizing an impossible specification. That distinction can change which system appears safe enough for further validation. Evidence: E001. High confidence.

The newly released EffectWorld represents each agent tool by what it reads, writes, and changes, including whether repeated calls are safe. An executable verifier can then check tool-use traces for unsafe effects without relying on human labels or another model as judge. Why it matters: If you build tool-using agents, this supports evaluation of actions such as duplicate writes or deletion without confirmation even when the final answer looks correct. It also offers machine-checkable training signals for reducing wasteful or unsafe tool sequences. Evidence: E006. High confidence.

LiveSearch, newly discovered by this feed, stores financial-search questions as executable verifier programs. The question remains fixed, but its current answer is generated through calls to a professional financial data service rather than frozen when the benchmark is authored. Why it matters: If you are choosing an evaluation for financial search agents, this design tests current retrieval and analysis instead of recall of stale answers. It changes the benchmark dependency from a static answer file to executable access to the underlying data service. Evidence: E090. High confidence.

FeatureArc, newly discovered by this feed, evaluates coding agents across successive extensions of the same feature. Each stage builds on the agent’s own earlier code, while executable checks test both new requirements and continuing compatibility. Why it matters: If your product relies on agents maintaining software over time, a one-request benchmark can miss regressions caused by earlier design choices. FeatureArc provides a way to compare agents on cumulative maintenance rather than isolated patch completion. Evidence: E095. High confidence.

A new release introduces Bipartite Attribution, or BiPA, for auditing agent skill optimizers. It reruns an optimizer’s acceptance rule on candidates identical to the starting procedure, revealing gains produced by noisy selection alone, and traces the extra input tokens associated with accepted edits. Why it matters: If you evaluate systems that automatically rewrite an agent’s instructions, this separates actual procedural improvement from chance acceptance on a small development set. It also makes token cost part of the comparison rather than treating task success as the only outcome. Evidence: E041. High confidence.

A new audit in this feed examines 51 multilingual benchmarks covering 242 datasets and 219 languages. It reports that 36% of represented languages occur in only one benchmark, while some regions receive almost no coverage and lower-resource languages span far fewer task categories. Why it matters: If you are selecting a multilingual evaluation suite, language count alone can overstate coverage. The audit supports comparing geographic representation and task variety before using aggregate multilingual scores to make model-selection claims. Evidence: E003. High confidence.

The new CogArena benchmark runs agents through ten behavioral experiments in a standard web browser, using the same visual stimuli and response interfaces encountered by human participants instead of converting the experiments into text prompts. Why it matters: If you study model behavior using human experimental paradigms, CogArena lets you test whether conclusions survive the visual interface and timing conditions. This can change whether a text-only result is treated as evidence about behavior in the original experiment. Evidence: E002. High confidence.

The newly released ETC-Bench evaluates transcript canonicalization: converting different written forms of the same speech into one comparison form when the audio cannot determine the difference. It covers 181 phenomenon types across 12 languages and tests both normalization and preservation of meaning. Why it matters: If you compare speech-recognition systems, this can separate genuine recognition errors from harmless spelling, formatting, or transcription conventions. That may change model rankings when conventional exact-text scoring penalizes equivalent transcripts. Evidence: E013. High confidence.
bullets_zh: 本信息流中的新发布项目 OpenGray 评估放射治疗规划智能体是否做出正确决策，而不只是生成有利的剂量计划。其答案已知的任务包括治疗目标相互冲突的情形，此时智能体应识别出不存在有效计划；还包括一个可行的对照情形，其中存储了一份满足所有硬性目标的计划。Why it matters: 如果您评估临床规划智能体，OpenGray 可用于测试智能体是否会适当地请求审核或停止，而不是因其优化一个不可能实现的规范而给予奖励。这一区别可能会改变哪个系统看起来足够安全、可以接受进一步验证。Evidence: E001. High confidence.

新发布的 EffectWorld 根据每个智能体工具读取、写入和更改的内容来表示该工具，包括重复调用是否安全。随后，可执行验证器可以检查工具使用轨迹中是否存在不安全影响，而无须依赖人工标签或另一个模型充当裁判。Why it matters: 如果您构建使用工具的智能体，这种方法可以支持评估重复写入或未经确认即删除等操作，即使最终答案看起来正确。它还可为减少浪费资源或不安全的工具调用序列提供机器可检验的训练信号。Evidence: E006. High confidence.

本信息流新发现的 LiveSearch 将金融搜索问题存储为可执行验证器程序。问题保持不变，但其当前答案通过调用专业金融数据服务生成，而不是在编写基准时被冻结。Why it matters: 如果您正在为金融搜索智能体选择评估方案，这种设计测试的是当前信息的检索与分析，而不是对陈旧答案的回忆。它使基准所依赖的对象从静态答案文件变为对底层数据服务的可执行访问。Evidence: E090. High confidence.

本信息流新发现的 FeatureArc 在对同一功能进行连续扩展的过程中评估编码智能体。每个阶段都建立在智能体自己先前编写的代码之上，同时通过可执行检查测试新需求和持续兼容性。Why it matters: 如果您的产品依赖智能体长期维护软件，单次请求式基准可能无法发现由早期设计选择引发的回归。FeatureArc 提供了一种按累积维护能力而非孤立补丁完成情况比较智能体的方法。Evidence: E095. High confidence.

一项新发布的工作引入了 Bipartite Attribution（即 BiPA），用于审计智能体技能优化器。它会对与初始程序完全相同的候选方案重新运行优化器的接受规则，从而揭示仅由有噪声的选择过程产生的增益，并追踪与已接受编辑相关的额外输入 token。Why it matters: 如果您评估会自动改写智能体指令的系统，这种方法可以将实际的程序性改进与在小型开发集上因偶然而被接受区分开来。它还将 token 成本纳入比较，而不是把任务成功视为唯一结果。Evidence: E041. High confidence.

本信息流中的一项新审计考察了涵盖 242 个数据集和 219 种语言的 51 个多语言基准。审计报告称，所涵盖语言中的 36% 仅出现在单个基准中，而某些地区几乎完全没有覆盖，资源较少的语言所涉及的任务类别也少得多。Why it matters: 如果您正在选择多语言评估套件，仅凭语言数量可能会夸大覆盖范围。该审计支持在使用多语言汇总分数提出模型选择结论之前，对地理代表性和任务多样性进行比较。Evidence: E003. High confidence.

新的 CogArena 基准让智能体在标准网页浏览器中完成 ten 项行为实验，使用与人类参与者所接触到的相同视觉刺激和作答界面，而不是将实验转换为文本提示。Why it matters: 如果您使用人类实验范式研究模型行为，CogArena 可用于测试相关结论在视觉界面和计时条件下是否仍然成立。这可能会改变人们是否将纯文本结果视为有关原始实验中行为的证据。Evidence: E002. High confidence.

新发布的 ETC-Bench 评估转录文本规范化：当音频无法判定不同书写形式之间的差异时，将同一语音的不同书写形式转换为统一的比较形式。它涵盖 12 种语言中的 181 类现象，同时测试规范化和语义保留能力。Why it matters: 如果您比较语音识别系统，这种方法可以将真正的识别错误与无关紧要的拼写、格式或转录惯例差异区分开来。当传统的精确文本评分对等价转录文本进行惩罚时，这可能会改变模型排名。Evidence: E013. High confidence.
briefing.caveat: These findings describe a keyword-filtered feed, not the AI field as a whole. Only 152 ranked evidence records were supplied from today’s 573-record corpus, so lower-ranked artifacts were not reviewed here. Brave, OpenReview, and Semantic Scholar were unavailable, and some attention collectors reported unread or stale records; no attention-based conclusion is included.
briefing.caveat_zh: 这些发现描述的是一个经过关键词筛选的信息流，而非整个人工智能领域。今天包含 573 条记录的语料库仅提供了 152 条已排序的证据记录，因此此处未审查排名较低的材料。Brave、OpenReview 和 Semantic Scholar 均不可用，且部分关注度采集器报告了未读或过期记录；因此未纳入任何基于关注度的结论。

evidence_items.summary: Background and purpose: Radiotherapy planning agents based on large language models (LLMs) decide when to submit a plan or request review but are evaluated mainly by dose. This study developed OpenGray, a benchmark of planning tasks with known correct decisions. Materials and methods: OpenGray adds tasks with known answers to the OpenKBP-Opt head-and-neck dataset, including two contradictions with dose goals proven incompatible and a feasible control with a stored plan meeting every hard goal. Four systems, from a rule-based planning script to a full LLM agent, were evaluated on 30 patients, the LLM-based ones with a commercial (Terra) and a local (Ministral 3 8B) LLM. Decisions, achieved dose, problem recognition, and technical failures were recorded and also read from logs of 39 stereotactic radiosurgery runs of SAGE, a clinical LLM agent. Results: With Terra, the script preceded by an LLM review and the full agent had decision accuracies of 95.4% and 92.1%, respectively, yet escalated only 50% (95% confidence interval, 25-75%) and 25% (10-40%) of overlap contradictions, which required arithmetic on the anatomy. All four systems submitted every feasible control, but 24% of these plans missed a hard goal that the stored plan had met. In four SAGE runs, one goal failed at every attempt; the agent identified it in every reply but had no action for stopping. Conclusions: Favorable aggregate scores concealed specific decision failures. Planning agents should be evaluated on their decisions as well as their dose and given an explicit action for stopping and requesting review.
evidence_items.title: OpenGray: a benchmark for evaluating the decisions of radiotherapy planning agents

evidence_items.summary: Claims about the cognitive capabilities of large language models are typically tested by translating behavioral paradigms into text prompts, bypassing the visual interfaces and time pressure through which human participants actually engage with experiments. At the same time, AI agents can now complete online behavioral tasks and produce human-like data, which raises concerns that online datasets in the social and behavioral sciences are increasingly open to contamination. We introduce CogArena, a benchmark of ten experimental paradigms from the social and behavioral sciences. Agents complete the experiments through a standard web browser, working with the same visual stimuli and response interfaces that online participants use. A three-level scoring procedure evaluates whether the agent completed the task, how accurately it performed, and whether its data show the behavioral signatures each paradigm reliably produces in people. Across four multimodal models, each run ten times per task, we find that finishing an experiment and reproducing its signatures are different things. Many sessions did not finish, and those that did reproduced some signatures reliably and others not at all. CogArena provides the tasks, scoring code, and a public leaderboard for new submissions.
evidence_items.title: CogArena: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents on Interactive Behavioral Experiments

evidence_items.summary: Multilingual evaluation benchmarks are the primary instrument for assessing whether large language models generalize beyond English, yet the adequacy of these benchmarks has received little systematic scrutiny. We present a data-driven audit of 51 recent multilingual benchmarks spanning 242 datasets and 219 languages, organized around three pillars: coverage, representativeness, and rigor. Our analysis reveals that coverage is wide but thin with 36% of evaluated languages appearing in only a single benchmark, entire regions (Oceania, the Americas, Central Asia) are near-zero, and a stark task equity gap leaves low-resource languages evaluated on only 1-3 task categories versus 14 for high-resource languages. Representativeness is structurally compromised: translation from English remains the dominant construction strategy where 56% of all dataset-language instances are translated introducing artifacts and English-centric framing, while culturally grounded content is concentrated in a handful of community-driven benchmarks with narrow language scope. The ecosystem thus forces a trade-off between breadth and validity. Rigor is undermined by benchmark contamination, including translated benchmark leakage and parallel corpus overlap that evade surface-form detection. We synthesize these findings into concrete recommendations for building evaluation frameworks that are natively constructed, culturally grounded, contamination-aware, and designed to serve the communities whose languages they claim to evaluate. The dashboard with all the metadata collected can be found at https://aka.ms/multilingual-evals.
evidence_items.title: The State and Fate of Multilingual, Contextual Evaluation in the NLP World

evidence_items.summary: Derivative-free optimization (DFO) addresses problems where derivatives are unavailable or costly to obtain. This setting often arises in simulation-based and experimental applications, where evaluating the black-box objective can itself be costly. Thus, it remains a central challenge in DFO to effectively exploit accumulated observations to select informative evaluation points under a limited budget. In this light, we introduce the NextEval solver, an agent-based DFO solver, which integrates the capabilities of a large language model (LLM) to guide the sequential selection of evaluation points. Specifically, we establish a system that combines an LLM agent with a numerical environment. The environment provides tools for analyzing past evaluations and executing numerical methods, while maintaining a shared evaluation history and method-specific state to support continuation across method switches. Using observations and tool feedback, the LLM agent selects tools, configures their parameters, and allocates the evaluation budget, while numerical methods compute and evaluate candidate points. Building on this system, we also introduce NextEval Bench, a benchmark protocol for comparing agent configurations on shared DFO tasks using the same numerical tools under matched evaluation budgets and information constraints. Numerical results on low-dimensional DFO problems demonstrate that the NextEval solver outperforms the state-of-the-art DFO baselines in function-evaluation efficiency.
evidence_items.title: NextEval: An Agent-Based Solver and Benchmark for Derivative-Free Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Small open language models can call tools, but they do not reason about what a call does: they delete without asking, repeat writes, re-read state they already hold, and issue one call per turn where a short program would do. We introduce EffectWorld, an executable world of effect-typed tools in which every tool declares its effect, whether it is idempotent, and which resources it reads and writes. These declarations let a replay verifier decide whether a trace is effect-safe without labels or judge models, let an executor run tool programs of several dependent calls in one turn, and let a compiler-style optimizer turn wasteful traces into verified training signal; together they make EffectWorld a benchmark of effect safety and call efficiency. Low-rank adapters trained on this data deliver large gains: on Qwen3-4B, they raise task success from 53% to 99% in distribution, from 52% to 81% on a held-out split with unseen task kinds and distractor tools, and from 74% to 83% on an unseen domain, with about a third of the output tokens. The gains carry over to other model families. On the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard (BFCL), the adapter matches the base model's live accuracy and raises multi-turn accuracy from 21.9 to 26.6, and a recipe with near-miss declines lifts the BFCL average above the base model's while matching its irrelevance detection. Along the way we uncover and fix a pitfall that in-domain evaluation alone would miss: refusal templates in widely used public tool-use corpora teach a small model not to call tools, cutting BFCL non-live accuracy from 88.0 to 31.4, and filtering them restores 84.8. We also find that positive examples, not negative ones, carry the learning: suppression and preference objectives on the verified negatives add nothing over an SFT-only control, while targeted positives move exactly the behaviour they show.
evidence_items.title: Small agents should know what their tools do

evidence_items.summary: Abstract While deep learning has significantly advanced image reconstruction of electrical capacitance tomography (ECT), most public datasets retain only capacitance vectors and permittivity distributions and do not expose the excitation-wise electric potential field, a physical intermediate in the forward mapping. To address this, we present an electric-potential-augmented ECT benchmark dataset generated via a COMSOL–MATLAB pipeline for a fixed eight-electrode sensor. The dataset comprises 20 000 randomized samples across four typical flow-pattern families. Alongside conventional capacitance vectors and permittivity images, each sample preserves eight spatially registered full-field potential maps. Governing equations and field-perturbation visualizations characterize the relation between potential and dielectric structure. As an initial use of this physical information, we introduce potential-field intermediate supervision to guide representation learning in simple forward and inverse models. Under sample-disjoint independent and identically distributed (IID) and fully held-out two-bar out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation, potential supervision reduces forward capacitance-prediction mean squared error (MSE) by 56.8% and 74.6%, respectively, relative to a structure- and capacity-aligned control. In an exploratory forward experiment, a low-weight partial differential equation residual yields 5.3%–8.3% lower mean potential-prediction MSE. For inverse reconstruction, the simple model reduces mean MSE by 14.3% and 3.0% on IID and OOD data, respectively, relative to the same control. The more modest inverse gains are consistent with the difficulty of recovering dense potential maps from limited capacitance measurements. These results provide initial controlled evidence for the value of potential-field supervision.
evidence_items.title: An electric-potential-augmented benchmark dataset for electrical capacitance tomography: electric-potential supervision for future physics-guided learning

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Specialist agents such as Biomni, STELLA and ToolsGenie wrap large language models in curated tools and multi-agent scaffolds for bioinformatics. We asked whether a current frontier model in an off-the-shelf coding harness still needs them. Claude Opus 5.5 (high effort) in Claude Code solved all 244 tasks of PromptBio-Bench, whose free-form output files are scored against expert references. It was run with and without 667 bioinformatics Agent Skills (bioSkills, ClawBio). Under the original evaluation framework with GPT-5.6 judges, Claude with skills completed every task and reached 0.869 accuracy, against 0.758 for Biomni and ToolsGenie and 0.717 for STELLA (paired McNemar p ≤ 2 × 10−4). Its failures exposed eleven evaluator defects and several incorrect reference answers. With these defects fixed, Claude reached 0.918 to 0.926 with skills and 0.873 to 0.902 without, across GPT and Claude judges that agreed on 95 to 98% of tasks. Skills added only 2.5 to 4.5 points, yet transcripts showed the agent never invoked one; the gap traces to run-to-run variation in a few judgement calls. Of the 18 tasks still failed, 11 trace to defective references or unstated settings, and most of the rest are defensible alternatives to the reference. A general-purpose frontier model now matches or exceeds purpose-built bioinformatics agents on realistic analyses; benchmark reliability, not agent capability, has become the main limit on measuring progress.
evidence_items.title: The Generalist Strikes Back:\\A General LLM Agent Outperforms Specialist Bioinformatics Agents on Free-Form, End-to-End Benchmark Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Coverage-evaluation benchmarks quantify whether retrieved evidence covers the different pieces of information needed to satisfy an information need. Existing benchmarks mostly consider factual claims that may already be known to pretrained retrieval components, leaving open whether retrievers find corpus evidence when it contradicts those priors. We study how retrievers behave when their parametric knowledge and the information in a corpus disagree. To do so, we develop a process to augment a nugget-based coverage benchmark with controlled contradictions. For each nugget, we create a negated counterpart and edit its supporting documents to support that negation while preserving the context. Applying this process to CoverageBench, a benchmark measuring information coverage, we create CoverageBench-Negate, spanning six datasets and roughly 63,000 original-edited evidence pairs (one per nugget-document link). We attach rich construction metadata to every pair and additionally provide out-of-family LLM judgments over all pairs and a human audit of a sample. In baseline experiments, BM25 separates original from edited near-twin evidence substantially better than dense retrievers (Qwen3 and Jina), which stay near chance. We release the benchmark on Hugging Face Datasets (nuggets, documents, pairs) together with the construction materials, including the prompts used to create it.
evidence_items.title: Coverage Under Contradiction: A Benchmark for Negation-Aware Retrieval

evidence_items.summary: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
evidence_items.title: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Benchmark researchers and developers of large language models (LLMs) and other AI systems need to find relevant evaluations, locate their benchmark datasets and code, and understand the settings behind reported scores. We present Benchmark Radar, a living database and search engine for retrieval and discovery of AI benchmarks, covering LLM evaluation, agentic and tool-use benchmarks, coding, reasoning, safety, and domain-specific evaluations. The system combines daily discovery of benchmark papers, repositories, datasets, and releases with a searchable benchmark catalog, mentions in model cards and technical reports, and score histories. It retains source identities and citations so readers can inspect candidate benchmarks and their evaluation evidence. Daily discovery draws on 37 sources: 13 direct connectors and 24 first-party research and engineering feeds. The catalog contains 1,283 source records drawn from 4 benchmark catalogs and 12,916 numeric observations on 790 records. We describe collection and retrieval, audit the full catalog, and examine benchmark saturation, adoption trends, and the limits of score comparisons. A worked example walks through a complete prior-art search, showing how to query the catalog and inspect benchmark evidence when designing a new evaluation. We release the web dashboard with a benchmark leaderboard, a Pareto frontier view of score against measured use, saturation and trend views, daily feeds, downloadable evidence, a command-line interface (CLI) for offline queries, and reproducible analysis.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark Radar: A Living Database and Search Engine for AI Benchmarks and Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) rely on static pretraining corpora, resulting in outdated knowledge over time. Existing approaches for evaluating knowledge edits either suffer from rapid contamination or rely on counterfactual edits that conflict with rigid existing knowledge. In this work, we propose a simulation-driven approach for evaluating and training LLMs on knowledge insertions. We introduce PARALLELEVENTS, a benchmark that simulates coherent trajectories of fictional yet realistic future events, enabling controlled evaluation without data contamination or conflicts with existing knowledge. We further propose SYNAPSE, a training framework that leverages model-generated data to integrate new knowledge into model parameters via instruction tuning. This synthetic pipeline enables scalable knowledge integration without costly human-curated data. SYNAPSE improves QA accuracy by 14.23 points over prior methods, indicating that simulation-based synthetic training yields robust, coherent knowledge insertion.
evidence_items.title: Parallel Universes for Temporal Evaluation and Knowledge Updating in LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable performance in Visually Rich Document Understanding (VRDU) tasks, but their capabilities are mainly evaluated on pristine, well-structured document images. We consider content restoration from shredded fragments, a challenging VRDU setting that requires integrating visual pattern recognition with semantic reasoning under significant content discontinuities. To facilitate systematic evaluation of complex VRDU tasks, we introduce ShredBench, a benchmark supported by an automated generation pipeline that renders fragmented documents directly from Markdown. The proposed pipeline ensures evaluation validity by allowing the flexible integration of latest or unseen textual sources to prevent training data contamination. ShredBench assesses four scenarios (English, Chinese, Code, Table) with three fragmentation granularities (8, 12, 16 pieces). Empirical evaluations on state-of-the-art MLLMs reveal a significant performance gap: The method is effective on intact documents; however, once the document is shredded, restoration becomes a significant challenge, with NED dropping sharply as fragmentation increases. Our findings highlight that current MLLMs lack the fine-grained cross-modal reasoning required to bridge visual discontinuities, identifying a critical gap in robust VRDU research.
evidence_items.title: ShredBench: Evaluating the Semantic Reasoning Capabilities of Multimodal LLMs in Document Reconstruction

evidence_items.summary: PURPOSE: Accurate dose calculation is a fundamental component of modern radiotherapy, enabling precise tumor irradiation while sparing surrounding healthy tissue. With the increasing adoption of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided radiotherapy and growing interest in real-time adaptive radiotherapy, there is a demand for fast and accurate dose calculation techniques on both computed tomography (CT) and MRI. To facilitate research in this area, the DoseRAD2026 dataset and accompanying challenge introduce a publicly available benchmark dataset comprising paired CT and MRI data with corresponding beam-level photon and proton Monte Carlo (MC) dose distributions, enabling the development and systematic evaluation of advanced dose calculation and prediction methods. ACQUISITION AND VALIDATION METHODS: The DoseRAD2026 dataset comprises paired CT and MRI data from 115 patients (75 training, 40 testing) treated on a hybrid MRI-linear accelerator (MRI-linac) for thoracic or abdominal lesions and is derived from the SynthRAD2025 dataset. Image pre-processing included deformable image registration, air-cavity correction and resampling. Ground-truth photon (6 MV) and proton dose distributions were generated using open-source MC dose calculation algorithms and resulted in a training dataset of 40,500 photon beams and 81,000 proton beamlets. DATA FORMAT AND USAGE NOTES: The dataset is organized into photon and proton subsets, each comprising paired CT-MRI images, beam-level dose distributions, and JSON files specifying patient-specific beam configurations. Data are provided in compressed MetaImage (.mha) format with standardized naming linking dose files to beam parameters in the JSON files. The dataset is released under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license, with the training set available from April 2026 and the test set withheld until March 2030.
evidence_items.title: DoseRAD2026: A benchmark dataset for AI-accelerated photon and proton dose calculation in radiotherapy.

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Heads of Security (HoS), a prompt injection defense that enforces instruction-data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. HoS learns how each head should redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. We evaluate HoS on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B. We compare it against SecAlign++, a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense, and ASIDE, a defense that, like ours, builds instruction-data separation into the model architecture. We show that HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. More specifically, the black-box RL-Hammer attack reaches 97% ASR against GPT-OSS-20B and 85% against SecAlign, but only 10% against HoS. Claudini, a state-of-the-art white-box attack, strengthened against HoS through autoresearch, requires 3 times more FLOPs to reach the same ASR on HoS as it does on GPT-OSS-20B or SecAlign. HoS preserves base-model utility across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, whereas SecAlign and ASIDE degrade in few-shot settings. On agentic benchmarks with static attacks, HoS and SecAlign perform similarly and substantially improve the security-utility trade-off over the base model. ASIDE struggles with tool use, achieving only 10% utility. These results show that prompt injection robustness can be achieved and improved through targeted attention interventions.
evidence_items.title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness

evidence_items.summary: Semi-supervised semantic segmentation, which aims to utilize large volumes of unlabeled images to achieve accurate segmentation results with fewer human annotations, has attracted increasing attention. Prior methods were primarily based on the assumption that the pseudo-labels generated by each branch were sufficiently reliable to supervise the remaining branches. However, there is a concern that the errors in pseudo-labels could accumulate during co-training, potentially resulting in suboptimal performance. To this end, we present a novel framework called heterogeneous dual-branch voting supervision (HDVS), which is designed to enhance the reliability of pseudo-labels and mitigate the issues arising from pseudo-labeling. Specifically, based on the cross-supervision framework, we introduce a voting mechanism that correlates pseudo-labels from heterogeneous branches to produce pseudo-labels with enhanced reliability. Concurrently, we employ a feature communication module to introduce perturbations at the feature level in each branch to maximize prediction diversity across the dual branches while maintaining convergence. Comprehensive evaluations of the proposed HDVS on two benchmark datasets (PASCAL VOC 2012 and Cityscapes) demonstrate its superiority to the state-of-the-art approaches.
evidence_items.title: HDVS: semi-supervised semantic segmentation via heterogeneous dual-branch voting supervision

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) derives its learning signal from binary rewards via on-policy exploration and becomes a powerful paradigm for improving the reasoning of large language models. Yet it faces a learning cliff on problems beyond model's current ability: when every rollout fails, the samples reveal nothing about a correct solution, and group-relative estimators (e.g., GRPO, RLOO) collapse the update to zero advantage. Expert trajectories offer a remedy, but they are incompatible with the current policy and often lie in the student's low-probability regions, so the surviving updates demand large parameter shifts and decay into surface-level imitation rather than transferable reasoning. We argue that a useful learning signal on hard problems must be both verifiably correct and sufficiently compatible with the current policy. We propose Policy-Compatible Reinforcement Learning (PICO), which performs distribution-constrained joint decoding: expert data guides decoding at the token level while preserving the student's relative token probabilities, and a dynamic top-k mechanism confines the sampling distribution under a finite divergence budget, yielding trajectories that are verified and policy-compatible by construction. These trajectories are optimized jointly with on-policy rollouts under a mixed-behavior objective that mitigates their distribution mismatch via importance sampling. Experiments across reasoning diverse datasets and agentic benchmarks demonstrate that PICO consistently outperforms standard RLVR and prior off-policy baselines.
evidence_items.title: When All Rollouts Fail: Policy-Compatible Joint Decoding for Hard-Problem Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Written transcripts of the same speech can differ in ways that are not uniquely determined by the speech signal. We formulate evaluation-side transcript canonicalization (ETC), which maps multiple surface forms to a single canonical form when their differences are not determined by speech. To our knowledge, ETC-Bench is the first and most comprehensive multilingual benchmark for evaluation-side transcript canonicalization, covering 181 phenomenon types across 12 languages. Each instance is a minimal pair that shares a sentence context and differs only in a target span exhibiting one phenomenon. To evaluate both canonicalization success and semantic preservation, we propose Semantic-preserving Exact-match Normalization Accuracy (SENA), which combines exact agreement between independently canonicalized pair members with a pair-relative BERTScore constraint against information loss. We further introduce the Taxonomy-guided Agent Canonicalization Skill (TACS), which provides LLM agents with phenomenon descriptions and explicit canonicalization contracts. Experiments with five baseline configurations and three TACS-based agents show that the agents outperform the baseline systems on shared languages. ETC-Bench provides a systematic testbed for evaluation-side transcript canonicalization across languages.
evidence_items.title: ETC-Bench: A Multilingual Benchmark for Evaluation-Side Transcript Canonicalization

evidence_items.summary: Depth sensors are widely deployed across robotic platforms, and advances in fast, high-fidelity depth simulation have enabled robotic policies trained on depth observations to achieve robust sim-to-real transfer for a wide range of tasks. Despite this, representation learning for depth modality remains underexplored compared to RGB, where large-scale foundation models now define the state of the art. To address this gap, we present DeFM, a self-supervised foundation model trained entirely on depth images for robotic applications. Using a DINO-style self-distillation objective on a curated dataset of 60M depth images, DeFM learns geometric and semantic representations that generalize to diverse environments, tasks, and sensors. To retain metric awareness across multiple scales, we introduce a novel input normalization strategy. We further distill DeFM into compact models suitable for resource-constrained robotic systems. When evaluated on depth-based classification, segmentation, navigation, locomotion, and manipulation benchmarks, DeFM achieves state-of-the-art performance and demonstrates strong generalization from simulation to real-world environments. We release all our pretrained models, which can be adopted off-the-shelf for depth-based robotic learning without task-specific fine-tuning. Webpage: https://de-fm.github.io/
evidence_items.title: DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics

evidence_items.summary: CARDIO-REVIEW: Research Data and Reproducibility Package This dataset accompanies CARDIO-REVIEW, a clinical artificial intelligence safety benchmark evaluating large language model (LLM) generation and automated review of clinician-authored synthetic cardiovascular scenarios. The study comprises 60 synthetic clinical scenarios organised into 30 matched A/B case pairs, with an independent repeatability assessment involving 12 scenarios from six matched pairs. Clinical safety classifications independently assessed by cardiologist investigators and final adjudicated severity ratings. Reviewer ACCEPT/REVISE decisions, source-to-review linkages, and clinical safety transitions. Frozen model configurations, prompt templates, and methodological documentation. Six R analysis scripts and reference outputs supporting reproduction of the reported descriptive statistics, reviewer analyses, 20,000-draw matched-pair cluster bootstrap confidence intervals, and repeatability assessments. A data dictionary, reproducibility instructions, and SHA-256 integrity verification tools. Reproducibility The supplied R scripts reproduce the reported analyses from the released linked and adjudicated data tables. The repository also preserves model response texts and synthetic case descriptions. Automated reconstruction of every intermediate analysis table from the original provider-level acquisition files and internal historical adjudication workbooks is outside the scope of this public release. Data protection and intended use All clinical scenarios are fictional. No real patient records are included. Direct clinician identifiers, confidential operational metadata, API credentials, and internal blinding records have been excluded. Some preserved model responses contain clinically unsafe recommendations.

evidence_items.summary: In finance, the answer that matters is usually the current one: prices, rates, and disclosures hold only as of a given day, so retrieving up-to-date facts is a core capability of a financial agent. Yet most financial benchmarks overlook timeliness. They fix each answer at annotation time, so the gold goes stale as markets move and, once leaked into training data, rewards recall rather than search and analysis. We introduce LiveSearch, a live benchmark that stores each question as executable verifier code: a typed program of calls to a professional financial data service, followed by a declarative extractor. The question is frozen, while its gold answer is determined by executing the program against professional financial data at evaluation time, and a daily job re-executes it with no human or language model in the loop. A memorized answer is thus likely outdated, and a model must reach the current one through tools and analysis. Construction is equally automatic: a language model only verbalizes programs enumerated from real tool responses and never chooses an answer. Under general web search, six contemporary tool-calling models reach 70.9% to 76.7% answer accuracy. Over three consecutive days, 70% of served questions change their gold value, and even under tolerance-aware matching, a literally reused earlier snapshot fails on a majority of questions within a single day. Per-question tracking uncovers dynamic shifts in correctness masked by aggregate accuracy.
evidence_items.title: LiveSearch: Questions as Executable Verifier Code for a Live Benchmark of Professional-Source Financial Search Agents

evidence_items.summary: Abstract — Synthetic medical tabular data generation has become essential for developing and validating computer-based medical systems (CBMSs) when real clinical data is restricted due to privacy, ethical, or data availability limitations. Existing probabilistic and deep generative models often lack interpretability and fail to preserve clinically meaningful dependencies, limiting their suitability for safety-critical applications. This paper proposes a novel application of Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) in a framework for synthetic medical tabular data generation with explicit causality and privacy preservation. Clinical features are described using linguistically interpretable fuzzy sets, and inter-feature dependencies are encoded as FCM edge weights computed from fuzzy set intersections. Synthetic patient records are generated by propagating randomly initialized linguistic activation vectors through the FCM until convergence, followed by defuzzification to produce clinically coherent numerical values.  The approach natively handles mixed data types, and domain constraints common in health records. Experimental evaluation on UCI medical benchmark datasets demonstrates competitive performance under a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) protocol. The proposed method achieves accuracy of up to 0.81 and AUROC of up to 0.90 on the Heart Disease dataset, matching or exceeding TVAE and Gaussian Copula baselines while running exclusively on CPU. Fidelity metrics including KS Complement (up to 0.91) and Correlation Similarity (up to 0.95) confirm strong statistical coherence, and DCR Baseline Protection scores consistently exceed those of TVAE, confirming adequate privacy guarantees. These results demonstrate that causally grounded, interpretable fuzzy modeling offers a computationally efficient and transparent alternative to deep generative models for trustworthy synthetic data generation in CBMSs.
evidence_items.title: Interpretable Synthetic Medical Tabular Data Generation for Clinical Decision Support Using Fuzzy Cognitive Maps

evidence_items.summary: Progress in natural language processing and information retrieval increasingly depends on large-scale evaluation data grounded in authentic high-quality human judgment. Such data are most valuable in high-stakes domains where annotation requires niche expertise, and they are becoming harder to obtain as generative AI and AI-assisted annotation tools make it difficult to guarantee that newly created datasets reflect genuine human decisions rather than synthetic or model-influenced labels. Here we present SYNERGY+, a curated collection of 119 SLR datasets comprising 494,201 screened records across four research domains (Health Sciences, Social Sciences, Physical Sciences, and Life Sciences), in which every record was evaluated by at least one human domain expert. Each dataset was selected from an initial pool of 212 candidates through a rigorous quality assessment covering licensing, data completeness, and publication integrity. These SLRs and their datasets were published between 2011 and 2025, predating the use of generative AI in screening. All records are enriched with bibliographic metadata via hierarchical matching against OpenAlex. SYNERGY+ is released under a CC0 license, with abstracts included for 168,969 open-access records where redistribution was permitted. The dataset is distributed through a Python package with a predefined stratified train/test split for standardized benchmarking. SYNERGY+ represents, to our knowledge, the largest and most methodologically rigorous benchmark for AI-assisted title and abstract screening to date, supporting applications spanning technology assisted SLRs, large language model evaluation, and evidence synthesis research.
evidence_items.title: SYNERGY+: A Large-Scale, Curated Benchmark Dataset of Expert Screening Decisions for Systematic Reviews

evidence_items.summary: OpenDUck is an open source implementation of Dynamic Undocking (DUck). OpenDUck can be found at https://github.com/CBDD/openduck. DUck is a particular application of steered molecular dynamics where the work needed to bring the main hydrogen bond in a protein-ligand complex to the quasi-bound state is evaluated 1. The quasi-bound work (WQB) is a measure of the structural stability of the complex and relates with the first dissociation barrier. DUck was designed as a filtering step in virtual screening campaigns and shows enrichment of docking results up to 40% for completely novel chemotypes. Due to its fast and cheap nature, it has been used in various screening pipelines like DUckCov2 for covalent docking or in fragment-based drug discovery3. Recently, new applications of structural stability have emerged. Maciej & Barril4 showed good binding mode prediction results and Miñarro et al.5 have deepened the understanding of modulation of protein-protein interactions by molecular glues. With the success of structural stability and the prospect of new applications, a push towards an open source, flexible and accessible implementation of Dynamic Undocking became imperative. OpenDUck has been developed as a python library to capitalize on big open source initiatives in computational chemistry such as OpenMM and OpenForcefield. While minimizing the external dependencies, we have been able to harness the development effort from those initiatives to provide as much flexibility as possible. We also aim to ease the maintenance and future updating of the code and protocol, by compartmentalizing the different DUck steps and parameters. OpenDUck comes with an executable openduck with all the necessary utilities and parameters to launch and evaluate Dynamic Undocking both in AMBER or in OpenMM. In addition to that, the openduck library can also be used to develop custom protocols with just a few lines of code.

evidence_items.summary: Hundreds of degraded textile fragments from the Viking Age Oseberg ship burial (834 CE) still await reconstruction. Deep puzzle solvers perform well on clean natural images, but no historical textile dataset existed to train or test them. We present TEXMET, a curated dataset of 18,644 CC0-licensed historical textile images from the Metropolitan Museum of Art and, to our knowledge, the first textile-specific benchmark for puzzle solving, and use it to evaluate three state-of-the-art solvers: JPDVT, FCViT and DiffAssemble. Our results show that domain data, not architecture alone, limits transfer. Transformer models trained on natural images lose up to 60 points of puzzle accuracy on textiles, while the graph-based DiffAssemble, fine-tuned on TEXMET, reaches 85.89% on textiles and improves from 26.67% to 64.44% on 45 photographs of real Oseberg fragments, each cut into a 3×3 grid and reassembled in isolation. This short paper summarizes our article in the ACM JOCCH Special Issue on Visual Heritage.
evidence_items.title: TEXMET: A Curated Dataset and Deep Learning Benchmark for Archaeological Textile Reconstruction

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion video models produce striking clips, but they cannot reliably render an exact formula, a correct chart, a rule-consistent game or narration synchronized to on-screen events. A different route is emerging: multimodal agents that write code to render every frame and synthesize every sound. We introduce VibeVideoBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents on code-driven video generation. Its 239 self-contained tasks in English and Chinese span 12 categories, from data stories and music-driven pieces to classroom lessons and paper explainers; each asks an agent, running in its native harness inside a sandbox with no image or video generation model, to deliver a finished MP4 with sound within one hour. Evaluation is hierarchical and evidence-based: program checks of the delivery spec, about 13k task-specific rubric checks traced to the requirements they enforce, and five quality dimensions anchored per task, scored by three VLM judge panels. Across nine frontier agent systems and 2,151 scored rollouts, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 rank first and second with both the judges and human annotators, and the strongest system satisfies every core requirement on 76.3% of tasks. Delivery is a second axis: counting missing videos as zero changes the ranking, and three quarters of the lost videos are final renders that started too late, ran too slowly or never started, a failure of how agents plan their hour. Agents build their own rendering pipelines and inspect their own frames, yet how much they look does not predict quality. The judges' ranking of the systems closely matches blind human preferences.
evidence_items.title: VibeVideoBench: Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Code-Driven Video Generation

evidence_items.summary: Low-cost arms such as the SO-101 have become the most common entry point to robot learning, yet no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on them out of the box, and existing SO-101 benchmarks run only on physical hardware with simple tasks and few held-out objects. We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation built on an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It has four tasks scored as five families, 138 objects in seen, unseen-instance and unseen-class splits, 916 evaluation episodes with subsets for held-out appearances, rotate-to-fit planning and occlusion memory, and 3,629 simulated demonstrations on which every learned policy is fine-tuned under an equal compute budget. The twin ranks policies as the real robot does: five policies trained without real data, four VLAs and an LLM agent, keep their exact ranking when the same weights run on the physical arm in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman rho = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates success. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the best learned policies score near 61%, with spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remaining open. An LLM agent that writes code and hands grasping to a learned policy scores 83.2%, and an ablation shows that this lead comes from the choice of harness and the choice of language model.
evidence_items.title: SO-101 Bench: Accessible Spatial Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating deformable 3D reconstruction requires ground truth linking camera motion, surface deformation, material correspondence and image appearance. We introduce the Synthetic Deformable Tubular Benchmark, generated with LumenMorph, an open-source toolkit for creating, annotating and evaluating tubular scenes. The release contains 5,580 RGB images. Its baseline crosses three surface-motion conditions with moving and stationary cameras in six scene families; matched appearance variants cover only moving-camera finite-element actions in four families. Documented public and evaluation interfaces expose camera poses, geometry, depth, deformation fields, persistent material correspondences and discrete finite-element records. Persistent triangle identities and material weights let users track the same surface location across frames and query its three-dimensional trajectory. Separately implemented geometric and mechanical checks assess annotation consistency with the generating models. Structure-from-motion, optical-flow and supplied-geometry displacement-interpolation studies demonstrate how the resource distinguishes registration coverage from geometric accuracy, exposes camera- and surface-motion effects, and tests the benefits and mismatch of mechanical priors. Public readers, evaluation contracts and the configurable generator support reuse and extension. Data integrity, fixed-environment repeatability and retained-prediction score replay have distinct verification scopes. The benchmark provides a controlled synthetic reference without claiming anatomical or clinical realism.
evidence_items.title: Synthetic Deformable Tubular Benchmark: A mechanically annotated dataset for evaluating deformable 3D reconstruction

evidence_items.summary: Retinal vessel segmentation is widely used in retinal image analysis, yet model selection based only on aggregate overlap scores can overlook structural fidelity, cross-dataset robustness, and application-specific error costs. We evaluated five executable binary vessel-segmentation pipelines (FSG-Net, SA-UNetv2, DCP-1024, GAVE, and FR-UNet) on 244 images from six public datasets using pixel-level agreement, cross-dataset stability, thin-vessel retention, structural metrics, error composition, and available computational evidence. Results were aggregated with equal weighting across datasets. No pipeline was optimal in every setting. FSG-Net achieved the highest equal-dataset mean Macro-F1 (0.77), IoU (0.63), clDice (0.83), and Skeleton F1 (0.78), whereas SA-UNetv2 achieved the highest mean sensitivity (0.85) and Thin-Vessel Sensitivity (0.63). Differences across datasets were often larger than those among the leading pipelines, and errors shared by all five methods were concentrated near annotated vessel boundaries and faint peripheral vessels. In an ancillary analysis on 45 HRF images, segmentation masks were converted into 11 ring-wise vascular features for leave-one-out classification. Controlled perturbations showed that local mask errors can be amplified in downstream features, while targeted stabilization reduced sensitivity for five features. The results support task-conditioned, benchmark-relative pipeline selection rather than a single universal ranking and highlight the need to validate the selected pipeline on the intended target domain.
evidence_items.title: Evidence-Guided Selection of Retinal Vessel Segmentation Pipelines: A Cross-Dataset Benchmark of Performance, Structure, Failure Modes, and Reproducibility

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Causality extraction—the identification of cause–effect relations in natural language text—has been approached through three successive methodological paradigms: rule-based systems relying on lexical and syntactic cues, deep learning models exploiting neural architectures and pre-trained encoders, and, most recently, large language models (LLMs) applied through prompting or fine-tuning. Each paradigm has been evaluated on different datasets, under different annotation schemes, and with different metrics, making it difficult to determine how far apparent performance differences reflect genuine methodological advantages rather than benchmark artifacts. This study addresses that problem by constructing a unified benchmark for comparative evaluation of rule-based, deep learning, and LLM approaches to causality extraction. We consolidate multiple existing corpora—covering news, biomedical, and safety-incident text—into a harmonized annotation format, re-annotate a stratified subset to ensure consistent treatment of implicit and explicit causal relations, and evaluate representative methods from each paradigm under identical preprocessing, train–test splits, and evaluation protocols. We report span-level precision, recall, and F1, document-level F1, calibration error, inference cost, and annotation efficiency, and we conduct cross-domain transfer experiments to assess generalization. Results are analyzed to disentangle the contributions of architecture, training data, and task formulation, with particular attention to the conditions under which each paradigm retains a comparative advantage. We further examine error profiles across paradigms, identifying whether failures are concentrated in explicit versus implicit relations, local versus distributed constructions, and domain-specific versus general-language contexts.
evidence_items.title: Comparative Analysis of Rule-Based, Deep Learning, and LLM Approaches for Causality Extraction: A Unified Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Reproducible offline benchmarks for electric vehicle charging require explicit transition definitions and auditable data processing. We introduce IoEV-MARL, comprising 157,071 decision-level transitions from SUMO simulations of the road network of Tangier, Morocco, organized in a 62-column table. The corpus covers 700 collection episodes, seven seeds, four traffic regimes, and five behavioral arms: NEAREST, WEIGHTED, tabular Independent Q-Learning, and two QMIX checkpoint/exploration configurations. Learned collection policies originate from 120-episode training campaigns. A three-layer contract distinguishes decision-time observations, inter-decision elapsed time, and outcome/evaluation fields. Elapsed time is missing when no subsequent decision is recorded. The ETL protocol documents horizon censoring, missing successors, dimensional grain, and file-level provenance. Seven-fold leave-one-seed-out evaluations benchmark Behavior Cloning and offline Implicit Q-Learning on accept/reject decisions conditional on the selected station. Mean Behavior Cloning balanced accuracy ranges from 0.758 to 0.928 across tiers and feature sets, measuring imitation rather than operational performance. In matched greedy evaluation, QMIX has lower station-load dispersion in 7/7 seeds under Normal traffic, versus 2/7, 4/7, and 4/7 under Light, Peak, and Surge. Discrete-state audits characterize coverage gaps and structural reachability constraints. IoEV-MARL supports offline decision-learning research without establishing closed-loop performance gains.
evidence_items.title: IoEV-MARL: A Reproducible Offline Dataset and Benchmark for Electric Vehicle Charging Coordination Under Centralized and Decentralized Training

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We develop mapping-induced state dependence (MISD), an architecture in which a fixed non-material preference parameter helps determine complementary weights on the underlying utilities of actions. These weights vary with the underlying-utility difference between actions (extra costs). MISD can accommodate considerations such as honesty, intrinsic motivation, or work ethic. We apply it to a dynamic network cooperation game. Relative to a fixed-weight benchmark, MISD predicts more cooperation at low-to-intermediate extra costs but potentially less at high costs across networks. Misrepresenting the network or the behavioral mapping can distort policy evaluation and design, producing errors in estimated effects, intervention intensity, and targeting. Keywords : Non-material preferences; State-dependent behavior; Behavioral reversals; Tipping points; Social networks. JEL Classification : C73, D63, D85, D91.
evidence_items.title: Morality under Pressure: Mapping-Induced State Dependence and Cooperation in Social Dilemmas

evidence_items.summary: Differentiating Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) respiratory syndromes requires weighing overlapping symptoms together with tongue and pulse findings, a task that most AI systems for TCM perform end-to-end but without an interpretable intermediate representation. In this study, we addressed this gap with LEAF (LLM extraction and multiobjective feature selection), a two-stage modular framework evaluated on 3,253 records covering 14 respiratory syndromes from the TCM-SD benchmark. Its first large language model (LLM) stage extracted a 35-item symptom ontology that was built entirely from public TCM sources; among three interchangeable LLMs, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct was ranked as the best, followed by Phi-4 and the TCM domain model BianCang. Its second evolutionary-computation stage benchmarked four multiobjective evolutionary algorithms [non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm-II (NSGA-II), strength Pareto evolutionary algorithm 2 (SPEA2), competitive mechanism-based multiobjective particle swarm optimizer (CMOPSO), and non-dominated sorting differential evolution (NSDE)] over 10 seeds, and they were compared using Friedman’s and Nemenyi’s testing in terms of both classification outcome and search-process quality. The four algorithms showed no significant separation on held-out macro-F1, although NSDE led nominally, and none exceeded the full-feature baseline on point estimates. In contrast, hypervolume differed significantly and favored NSGA-II, the weakest of the four on held-out macro-F1. A four-classifier panel found no algorithm to be significantly different from either the full-feature baseline or a random-feature control, which was significantly outperformed only by the full-feature baseline. Applying NSDE to the remaining two LLM pipelines reproduced the original ranking, and its representative solution was fully attested against the knowledge base of TCM-SD, although not typically so across all the 10 seeds.
evidence_items.title: LEAF: benchmarking multiobjective evolutionary feature selection over large language model–extracted symptoms for interpretable Traditional Chinese Medicine respiratory syndrome differentiation

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for oncology decision support, but their performance in colorectal cancer with peritoneal metastases (CRC-PM) remains uncertain. We benchmarked 10 contemporary LLMs against an expert-consensus framework. Methods Forty-eight synthetic vignettes were derived from a 2026 CRC-PM consensus guideline, including 36 primary scenarios and 12 counterfactual scenarios forming six pairs. Each model completed every vignette three times using a frozen zero-shot structured prompt. The primary endpoint was prompt-aligned structured Full concordance; contradiction-only and full-semantic adjudication were sensitivity analyses. Two blinded attending colorectal surgeons, each with 5 years of clinical experience, independently validated the reference classifications. Results Among 1,080 primary responses, structured scoring classified 609 (56.4%) as Full, 117 (10.8%) as Partial, and 354 (32.8%) as Discordant. Model-specific structured Full concordance ranged from 49.1% to 63.0%; neither the Friedman test ( P = .104) nor clustered GEE ( P = .186) supported a robust model effect. Contradiction-only scoring was similar (56.2% Full), whereas full-semantic adjudication reduced Full concordance to 45.5%. Excluding prompt-development scenarios lowered absolute concordance but did not change the inferential conclusion. Expert agreement was 93.8%–97.9% across decision domains (Cohen kappa 0.898–0.948). Counterfactual and metachronous risk-management analyses showed wide uncertainty, and 21 clinically consequential discordance flags arose from five scenarios. Conclusions LLM performance in CRC-PM was sensitive to scoring definition and did not establish a stable between-model hierarchy. Prospective clinician-plus-LLM studies are required before clinical benefit can be inferred.
evidence_items.title: Large language models for complex decision-making in colorectal cancer with peritoneal metastases

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Dependable comparisons of minimum weighted feedback arc set (MWFAS) heuristics require consistent inputs, computational budgets, and treatment of incomplete runs. We present an audited benchmark linking weighted graphs and source-parent relationships to validated saved orders, original outcomes, and numerical optimization references. This resource extends an earlier metrics-only release and supports comparisons across graph families, paired weight regimes, and empirical sources. Incumbent-protected strongly connected component neighborhood search (IPSNS) showed family-dependent gains over its better initializer. Across all tested graph--seed groups in two generated-graph campaigns, ten iterations produced the same saved objectives and permutations as every larger tested budget. In the replicated campaign, family median process-wall ratios relative to the selected initializer were 1.27--1.60 at ten iterations, compared with 3.19--9.82 at 200. This observed trade-off is not a convergence or stopping guarantee. Under matched wall-clock horizons, IPSNS seed~1 beat RASstar on seven of nine selected synthetic topologies but only one of four selected empirical parents. At 300~s, single-node insertion from either evaluated initializer beat IPSNS seed~1 on all four parents. In a separate empirical campaign, complete 200-iteration comparisons covered only 18 of 38 views, all from one source parent. These findings show how budget, availability, dependence, and comparator choice affect interpretation. Public saved-output replay covers all ten numerical tables, Figure~2, and 11/17 tracked claim groups; six broader groups and historical-source reconstruction remain unresolved. The evidence supports scoped comparisons of existing methods rather than a universal ranking.
evidence_items.title: An Audited Benchmark for Minimum Weighted Feedback Arc Set: Graph Identity, Algorithm Comparison, and Reproducibility

organizations: School of Electrical & Computer Engineering, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Beer-Sheva 8410501, Israel

evidence_items.summary: Organic and polymer semiconductors are central to modern electronic and optoelectronic technologies, including organic thin-film transistors (OTFTs), solar cells, and bioelectronic devices. Controlling thin-film morphology is critical for optimizing the performance of organic electronic devices. However, the spin-coating process provides limited morphological control, and conventional characterization tools such as X-ray diffraction (XRD) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) are often insensitive to subtle structural changes that strongly influence charge transport. In this work, we demonstrate that spectroscopic ellipsometry (SE) combined with critical point (CP) analysis enables rapid, non-destructive assessment of microstructural evolution in regioregular poly(3-hexylthiophene) (rr-P3HT) thin films during thermal annealing. OTFTs based on P3HT were selected as a benchmark system due to their simple device architecture and well-defined structure–property relationships. The CP model provides physically meaningful optical parameters (transition energy, amplitude, broadening, and dimensionality) that correlate with electrical performance. Our results reveal a distinct shift in dimensionality of the primary optical transition upon annealing, indicating increased molecular ordering and reduced energetic disorder. These optically derived descriptors complement conventional structural probes and correlate with the observed improvements in charge transport. These findings offer a practical, non-destructive materials-focused approach for early-stage evaluation and process monitoring in organic electronics.
evidence_items.title: From Optical Transitions Through Morphology Changes to Charge Transport: A P3HT Benchmark Study Using the Critical Point Model

organizations: School of Computer and Mathematical Sciences, University of Nottingham Malaysia

evidence_items.summary: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) for oral screening is usually judged by aggregate detection metrics on public benchmarks whose partitions, labels, and relevance to users are rarely checked. Methods We audited a prototype combining a YOLOv8m detector for six conditions (1,500 test images), a DenseNet169 histopathology network, and a ResNet18 router. Under a pre-specified plan, we measured duplication across partitions, tested removal of duplicated test images against 10,000 matched controls, compared duplicated copies' labels and predictions, compared the library versions, and ran every test image through the application pipeline. Results Near-duplicates of training images accounted for 17.3% of test and 17.1% of validation images (lower bounds). Removing duplicated test images changed mean average precision (mAP)@0.5 by +0.001 (95% confidence interval [CI] −0.012 to +0.014). Only 22% of duplicated photographs had identical labels on both copies; exploratory analysis suggested memorization of training labels in orientations seen in training. A library update moved mAP@0.5:0.95 by −0.012 with identical predictions. The router rejected 23% of in-domain photographs and 51% of photographs with ulcers, so ulcer sensitivity per image was 0.36 despite the highest benchmark recall (0.91). A class-mapping defect, still live in a public demonstration in September 2026, gave the wrong name to 73% of findings. The histopathology classifier classified every image as positive; its label was not a diagnosis. Conclusion Duplication compromised the benchmark's independence without detectably changing aggregate mAP; the defects that changed what was reported or displayed lay in the labels, evaluation software, and pipeline. Evaluations should verify partitions and labels, pin the library, and test deployed systems end to end.
evidence_items.title: From benchmark to user: an end-to-end evaluation audit of an AI-based oral health screening prototype

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Materials literature contains detailed experimental knowledge, but procedures, chemical entities and measurements remain difficult to aggregate because they are reported in heterogeneous forms and depend on process-specific context. We present SciKGExtract, a schema-guided framework that combines large-language-model extraction with chemical normalization and agent-based evaluation and refinement before knowledge-graph integration. We evaluate the framework on 176 atomic-layer-deposition papers describing zinc oxide (ZnO) and indium--gallium--zinc oxide (IGZO), together with an expert-annotated full-schema subset. PubChem normalization improves exact-match extraction F1 for every tested model. For ZnO, the best F1 increases from 0.591 for direct normalized extraction to 0.805 with agentic refinement, whereas the best IGZO result is 0.344, revealing the greater difficulty of multicomponent supercycle processes. Evaluation against a deeply nested schema containing 65 experimental properties and 155 quantitative measurement nodes further exposes errors in process segmentation and numerical assignment. These results show that chemical canonicalization and targeted agentic verification provide complementary controls for converting complex materials literature into reusable, machine-actionable experimental knowledge.
evidence_items.title: Agentic schema-guided extraction of materials process knowledge from scientific literature

evidence_items.summary: Parametric knowledge in large language models (LLMs) is a cornerstone of their success, yet remains poorly understood. Existing knowledge benchmarks typically rely on predefined questions (e.g., "What is the birth date of M.L. King?"), evaluating only knowledge that benchmark designers explicitly choose to query, a problematic availability bias. In this paper, we introduce open knowledge evaluation, a new paradigm for benchmarking the stated knowledge of LLMs. Instead of asking narrow questions, it evaluates models on the knowledge they choose to surface in response to open-ended elicitation prompts (e.g., "Tell me everything you know about M.L. King"). This shifts the focus from predefined answer retrieval toward characterizing the knowledge models naturally express. We instantiate this paradigm with BeQu (Beyond Questions), a benchmark of 10,000 entities paired with reference corpora for statement verification. Using BeQu, we evaluate a broad range of language models and analyze the effects of reasoning effort, model scale, prompt format, and knowledge domain. Data and leaderboard are available on this work's GitHub repository and at ANONYMIZED.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Questions: Evaluating the Stated Knowledge of LLMs

evidence_items.summary: This study presents a comprehensive benchmarking evaluation of large language models(LLMs) and agentic coding systems for automated analysis and visualization workflows for transcriptomic data, in particular human responses to COVID-19 infection. Multiple models, including ChatGPT 5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1, and Llama4-Scout, were assessed across a series of scientific prompts designed to test their ability to reproduce workflow components such as dimensionality reduction, clustering, outlier detection, reproducibility, and code generation. The benchmark protocol involved varying prompt specificity and examined both quantitative metrics such as clustering scores and outlier counts as well as qualitative aspects such as code quality and reproducibility. Results indicate that prompt specificity improves code structure and methodological correctness, but quantitative performance depends heavily on preprocessing choices and execution environment. While some models produced strong code and reproducible outputs, alignment with scientific targets like label-based clustering was inconsistent. The findings highlight the promise and limitations of current LLMs for automating scientific data analysis and visualization and suggest directions for future benchmarking and workflow standardization.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Transcriptomic Data Analysis and Visualization: Multi-Model Workflow Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Plant metabolism produces a vast diversity of molecules, yet identifying the enzymes that catalyse biosynthetic reactions remains a major open problem. Existing benchmarks typically reduce this problem to isolated enzyme–reaction pairs, overlooking pathway and metabolite context that determines biological plausibility, leaving no standardised way to evaluate approaches that exploit this richer multimodal and relational structure. We present PlantMetBench, a multimodal graph benchmark built on PlantMetWiki, a curated knowledge graph of plant metabolism spanning 424 organisms. The resulting benchmark graph comprises 13,682 proteins, 2,741 genes, 4,577 metabolites, and 11,980 experimentally curated enzyme–reaction pairs. PlantMetBench frames enzyme–reaction prediction as an organism-disjoint link-prediction task and provides graph-native dataset splits, precomputed multi-modal node features, and evaluation protocols. Using PlantMetBench, we evaluate heterogeneous graph neural networks, standard architectures (HeteroSAGE, GAT, HGT, and R-GCN), alongside residual and jumping-knowledge variants, against non-graph models. Most heterogeneous graph architectures consistently outperform non-graph baselines on our rank-based evaluation, suggesting the value of relational context for enzyme–reaction prediction. Yet, performance remains far from saturated, indicating substantial room for improved representations and modelling strategies. Also, we show that benchmark design choices (shortcuts, splits, and metrics) are key to aligning evaluation with biologically meaningful tasks. PlantMetBench provides a standardised, reproducible framework to evaluate multimodal biosynthetic data, establishing a foundation for future work on graph-based architectures for enzyme–reaction prediction. Code and data are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: PLANTMETBENCH: A MULTIMODAL KNOWLEDGE GRAPH BENCHMARK FOR BIOSYNTHESIS PREDICTION

evidence_items.summary: Reliable heat transfer correlations are needed in the thermal-hydraulic design and safety analysis of advanced nuclear energy systems, especially liquid-metal fast reactors. Liquid-metal coolants, such as sodium, have high thermal conductivity and strong heat removal capability, which makes the prediction of heat transfer behavior an important issue in reactor analysis. In practical calculations, empirical heat transfer correlations are still commonly used because they are simple and computationally inexpensive. However, these correlations were obtained from different experiments and were reported with different applicability ranges, so a direct comparison without considering these ranges may be misleading. This study presents a validity-range-based benchmark for 11 classical empirical heat transfer correlations for axial liquid-metal flow in triangular rod bundles, as summarized in the Sodium Coolant Handbook. A reconstructed benchmark dataset with 597 data points is used, including pitch-to-diameter ratio <i>P/D</i>, Peclet number <i>Pe</i>, and experimentally measured Nusselt number Nu. In the strict in-domain assessment, only correlations expressed as functions of <i>P/D</i> and <i>Pe</i> and having applicability ranges defined by the same variables are considered. Prediction performance is evaluated using multiple statistical indicators. The <i>P/D–Pe</i> parameter space is also divided into grid cells according to the reported validity limits, so that the locally best-performing correlation can be identified in each region. The resulting benchmark gives a reproducible basis for comparing empirical heat transfer correlations and may also serve as a reference for assessing empirical models in other advanced energy systems.
evidence_items.title: A validity-range-based benchmark of liquid-metal heat transfer correlations for nuclear energy systems

evidence_items.summary: Permission-based static analysis is still one of the lightest methods for catching ransomware prior to installation, and ransomware is continuing to become more sophisticated on the Android platform. In a previous work, a well-balanced set of 1,990 Android applications (995 for ransomware and 995 for benign) and 365 permission attributes was collected, and Logistic Regression to achieve an accuracy of 97.69% under 10-fold cross validation had been obtained. This paper is along two lines of extension, scale and algorithmic breadth, of this study. The 20,012 applications in the permission dataset are a public-permission version that has been substantially-expanded from the known ransomware/benign dataset included with the publication, and are defined by 2,317 cleaned binary permission/Api Usage features used on each sample; we test the performance of six popular supervised learning algorithms (Random Forest, XGBoost, linear-kernel SVC, MLP, a single decision tree, and linear regression). A common preprocessing pipeline was performed across all models and training was performed on a synthesis of a 70/30 split and 10-fold stratified cross-validation. We present accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, ROC area, false positive rate, confusion matrix, training time and a gini impurity feature ranking. The MLP, Linear SVM, and Random Forest achieved comparable results as Random Forest is the second best (91.72% ± 0.72% accuracy under cross-validation and 91.72% when performing a held-out test on the train/test split, with an F1-score of 0.922 and an ROC-AUC score of 0.942). The single Decision Tree model was once again the most poor with thresholded Linear Regression being not far behind the dedicated classifiers, meaning that many of the signals in permission space are approximately linear — as seen in our previous study where Logistic Regression performed well.
evidence_items.title: A Baseline Machine Learning Benchmark for Permission-Based Android Ransomware Detection: Comparative Evaluation of Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machines, Neural Networks, Decision Trees, and Linear Regression
