evidence_items.summary: Speaking-style captioning (SSC) aims to generate natural language descriptions of how speech is delivered, capturing paralinguistic attributes such as vocal timbre, prosody, and expressivity. Many downstream applications, including conversational AI agents, controllable speech generation, and large-scale audio annotation, require dimension-specific style captions that describe targeted aspects of speech (e.g., speaker traits, emotion, or delivery style), rather than a single undifferentiated description. However, existing work lacks a unified formulation for controllable speaking-style captioning. We address this gap by formulating SSC as an instruction-following audio-language task, where explicit instructions specify the speaking-style dimensions to be described. We introduce StyleInstructCaps, the first standardized benchmark for controllable speaking-style captioning in audio-language models. StyleInstructCaps provides a dataset and evaluation framework that measures metadata groundedness, hallucination, instruction-following ability, generalization to unseen instructions and audio datasets, and speaker-style consistency. Across nine state-of-the-art audio-language models, we find that strong instruction-following ability does not necessarily imply grounded speaking-style understanding, and that SSC-specific instruction-diverse training substantially improves groundedness, controllability, and speaker consistency.
evidence_items.title: A Benchmark for Controllable Speaking-Style Captioning in Audio-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Analogical reasoning is widely considered a fundamental component of human intelligence. Few benchmarks are designed to explicitly test far analogical reasoning - reasoning between domains that are superficially dissimilar yet share deep relational or structural similarities. In this work, we introduce an analogical reasoning benchmark called Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus of ANAlogy (ARCANA). The tasks of ARCANA require performing far analogical mappings from real-world objects or physical phenomena to abstract grid-based transformations, different from the well-known ARC-AGI benchmark which primarily emphasized innate human priors. We validate ARCANA through a human study, demonstrating that humans solve these tasks reliably. In contrast, evaluations across a range of large language models show a distinct performance gap compared to humans, revealing systematic failure modes that remain challenging for current models. To address this gap, we propose ConceptSIR, a reasoning framework based on concept slippage, introspection, and reflection. Experiments demonstrate that ConceptSIR enables standard LLMs to solve several challenging ARCANA tasks that were unsolved by direct prompting in our evaluation. Overall, our results suggest that far analogical reasoning remains an open problem for contemporary LLMs. All the materials are available at sites.google.com/view/arcanacogtest. The complete codebase, including benchmark, and ConceptSIR, is publicly available at https://github.com/density-11/arcana-test. All ARCANA data and task instances can be accessed and explored at https://arcanacogtest.org/.
evidence_items.title: ARCANA: A Benchmark for Abstraction and Analogical Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents BanglaBBQ, a question-answering bias benchmark designed to capture stereotypes grounded in the Bangladeshi context, in both Bangla and English. Following KoBBQ and PakBBQ, BanglaBBQ adapts the original Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) by classifying its templates into three groups: directly translated (DT), modified to align target groups or contexts with Bangladesh (TM), and removed when deemed unsuitable for the Bangladeshi context (SR). This process retains 140 templates across six categories, comprising 76 DT and 64 TM templates. Five newly authored (NA) categories, based on stereotypes common in Bangladeshi society, are then added: marital status, age and political perception, regional origin, educational background, and mental-health status. Native Bangladeshi annotators judged all 466 newly authored templates, and 372 were retained because a strict majority of English annotators identified the intended target and rated the attitude as common enough. Each newly authored template is linked to a documented source and a verbatim quote from it. Each evaluated template also has a counter-stereotypical version of its disambiguated context. The dataset was evaluated using two open-weight models (Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B) and two closed models (GPT-4.1-mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash). All four lean towards the stereotyped person when the context is ambiguous, in both languages, and the effect of language differs by model, so English results do not predict behaviour in Bangla. On the adapted BBQ templates, both Qwen3 models are also less accurate when the context contradicts a stereotype than when it confirms it. On the newly authored templates, the closed models follow counter-stereotypical evidence almost perfectly, and all four models are more biased on the templates that annotators validated than on those they rejected.
evidence_items.title: BanglaBBQ: A Bias Benchmark for Question Answering in the Bangladeshi Context

evidence_items.summary: Software teams evaluating coding agents need evidence that reflects the changes they expect those agents to make. Benchmark scores summarize how often an agent resolves tasks under broad labels such as bug fixing and feature implementation, but provide little guidance on whether the evaluated work resembles a team's workload. To support this decision, we characterize 2,487 tasks from five public benchmarks and analyze 14,922 runs of six agent configurations. We introduce the Spread-Novelty-Centrality (SNC) profile to describe how the reference solution is distributed across files and directories, how much it adds relative to what it removes, and the dependencies, history, and complexity of the code it touches. We also compare the scope of agent patches and their file exploration. Every pair of benchmarks differs on at least two SNC axes, including benchmarks with the same task label. Among tasks resolved by Claude Opus 4.6, patches are larger than the reference on FeatBench and smaller on FeatureBench. Across the six configurations, resolved runs tend to involve less distributed changes and code with lower values on the Centrality indicators, while the patch sizes associated with resolution differ between the Claude and Qwen configurations. These observations suggest that practitioners should select evaluation tasks based on their change characteristics, inspect the information provided in task descriptions, and assess patch scope alongside test outcomes. We explain how teams can apply this analysis to completed changes and identify the additional evidence needed before using it for task assignment or review automation.
evidence_items.title: Choosing Coding-Agent Benchmarks for Practice: Lessons from Task Demands and Agent Behaviour

evidence_items.summary: Planning is central to LLM agents: before acting, an agent must decompose goals, select tools, reason over constraints, and decide when a task is infeasible. Yet existing agent evaluations often report only end-to-end success, making it difficult to determine whether failures stem from planning or execution. We introduce Agent Planning Benchmark (APB), a planning-specific diagnostic benchmark with 4,209 multimodal cases across 22 domains and five settings, covering holistic planning, feedback-conditioned step-wise planning, and robustness under extraneous tools, broken tools, and unsolvable tasks. Across 12 MLLMs, APB reveals systematic weaknesses in long-horizon planning, tool-noise robustness, calibrated refusal, and inference-time refinement. We further validate APB on 200 ToolSandbox tasks and 200 $\tau^2$-bench tasks, where APB-guided refinement consistently improves plan correctness, plan grade, and downstream execution metrics across three representative models. APB thus serves as an upstream diagnostic complement to execution benchmarks. The APB benchmark and code are available in \href{https://github.com/Mikivishy/AgentPlanningBenchmark}{this URL}.
evidence_items.title: Agent Planning Benchmark: A Diagnostic Framework for Planning Capabilities in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Web-scale 3D asset collections are abundant but rarely ready to ingest without cleanup, suffering from arbitrary metric scaling, incorrect pivots, brittle geometry, and incomplete textures, defects that limit their use in embodied AI, robotics, and spatial computing. We present AmaraSpatial-10K, a dataset of 10,071 synthetic 3D assets standardised for direct ingestion. Each asset ships as a metric-scaled, deterministically anchored .glb with separated PBR maps, a convex collision hull, a paired reference image, and multi-sentence text metadata. Alongside the dataset we introduce a reusable evaluation suite for 3D asset banks, a continuous Scale Plausibility Score (SPS), a keyword-based Concept Density metric, anchor-error auditing, and a cross-modal CLIP coherence protocol, and apply it to AmaraSpatial-10K alongside matched subsets of Objaverse, HSSD, ABO, and GSO. We check the annotations independently of the LLM/VLM pipeline that produced them: measured ABO object heights fall inside our scale intervals 88.7-90.7% of the time, and three non-author raters auditing a stratified sample of 314 assets judge 95.5% plausibly scaled and 99.7% correctly anchored. AmaraSpatial-10K improves CLIP Recall@5 by 3.4x over Objaverse (0.612 vs. 0.181, median rank 267 -> 3), achieves a 99.1% settling-stability rate under Habitat-Sim in static placement and collision tests, with ~20x lower per-load wall time, and as a drop-in Holodeck asset bank improves planned-scale matching and is preferred by blinded human raters in 27 of 40 paired scenes. Controlled ablations on the same asset bank attribute the retrieval gain to description richness.
evidence_items.title: AmaraSpatial-10K: A Spatially and Semantically Aligned 3D Dataset for Spatial Computing and Embodied AI

evidence_items.summary: The advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has catalyzed the development of autonomous agents capable of navigating complex environments. However, existing evaluations primarily adopt a deductive paradigm, where agents execute tasks based on explicitly provided rules and static goals, often within limited planning horizons. Crucially, this neglects the inductive necessity for agents to discover latent transition laws from experience autonomously, which is the cornerstone for enabling agentic foresight and sustaining strategic coherence. To bridge this gap, we introduce OdysseyArena, which re-centers agent evaluation on long-horizon, active, and inductive interactions. We formalize and instantiate four primitives, translating abstract transition dynamics into concrete interactive environments. Building upon this, we establish OdysseyArena-Lite for standardized benchmarking, providing a set of 120 tasks to measure an agent's inductive efficiency and long-horizon discovery. Pushing further, we introduce OdysseyArena-Challenge to stress-test agent stability across extreme interaction horizons (e.g., > 200 steps). Extensive experiments on 15+ leading LLMs reveal that even frontier models exhibit a deficiency in inductive scenarios, identifying a critical bottleneck in the pursuit of autonomous discovery in complex environments. Project homepage: https://os-copilot.github.io/OdysseyArena-Home/
evidence_items.title: OdysseyArena: Benchmarking Large Language Models For Long-Horizon, Active and Inductive Interactions

evidence_items.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) describe satellite images fluently but struggle with the quantitative spatial reasoning that remote sensing (RS) analysts perform routinely, such as counting buildings, measuring forest area in hectares and computing distances in meters. We introduce SQuID (Satellite Quantitative Intelligence Dataset), a benchmark of 2,000 questions over 587 images from four sources at 0.3 to 1.0 m ground sampling distance, covering 24 question types in three difficulty tiers. Answers are computed from curated segmentation masks or, for 50 questions, from human consensus, and numeric answers are scored against tolerance ranges informed by human annotations. SQuID also releases the reference masks behind its answers, so that modular systems can be evaluated using reference rather than predicted masks, and 75,687 training question-answer pairs on disjoint images (SQuID-Train). Among 15 evaluated systems, the best zero-shot end-to-end VLM reaches 28.1%, and RS-specialized VLMs score lower. As a baseline, we propose QASR (Quantitative Agentic Spatial Reasoning), in which an LLM writes a program that segments the image and measures the masks with geometric operators. QASR reaches 42.0%. On the 1,950 mask-derived questions, running its programs on the reference masks instead of predicted masks raises accuracy from 42.2% to 82.6%, so segmentation is its main source of error. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-7B on SQuID-Train raises its accuracy from 16.1% to 40.7%, close to QASR. Multi-condition questions (Tier 3) remain the hardest in every setting, at 62.0% for QASR with reference masks and 13.2% after fine-tuning. These results leave clear room for end-to-end models that learn metric spatial reasoning, and SQuID provides the data to train and evaluate them.
evidence_items.title: SQuID: A Benchmark for Quantitative Spatial Reasoning on Satellite Imagery

evidence_items.summary: Long-horizon agentic systems become long-context systems by accumulation rather than through a single long document, since every step reassembles a prompt from role instructions, tool and sub-agent descriptions, recalled memories, dialogue history, and previous tool outputs, separately for every agent. This paper studies how such accumulated context can be trained, evaluated, and managed in hierarchical multi-agent assistants. We present HiMA-Ecom, a hierarchical multi-agent benchmark for e-commerce assistants with 22.8K instances, of which 17.7K carry memory entries in context, pairing agent-specific supervised fine-tuning data with system-level supervision for end-to-end multi-agent reinforcement learning. Building upon it, HiMA-R1 keeps the context budget of a trajectory under control through Variance-Reduction Group Relative Policy Optimization (VR-GRPO), which samples along an initial trajectory so that sampling cost grows additively with trajectory length and updates the agents with the largest reward variance, together with an efficiency reward on trajectory length and a memory evolution mechanism that repurposes GRPO rewards as cost-free signals for what stays in context. Agents built upon 3B and 7B open-source models match DeepSeek-R1 and surpass DeepSeek-V3 by 6.0 points on average, while reward-driven memory reduces the update steps needed for convergence by roughly 55%.
evidence_items.title: HiMA-Ecom: A Long-Horizon Memory Benchmark for Hierarchical Multi-Agent E-commerce Assistants

evidence_items.summary: Existing code generation benchmarks primarily evaluate functional correctness, with limited focus on code efficiency and often restricted to a single language like Python. To address this gap, we introduce EffiBench-X, the first multi-language benchmark designed to measure the efficiency of LLM-generated code. EffiBench-X supports Python, C++, Java, JavaScript, Ruby, and Golang. It comprises competitive programming tasks with human-expert solutions as efficiency baselines. Evaluating state-of-the-art LLMs on EffiBench-X reveals that while models generate functionally correct code, they consistently underperform human experts in efficiency. Even the most efficient LLM-generated solutions (Qwen3-32B) achieve only around \textbf{62\%} of human efficiency on average, with significant language-specific variations. LLMs show better efficiency in Python, Ruby, and JavaScript than in Java, C++, and Golang. For instance, DeepSeek-R1's Python code is significantly more efficient than its Java code. These results highlight the critical need for research into LLM optimization techniques to improve code efficiency across diverse languages. The dataset and evaluation infrastructure are submitted and available at https://github.com/EffiBench/EffiBench-X.git and https://huggingface.co/datasets/EffiBench/effibench-x.
evidence_items.title: EffiBench-X: A Multi-Language Benchmark for Measuring Efficiency of LLM-Generated Code

evidence_items.summary: Developing on-device image models requires considering practical user needs, task types and device resource constraints. However, existing benchmarks provide limited guidance on identifying capability gaps between on-device models and server-side models. We introduce MoI-Bench, a benchmark grounded in mobile user needs, comprising 64 subtasks and 1150 samples. It defines 16 operations, such as removal and replacement, and eight visual target categories covering content such as portraits and text. These form two orthogonal axes whose applicable combinations define specific tasks, such as removing facial makeup. To better guide model improvement, we further propose MoI-Eval, which introduces task-specific criteria covering instruction following, visual quality and detail preservation. We further construct sample-level evaluation questions and aggregate their scores into overall quality and capability profiles along the operation, target and criteria axes. We evaluate representative on-device and server-side models and measure mobile deployment costs. Results show that this decoupled Operation x Target design provides finer-grained guidance for improving compact models. For example, it highlights the need to prioritize specific capability gaps (e.g., text-replacement) over broad application-level goals (e.g., improving text editing). Unlike conventional benchmarks that rank models using a single score, we introduce a two-dimensional Quality-Deployability capability map to assess models for practical mobile use. The map shows that current on-device models can achieve efficient generation or editing but expanding their task coverage deserves greater attention than further improving deployment efficiency. Further progress requires improving editing quality, particularly identity preservation and text rendering, while broadening task coverage.
evidence_items.title: MoI-Bench: A Benchmark for Image Generation and Editing on Mobile Devices

evidence_items.summary: Injecting new subjects naturally during streaming video generation requires integrating newly supplied visual references into the existing video while preserving established subjects and the scene. Encoding references independently of the current scene provides little guidance for this integration, while keeping their features in persistent memory can interfere with established context. We propose ReferStream, a framework that requires no additional training and combines reference construction using the current scene with transient cache injection. Joint Latent places reference latents in target regions of the latest scene latent, allowing reference features to be extracted in context. Cache Restoration uses these features to condition the injection chunk, then restores the overwritten global cache entries while retaining the newly generated history. This procedure incorporates new visual conditions without retraining the generator or revising emitted frames. We further introduce ReferStream Bench, a new benchmark with scheduled reference arrivals, evolving instructions, and explicit annotations of subject presence for InShot and MultiShot generation. Evaluation follows the event schedule and measures both the fidelity of new subjects and the preservation of established subjects, alongside video quality, text adherence, and count accuracy. Experiments on ReferStream Bench show higher scores for text adherence, subject similarity, and count accuracy than the compared baselines, including offline methods given all references in advance. Project page: https://xushuolin.github.io/ReferStream/.
evidence_items.title: ReferStream: Interactive Subject Injection for Streaming Video Generation

evidence_items.summary: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) syndrome differentiation is usually evaluated as static final-label selection over complete clinical records. This setting hides three diagnostic behaviors: whether a model distinguishes semantic-neighbor syndrome labels from easy random distractors, whether it updates predictions as evidence fields are revealed, and whether it should commit under uncertainty. We introduce TCM-DiagCommit, a benchmark derived from the public TCM-SD/ZY-BERT resource while retaining its source syndrome labels; it converts 1,834 source cases into 23,842 task rows over 148 syndrome labels. The benchmark combines random, profile-neighbor, and full-vocabulary candidate ladders with staged t1/t2/t3 evidence. It also includes fixed-label tongue/pulse perturbations and insufficient-evidence variants. A benchmark-defined action contract scores commit, acquire, defer, and abstain. Across five zero-shot DirectLLM calibrations, random10 top-1 accuracy is 63.2% to 66.4%, but hard20 falls to 24.7% to 30.3% and full148 to 14.8% to 22.3%; on hard20, WT(all) wrong-terminal commits remain 62.2% to 74.3%. These results show that final-answer accuracy alone is insufficient for diagnostic benchmark evaluation: answer selection, evidence use, and benchmark commitment scoring should be measured separately.
evidence_items.title: TCM-DiagCommit: A TCM-SD-Derived Benchmark for Evidence-Conditioned Syndrome Selection and Commitment

evidence_items.summary: Skill optimizers adapt an agent to long-horizon tasks, such as repairing a terminal environment, by rewriting its skill, a natural-language procedure in its context, and keeping the edits that raise success on a small dev set. On such tasks success is noisy, so a gain on a small dev set does not show that an edit helps, and a success score does not show what the edit costs. We introduce BiPA, which replays an optimizer's acceptance rule on candidates identical to its seed to measure what selection alone reports, and records each episode as a bipartite graph of turns and the text they read to trace extra input tokens to the behavior behind them. Across three optimizers, three agentic benchmarks and two models, the learned skills succeed about as often as their hand-written seed, 0.1 points higher on average. Their dev gains vanish on test: keeping the best of several candidates on at most 30 tasks reports gains this large even when none changed. They read about 16% more input tokens: the optimizers almost always add rules, half to re-check work and some to act one call at a time, and the agent follows them as extra turns, each re-sending the whole conversation. Four principles follow: accept an edit only if its gain exceeds what selection alone reports; charge it for the turns it adds, not for its length; let the editor delete and merge rules; show it what earlier rules cost. Code is available at https://github.com/valleysprings/BiPA.git.
evidence_items.title: Does Your Generalist Skill Optimizer Really Incentivize Agentic Tasks? Rethinking Skill Optimization via Bipartite Attribution

evidence_items.summary: Evaluation of Tamil handwritten character recognition (HCR) has largely focused on clean test images, and a standardized multi-corruption robustness benchmark for isolated Tamil HCR has not been established. We introduce uTHCD-C, a corruption-robustness benchmark based on the unconstrained Tamil Handwritten Character Database (uTHCD). The benchmark defines ten corruption types, including a handwriting-specific stroke-thinning corruption, at five severity levels. We evaluate nine convolutional and transformer-based architectures using five-fold stratified cross-validation and writer-independent testing. Robustness is quantified using mean Corruption Error (mCE), normalized against a VGG16-BN reference. We additionally compare parameter count, computational complexity, and inference throughput to characterize the computational requirements of the evaluated architectures. The results establish comparative robustness baselines for Tamil HCR, revealing substantial differences across architectures: ConvNeXt and Swin achieve the lowest mCE values (0.75 and 0.83, respectively), whereas ShuffleNet and MnasNet exhibit higher values (1.55 and 1.85, respectively). The accompanying efficiency measurements characterize the trade-offs between corruption robustness and computational requirements. By providing standardized corruption configurations, evaluation protocols, and comparative results, uTHCD-C establishes a reproducible basis for future research on robust and computationally efficient Tamil HCR.
evidence_items.title: uTHCD-C: A Corruption-Robustness Benchmark for Tamil Handwritten Character Recognition

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress on solving competition-level mathematics, yet their ability to verify natural-language mathematical proofs remains relatively underexplored. This gap is especially pronounced for Olympiad-level proofs, which require meticulous assessment of each claim in a long reasoning chain. Current proof verification thus primarily relies on expert inspection, which is costly to scale. In this paper, we present a systematic study of LLM-based verification in this setting. Specifically, we introduce a human-curated dataset of USAMO 2025 candidate solutions with expert grading, and conduct a broad evaluation of existing LLM verifiers across frontier models. We also propose TROJAN, an iterative self-critique pipeline for generating high-fidelity adversarial proofs at scale. Our comprehensive evaluation covers 20 models spanning seven metrics, two prompt styles, three inference methods, and three prompt templates, showing that state-of-the-art models still leave considerable room for improvement. To narrow this gap, we propose MABGrader, a Multi-Armed Bandit framework that reframes grading as arm selection over the discrete score space. MABGrader outperforms the SOTA ProofGrader by 26.4% in Quadratic Weighted Kappa and reduces grading error by 14%. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/aziksh-ospanov/TROJAN.
evidence_items.title: Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes over time (4D reconstruction) from a single moving camera is central to robotics and AR/VR applications, yet state-of the-art feed-forward methods rely solely on RGB frames and therefore inherit the failure modes of conventional cameras, including motion blur and temporal aliasing under fast or non-uniform camera and object motion. Event cameras report per-pixel brightness changes asynchronously at microsecond resolution, offering a complementary signal that is largely immune to these artifacts, but whether this modality can be incorporated into existing RGB based 4D reconstruction pipelines without a full architectural redesign remains an open question. In this preliminary study, we investigate a minimal extension: we augment Monst3R, an existing RGB-only 4D reconstruction model, with an additional event-camera input branch, leaving the rest of the architecture unchanged. Across 3 benchmark datasets, this simple RGB-event fusion reduces Abs Rel by 3.4% on average relative to the RGB-only Monst3R baseline, and a sensitivity analysis shows that the improvement grows with the magnitude of camera and object motion, with the largest gains observed under high object motion conditions where RGB-only reconstruction degrades most. These early results suggest that even a lightweight, non-invasive fusion of event data can meaningfully improve 4D reconstruction robustness, motivating a more thorough architectural investigation in future work.
evidence_items.title: 4D Reconstruction with Events & RGB

evidence_items.summary: Robotic agents operating in real-world environments must adapt continuously from a stream of multimodal demonstrations, often under constraints that preclude storing or revisiting past data. In this replay-free, single-pass lifelong imitation learning setting, sequential updates can progressively distort the representation space, making expert-based approaches particularly sensitive to routing interference, causing expert selection to degrade over time. We propose HIDRA, a structured routing framework that mitigates this issue through a hierarchical dual-attention mechanism, which decouples instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement. To further stabilize routing under representation drift, HIDRA introduces a key-level geometric regularization that enforces both alignment within tasks and separation across tasks. The resulting approach enables reliable expert selection while supporting an expandable set of experts for continual adaptation. We evaluate HIDRA on several LIBERO benchmark suites, including more challenging variants with heterogeneous task sequences and paraphrased language instructions. Our approach consistently outperforms both replay-free and replay-based baselines, improving AUC and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting, with stronger gains under high interference and language variation. The code is available at: https://github.com/yfqi/HIDRA.
evidence_items.title: HIDRA: Hierarchical Dual-Routing Attention for Replay-Free Lifelong Imitation Learning

evidence_items.summary: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.
evidence_items.title: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory

evidence_items.summary: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. However, few studies have developed benchmarks specifically tailored for dexterous manipulation, leaving the dexterous manipulation capabilities of existing models insufficiently characterized. In this paper, we present BiDex-100, a simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation that combines broad task coverage, multi-dimensional evaluation, and high-DoF hand embodiments. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness. In addition, the benchmark supports two embodiments and provides 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations, totaling 6.25 million frames. We evaluate seven recent Vision-Language-Action models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. The website is available at https://robbyant-research.github.io/BiDex-100/.
evidence_items.title: BiDex-100: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across 100+ Simulation Tasks

evidence_items.summary: Reliable probability estimates are critical in many machine learning applications, yet modern classifiers are often poorly calibrated. Post-hoc calibration provides a simple and widely used solution, but the large number of proposed methods, combined with small-scale and inconsistent evaluations, makes it difficult to determine which approaches are truly effective in practice. We introduce a large-scale, standardized benchmark for post-hoc calibration, covering nearly 2000 experiments across tabular and computer vision tasks, including binary, multiclass, and large-scale classification settings. Our benchmark aggregates predictions from a diverse set of classical models, modern deep learning architectures, and foundation models, and provides unified, reproducible implementations of dozens of calibration methods within a common evaluation framework. We argue that Post-Hoc Improvement (PHI) in proper scoring rules offers a principled alternative to traditional calibration error estimators for comparing post-hoc methods, capturing both calibration quality and potential degradation to the model's predictive performance. Using this framework, we conduct the most comprehensive empirical study of post-hoc calibration to date. Our results reveal consistent patterns across domains: smooth calibration functions outperform binning-based approaches, dedicated multiclass methods are essential in high-dimensional settings, and generic machine learning models are not competitive without calibration-specific design. To facilitate future research, we release all data, code, and evaluation tools, providing a plug-and-play benchmark for developing and comparing calibration methods.
evidence_items.title: CalArena: A Large-Scale Post-Hoc Calibration Benchmark

Authentic samples were obtained from the FFHQ dataset, while manipulated samples were generated using Stable Diffusion-based models. Pixel-level annotations were automatically generated during the manipulation process using a face-parsing model to identify the affected facial regions. The utility of the dataset was evaluated using different semantic segmentation architectures. This dataset is a derivative work based on the Flickr-Faces-HQ (FFHQ) dataset. evidence_items.summary: Clinical research over electronic health records depends on derived variables whose definitions sit outside the schema, in item codes, time windows, missingness rules, and output-grain choices that change cohorts and downstream conclusions. We introduce M4Bench, 28 clinical derivation tasks across 15 task families on MIMIC-IV and eICU, to test whether AI coding agents can reproduce such derivations and how clinician-reviewed agent skills change their results. Its controls decompose the value of skills into specification completeness, delivery format, and schema familiarity. In a Docker-isolated Codex campaign (GPT 5.4 Mini and GPT 5.5), skills raise reward by 0.136 over the no-skill baseline, with 26 of 28 tasks improving. Specification completeness accounts for most of this gain: on an eight-task control subset, an operational spec alone raises reward by 0.162, and skills add only 0.024 on top, indistinguishable from zero. On a ten-task subset, decoy skills score like no skill and raw reference SQL nearly matches targeted skills, arguing against generic context or the skill format as the explanation. Schema obfuscation and restructuring preserve 86% and 70% of the skill gain (GPT 5.4 Mini, 26 MIMIC-IV tasks), a descriptive robustness check rather than a bound on memorization. A descriptive Claude Code replication on all 28 tasks (Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 4.6, 560 runs) is directionally consistent (+0.120, 21 of 28 tasks improving). These gains are partial agreement with the reference, not completed tasks: only 25 of 280 with-skill and 13 of 280 no-skill Codex runs pass every strict check, and skills barely change which rows agents return (key F1 +0.003). Skills are released as a versioned, clinician-reviewable markdown delivery format, with a family-level reference-validity audit. M4Bench releases tasks, skills, evaluation code, and sanitized per-run evidence as an open-source benchmark.
evidence_items.title: M4Bench: Evaluating Procedural Specification for Clinical EHR Derivation Agents

evidence_items.summary: A software feature usually evolves over time: developers extend its first version as new use cases and requirements arrive, and each extension builds on code written earlier. Most feature benchmarks evaluate a single request on a fixed codebase. Feature evolution requires evaluating successive extensions on an agent's own earlier code and checking whether the feature remains correct. We introduce FeatureArc to evaluate coding agents on evolving features, together with a pipeline that constructs its tasks from repository histories. The benchmark combines dependencies between successive stages of the same feature, explicit requirements and interface contracts, and executable checks across four programming languages. The pipeline validates fail-to-pass (F2P) tests for new behavior and pass-to-pass (P2P) tests for existing behavior on the reference code before and after each stage. We evaluated 10 coding agents on 73 manually reviewed tasks of 2 to 10 stages. Each agent works in one persistent session and workspace without external test feedback or rollback. The evaluation reveals a gap between first-stage and whole-feature success: pooled success falls from 62.7% at the first stage to 28.5% when the whole feature is tested on the final code. Trajectory analysis identifies inherited defects as a common failure mechanism, present in 72.9% of failed later stages. These earlier errors often remain undetected: in stages following a failure, agents leave the earlier error unnoticed about 95% of the time, and their self-tests rarely revisit earlier stages. Evolving a feature autonomously, without human checks between stages, therefore remains a substantial challenge for current coding agents. At Tencent, the pipeline extends internal evaluations to this setting and guides the development of Hunyuan, Tencent's family of large language models.
evidence_items.title: FeatureArc: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Evolving Features

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) results for 217 synthetic question-answer pairs in Portuguese derived from the Brazilian Grid Code (ONS Procedimentos de Rede). Each pair has a direct question and a corresponding paraphrased question sharing the same reference answer. direct.jsonl: 217 records for direct questions, including scores from two domain experts. paraphrase.jsonl: 217 records for paraphrased questions. Each UTF-8 JSONL record includes the question, reference answer, original source passage, generated answer, ten ranked retrieved passages, source-documentmetadata, and automatic evaluation results. Matching qa id values link the corresponding cases across the two files. Automatic scores range from 0 to 1 and cover Contextual Recall, Contextual Precision, Faithfulness, Answer Relevancy, Answer Correctness (G-Eval), ANLS,BLEU-4, and ROUGE-L. The five LLM-based metrics include their automatic reasons; ANLS, BLEU-4, and ROUGE-L include scores only. Human scores are included only in direct.jsonl, under human scores. The entries expert 1 and expert 2 correspond to the first and second experts in the paper. Each entry contains: retrieval: 0 = insufficient retrieved evidence; 1 = sufficient evidence. generation: 0 = inadequate; 1 = partially adequate; 2 = technically adequate. The first expert manually assessed only a few selected paraphrased cases for the paper's qualitative analysis. This assessment did not cover all 217 paraphrased questions, so those human scores are not included in paraphrase.jsonl. The RAG system uses Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B for retrieval and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct for answer generation. The automatic LLM evaluator is GPT-5.4-mini. Reference answers were generated synthetically and retained without manual editing. The complete reference set was not independently validated by domain experts against the original Grid Code documents. The questions, reference answers, and generated answers are provided in Portuguese.

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are extending agent-mediated commerce on the Web from shopping for consumers to operating businesses for sellers. In online-to-offline (O2O) commerce, decisions are issued through Web-based platforms but realized through costly physical execution. Evaluating such agents requires going beyond individual transactions to ask whether decisions made online turn into sustained economic returns. We introduce AutoVend, a benchmark in which one LLM agent manages 20 vending machines across five site types through a Web-based operating interface for 180 simulated days. Its data-grounded simulator combines a shared warehouse, procurement lead times, paid replenishment, inventory expiration, and recurring operating costs. We evaluate five LLM agents against a rule-based inventory-control baseline and diagnose their site coordination, execution, and performance over time. Four of five evaluated LLM agents fall short of this baseline, and returns per dollar of inference cost rank models differently from returns alone. Operational analyses show that gains in individual metrics do not consistently yield stronger economic growth, as inventory and execution costs erode these gains. Trajectory analysis further reveals difficulties in grounding feasible actions, managing inventory commitments, and converting feedback into effective policy revisions.
evidence_items.title: AutoVend: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Autonomous Vending Operations

evidence_items.summary: Logging statements are central to debugging, failure diagnosis, and production observability, yet writing them requires developers to decide where to place a logging statement, which API and severity level to use, and what runtime information to expose. Automated logging aims to reduce this burden, but existing evidence remains dominated by Java-centric repositorysnapshot datasets. Thus, Java-centered benchmarks do not show whether findings on model behavior and model selection generalize to other programming languages or to real-world maintenance changes that introduce logging statements. This paper presents MultiLogBench, a multilingual benchmark and empirical study spanning six programming language ecosystems. MultiLogBench contains 63,965 production-code repository-snapshot instances, 744 revision-history cases where developers introduce logging statements during maintenance, and a paired transformed revision-history branch for robustness analysis. Using seven contemporary large language models under a unified protocol, we evaluate logging-site localization, frameworkanchor matching, severity prediction, message generation, variable recovery, and cascaded overall quality. Results show that automated logging is sensitive to language-ecosystem conditions. On repository-snapshot data, absolute performance levels and component profiles vary across language-specific subsets, with position prediction exhibiting the largest average withinmodel component gap. The six language-specific CCS leaderboards are nevertheless highly correlated, with a mean pairwise Spearman correlation of 0.912, and identify the same top two models; reordering is concentrated among the middle- and lower-tier models. Among the primary structural buckets, loop and nested-callable sites are the hardest.
evidence_items.title: Automated Logging Is Language-Sensitive: A Multilingual Benchmark and Empirical Study of LLMs

evidence_items.summary: This study evaluates a causal, six-target, 30 min forecasting component for diesel hydrotreating using campaign-separated synthetic data, not a deployed digital twin. An empirical, engineering-constrained simulator generated 30 original campaigns; the recovered code reproduced their datasets byte-for-byte but the simulator did not implement mechanistic balances. The archived AURA-SSM hybrid combines a frozen Ridge anchor, a released measurement observer, multiscale context, bounded corrections, and conditional empirical risk weights; despite its identifier, it has no learned state-space layer. On two previously inspected evaluation domains, frozen NRMSE was 0.16996 and 0.18085, versus ten-degradation means of 0.19170 and 0.20490. These retrospective improvements over leading frozen controls were below the prespecified 3% practical threshold; adaptive Ridge was more accurate on average. Additional matched controls, CRISP/TimeFormer adaptations, and a prespecified 16-campaign synthetic evaluation clarified limitations. On new common/modified simulator structures, AURA-SSM achieved ten-degradation NRMSE of 0.18804/0.20332, outperforming NLinear but not a fixed convex blend; context LightGBM was more accurate with clean measurements. A separately corrected observer passed causal tests and improved prolonged-outage prediction without replacing archived results. Interval undercoverage, lack of mechanistic validation, and absent independent industrial data constrain applicability.
evidence_items.title: Causal Multivariate Forecasting of Diesel Hydrotreating Variables on a Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence systems combine language-model interaction with tools that perform operations beyond text generation. In data analytics, an integrated workspace must support dataset handling, analytical computation, visualization, and controlled tool execution while making the limits of each capability clear. This paper presents Fabric, a software project intended to bring conversational model access and data-oriented workflows into a common workspace. The paper documents its architecture and a preliminary local evaluation on Windows 11 using Node.js v24.15.0. JavaScript syntax validation passed, and a targeted evaluation suite reported seven passing tests. A synthetic local benchmark processed 10,000 rows and verified a sum of 505,000. The broader test suite reported 415 passing tests and four failures, including a Windows filesystem-permission verification failure and spreadsheet-processing failures. These observations support only narrow claims about selected components. They do not establish end-to-end model accuracy, secure execution isolation, production readiness, or performance under real-world workloads. The paper reports the methodology, results, limitations, and further validation required for a rigorous assessment of Fabric as an AI-assisted data-analysis workspace.
evidence_items.title: Fabric: An Agentic AI Workspace for Natural-Language Data Analysis and Multi-Tool Task Execution

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains kinematic, electromyographic, force, and subjective strain data from a robot-based, quasi-static surrogate hammer-drilling study with 37 healthy participants. It documents how three design parameters of handle position and orientation (the relative angle between the handles about the push axis, their longitudinal distance along the push axis, and their lateral distance perpendicular to it) affect upper-limb load and strain during bimanual tool use. A six-axis industrial robot reproduced the degrees of freedom of a rotary hammer within a bore hole. Participants gripped two sensor-integrated handles mounted to the robot flange and had to statically maintain a prescribed total push force (135 N below shoulder, 155 N overhead) and a prescribed total grip force (130 N) for 15 s per trial. In the below-shoulder horizontal (BSH) task condition the rotational degree of freedom about the push axis was unconstrained, so the robot had to be stabilized. In the overhead vertical (OHV) task condition all degrees of freedom were constrained. Seven handle configurations, realizing the levels of the three design parameters, were tested in both task conditions with three repetitions each. Recorded measures comprise whole-body kinematics (17 inertial measurement units, 60 Hz), surface electromyography of six upper-limb muscles per side (2148 Hz), push and grip force per handle (4000 Hz), and perceived strain on the Borg CR10 scale. The dataset provides both cropped time series per trial and processed mean values per trial, together with participant demographics, anthropometry, and maximum voluntary push and grip forces. All data are provided as comma-separated CSV files, organized by measurement type with one subfolder per participant. A README and a data dictionary describing all files, variables, units, and processing levels are included.
evidence_items.title: Dataset to: "Mapping Handle Design Parameters to Upper-Limb Load and Strain for Design Evaluation - An Experimental Study Using a Reproducible Manual Task"

evidence_items.summary: Continual learning is the ability of LLM agents to improve over time by acquiring, refining, and applying knowledge from experience while retaining useful prior knowledge. It is essential for agents learning over long time horizons, yet current evaluations largely assess individual task performance rather than improvement through accumulated experience. We introduce Continual Learning Exam (CLE), a large-scale benchmark developed by 50+ domain experts to measure experience-driven improvement in realistic professional workflows. CLE comprises 120 human-authored tasks, each organised as a five-level ladder, yielding 600 levels spanning 89 professional roles across 12 occupational domains. Agents must pass each level to unlock the next, with later levels building on experience accumulated during earlier assignments. An evaluation agent assesses each submission against human-authored rubrics. We compare a single-submission setting with one that provides diagnostic feedback after failure and allows one revision. Across 17 harness-model configurations using frontier LLMs, feedback and revision yield a median completion gain of 5.3 percentage points. Yet the best-performing system clears only 47.7% of levels and completes all five levels in just 23.3% of tasks, highlighting the difficulty of sustained learning from experience for existing frontier LLMs. As such, the dataset can also be used to post-train LLMs to strengthen their continual learning capabilities.
evidence_items.title: Continual Learning Exam: Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Patent examination is a challenging real-world task that requires agents to discover sparse prior art, iteratively refine queries, inspect technical evidence, and produce novelty assessments documented in Office Actions (OAs) across heterogeneous scientific and technical domains. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on static and limited candidate sets, leaving the full search--reasoning--assessment process underexplored. We present PatEx-Gym, the first framework for developing and evaluating agents for patent examination, which integrates three components. First, PatEx-Bench provides 1K realistic examination tasks, two large-scale retrieval corpora containing over 1M patents and 52K scientific papers, and a harness runtime supporting iterative search, document visits, reasoning, and OA generation. Second, we introduce PASS, an annotation-free Prior-Art Agentic Search Trajectory Synthesis framework. Specifically, it exploits document visits as implicit relevance signals and evidence-acquisition anchors to model intra-turn query behavior, inter-turn search progression, and trajectory-level evidence and outcome quality, yielding PatEx-SynData. Third, we train PatEx-Agent at the 4B scale via supervised fine-tuning on the curated trajectories, establishing a lightweight baseline. Extensive experiments show that final decision accuracy alone does not fully reflect examination quality, while prior-art discovery remains difficult even for strong frontier models. Our PatEx-Agent achieves competitive performance against substantially larger general-purpose agents. These results show that training on PatEx-SynData enables a compact 4B model to serve as a competitive baseline for prior-art search and patent examination. We view patent examination as a demanding testbed for agentic search and deep research agents.
evidence_items.title: Novel or Not? PatEx-Gym: Agentic Prior-Art Search for Novelty Assessment in Patent Examination

evidence_items.summary: Background Automated dietary assessment increasingly struggles to evaluate industrial food processing levels, revealing a systemic gap between the visual presentation of meals and their underlying ultra-processed food composition. Although existing dietary monitoring tools can effectively track caloric and macronutrient intake, they lack the qualitative processing assessments required to identify hidden additives and map dietary risk triage quadrants. Methods This study introduces a modular, IoT-enabled multimodal dietary decision-support framework that decouples visual food recognition, standardized database retrieval, and qualitative language reasoning for automated NOVA processing classification and 2D decision matrix mapping. Operating on isolated single-dish meal instances, the system employs a four-phase cascaded pipeline that integrates vision-language models, database retrieval, and large language models (LLMs) with strict JSON schema enforcement. The platform was evaluated using the Nutrition-NOVA validation benchmark, a harmonized multimodal dataset constructed through dense vector-space semantic linkage between quantitative profiles from the Center for Food Safety database and qualitative NOVA tiers from Open Food Facts. This benchmark addresses a 75.0% metadata sparsity deficit identified in legacy repositories. Results In experimental evaluations on the Nutrition-NOVA benchmark, the baseline Qwen-VL-Max architecture achieved an adjacent accuracy of 77.7%. Furthermore, enforcing schema modularity enabled complete plug-and-play backend replaceability between commercial cloud application programming interfaces (APIs) and private, on-premises open-weight models without requiring architectural retraining. Discussion The proposed framework establishes an efficient, safety-first screening tool for digital healthcare decision support.
evidence_items.title: IoT-enabled multimodal large language model-based framework for compositional food recognition, nutrient profiling, NOVA classification, and cancer risk mitigation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The rapid expansion of mobile and digital financial services in Ethiopia has generated substantial user feedback, yet automated analysis remains challenging because reviews are multilingual, informal, code-switched, and weakly represented in existing language resources. This study develops and evaluates a reproducible multilingual natural language processing framework for classifying Ethiopian FinTech reviews into five service-oriented categories: General Praise or Suggestions (GPS), User Experience and Design Issues (UXD), Transaction and Payment Failures (TPF), Login and Authentication Problems (LAP), and Service and Support Complaints (SSC). An annotated corpus was constructed from publicly accessible reviews associated with 27 Ethiopian FinTech applications. The initial collection contained 8,387 records, of which 7,148 were retained after quality-control procedures. The corpus contains English, Amharic, and English-Amharic code-switched reviews. We benchmark conventional TF-IDF classifiers, neural architectures, and multilingual/African-language transformer models under a leakage-controlled experimental protocol in which random oversampling is restricted to the training partition. Using five-fold stratified cross-validation, repeated random seeds, held-out evaluation, confidence intervals, and paired bootstrap significance testing, AfroXLMR achieved the strongest performance, with 96.7% accuracy and 96.0% macro-F1, followed by AfriBERTa (96.5%, 95.8%) and XLM-R (96.2%, 95.4%). The strongest neural baseline, CNN, achieved 95.1% accuracy and 94.3% macro-F1, while XGBoost achieved 90.2% accuracy and 88.1% macro-F1. Minority-class recall improved substantially after training-only oversampling. Language-specific analysis indicated lower performance for English-Amharic code-switched reviews than for English and Amharic reviews.
evidence_items.title: Multilingual Artificial Intelligence for Classifying Ethiopian FinTech User Reviews

evidence_items.summary: Click-Through Rate (CTR) prediction is a critical task in recommender systems and online advertising, so CTR models design has been widely researched in both academia and industry. However, since the model parameters increase larger and their computations become more complex, the inefficiency severely hinders practical deployment and application. Especially, the lack of a unified benchmark for the computational efficiency of CTR models complicates matters. To address the issues, we propose a holistic efficiency benchmark for CTR models named EffBench. a) A comprehensive evaluation metric system is constructed for CTR models, including seven metrics to assess accuracy and strongly emphasize computational efficiency. b) EffBench benchmark is implemented based on industrial mainstream framework TensorFlow, to better align with real-world usage scenarios. c) An operator-level profiling tool in EffBench is designed to identify key performance bottlenecks. d) Based on the EffBench benchmark, we evaluate and analyze 30 representative models across three typical CTR task types on the three widely used real-world datasets. As the first benchmark aiming at improving CTR model efficiency, EffBench will facilitate researchers in CTR model evaluation, comparison, validation, and inspiring future model designs. Our benchmark source code is available at https://github.com/Yeedzhi/EffBench .
evidence_items.title: EffBench: A Holistic Efficiency Benchmark for CTR Models

evidence_items.summary: In this study, three software reliability tasks are considered: predicting defect prone modules, software incidents severity classification, and predicting deployment change failures, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is studied for those tasks. For four explicitly synthetic tabular datasets with 2,400 data points each, that is, 7,200 observations, four classifiers were tested: logistic regression, random forest, extremely randomized trees and histogram gradient boosting. We were able to generate 12 model task evaluations, with 600 instances left out for each task. The accuracy and the macro-F1 scores of logistic regression were 77.17% and 75.40% for defect prediction, 72.00% and 72.33% for incident severity classification, and 64.33% and 63.69% for change-failure prediction, respectively. There are three areas of examination in the evaluation: predictive performance analysis, error patterns analysis, and model interpretation analysis. The confusion matrix, the receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) and the balanced accuracy are all used to explore these areas, along with the Matthews correlation coefficient and the feature-importance analysis. Twenty publications on the topic are critically examined and used to put the benchmark into the context and its methodological choices. The study offers an evaluation protocol that conveys the explanation in terms that the reader can follow and a comparative simulation framework of three software engineering decision points, along with a discussion of the constraints of the shown tasks when it comes to deployment. It does not develop a new learning algorithm but rather it is methodological and comparative. The results reported here are only applicable to the data sets generated and external validity has not been established.
evidence_items.title: Explainable AI for Software Reliability: A Three-Dataset Benchmark of Defect, Incident-Severity and Change-Failure Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Robust 3D reconstruction across varying environmental conditions remains a critical challenge for robotic perception, particularly when transitioning between air and water. To address this, we introduce BALTIC, a controlled benchmark designed to systematically evaluate modern 3D reconstruction methods under variations in medium and lighting. The benchmark comprises 13 datasets spanning two media (air and water) and three lighting conditions (directional, artificial, and mixed), with additional variations in motion type, scanning pattern, and initialization trajectory, resulting in a diverse set of sequences. Our experimental setup features a custom water tank equipped with a monocular camera and an HTC Vive tracker, enabling accurate ground-truth pose estimation. We further investigate cross-domain reconstruction by augmenting underwater image sequences with a small number of in-air views captured under similar lighting conditions. We evaluate Structure-from-Motion reconstruction using COLMAP in terms of both trajectory accuracy and scene geometry, and use these reconstructions as input to Neural Radiance Fields and 3D Gaussian Splatting methods. The resulting models are assessed against ground-truth trajectories and in-air references, while rendered outputs are compared using perceptual and photometric metrics. Additionally, we perform a color restoration analysis to evaluate radiometric consistency across domains. Our results show that under controlled, texture-consistent conditions, Gaussian Splatting with simple preprocessing (e.g., white balance correction) can achieve performance comparable to specialized underwater methods, although its robustness decreases in more complex and heterogeneous real-world environments.
evidence_items.title: Baltic: A benchmark and cross-domain strategy for 3D reconstruction across air and underwater domains under varying illumination

evidence_items.summary: Reproducible evaluation frameworks are essential for translating machine learning advances into medical decision-support systems, yet comparisons of classical machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and automated machine learning (AutoML) often lack standardized preprocessing, consistent validation, and transparent runtime reporting. We present a reproducible, time-aware benchmark for heart disease detection using a unified tabular dataset merging four University of California Irvine (UCI) Heart Disease sources: Cleveland, Hungary, Switzerland, and Veterans Administration (VA) Long Beach. The framework applies shared preprocessing and evaluates ML, DL, and AutoML under nominal framework-level time limits of 180 and 60 s, while reporting predictive metrics, observed wall-clock runtime, memory usage, and serialized model size. In the original single-split benchmark, Extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) achieved an accuracy of 84.78%, an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of 91.79%, and an F1-score of 86.67% in the full regime. Under the lightweight regime, AutoGluon matched the accuracy and F1-score, increased area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) to 92.80%, and completed in 9.87 s, although with a larger serialized artifact. Robustness was assessed using repeated stratified 80/20 holdout evaluation across five pre-specified seeds. AutoGluon Light achieved the highest descriptive mean F1-score and ROC-AUC (83.97 ± 1.95% and 89.16 ± 2.29%, respectively), while ClassicML Light remained competitive (82.86 ± 2.68% F1-score; 88.09 ± 2.29% ROC-AUC) and achieved the shortest mean runtime (3.41 ± 3.52 s). Pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction showed no statistically significant differences among lightweight frameworks.
evidence_items.title: A time-aware reproducible benchmark of full and lightweight AutoML, machine learning, and deep learning frameworks for heart disease detection

evidence_items.summary: Abstract-: Verifying the authenticity of handwritten signatures remains a vital challenge in biometric security systems, especially in financial, legal, and administrative domains. This work presents a deep learning–based framework for automated offline signature authentication using transfer learning with MobileNetV2. The system distinguishes real from forged signatures through convolutional feature extraction and classification. Leveraging MobileNetV2’s lightweight architecture and ImageNet pretraining, the model is fine-tuned on a labelled signature dataset using data augmentation and adaptive training. The pipeline consists of four core modules: Data Preprocessing, CNN Feature Extraction, Transfer Learning Fine-Tuning, and Real-Time Signature Prediction. Evaluation on a real-world dataset achieves 96.46% accuracy, as shown in the confusion matrix. This framework provides a reliable, scalable solution for signature verification in practical security applications, especially where computational efficiency and high precision are essential.

evidence_items.summary: ## Dataset Description This dataset contains specimen-level experimental data generated during a study investigating the intra-build stability and inter-build repeatability of porosity, tensile properties, and fatigue performance in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of Ti–6Al–4V. The dataset includes: - Build-level manufacturing information - Porosity measurements - Tensile test results - Fatigue test results The data were used to evaluate variability within individual build (called stability) and between nominally identical builds (called repeatability) of samples manufactured using nominally identical processing conditions. Associated Original Publication Reijonen, J., Vaajoki, A., Puukko, P. Solin, J., Alhainen, J., Kivistö, A. Intra-build stability and inter-build repeatability of porosity, tensile properties and fatigue performance in laser powder bed fusion of Ti–6Al–4V. Progress in Additive Manufacturing (2026). DOI: 10.1007/s40964-026-01772-y ## Experimental Overview Ti–6Al–4V specimens were manufactured using laser powder bed fusion under nominally identical process conditions in multiple independent builds. The study investigated: 1. Within-build variability in one build job called stability, with specimens grouped into five locations (1-5) on the build plate: center and all four corners 2. Build-to-build repeatability in three build jobs called R1-3, with specimens grouped to two locations 3, 5 that were identified to be the best and worts location groups in step 1. The specimen population included tensile, fatigue and porosity specimens in each said location group. Detailed manufacturing procedures, specimen geometries, location of each individual specimen, testing methods, and statistical analyses are described in the associated publication.

evidence_items.summary: Stair Gait Analysis (Lower-Limb Step-Up and Step-Down Movement) This dataset comprises two-dimensional pose-annotation data, knee joint angles and gait phase labels collected from healthy young adults performing step-up and step-down activities. The dataset was developed to support research in lower-limb movement analysis, human pose estimation, gait assessment, gait phase detection, joint-angle estimation, spatiotemporal parameter extraction, and machine-learning-based movement classification. A total of nineteen healthy participants, aged between 20 and 25 years, voluntarily participated in the study. The participants had no reported history of neurodegenerative disorders, musculoskeletal conditions, or abnormal gait and were physically capable of performing the experimental activities independently without external support. Each participant performed step-up and step-down movements on a staircase, paced by a metronome set to 90 beats per minute. The lower-limb movements were recorded using a Sony Alpha 6000 series mirrorless camera, positioned perpendicular to the participant's sagittal plane. Ground-truth anatomical landmark trajectories were subsequently generated using Kinovea version 2023.1.2. Three anatomical keypoints (Left Hip, Left Knee, and Left Ankle) were selected for the lower-limb movement analysis. The selected anatomical landmarks were manually identified in the video and tracked throughout the recorded sequences using Kinovea. The tracked trajectories were reviewed across the video frames to verify the consistency and accuracy of the landmark positions. The dataset contains two sets of files: 1. Keypoint coordinate files (subject1.csv to subject17.csv): frame-wise X and Y image-plane coordinates of the Left Hip, Left Knee, and Left Ankle keypoints for Subjects 1 to 17. 2. Knee angle and gait phase files (subject1 knee angle phase.csv to subject19 knee angle phase.csv): frame-wise knee joint angle and gait phase label for Subjects 1 to 19.
evidence_items.title: Stair Gait Analysis

evidence_items.summary: As large language model agents increasingly compile natural-language requirements into repository-level code, requirement-to-test generation grows in importance to provide validation constraints (or harness) to guide code generation. Yet it remains unclear whether current agents can generate tests that validate the required behavior when the implementation of that behavior is withheld. Existing test-generation benchmarks mostly focus on white-box testing, whereas the requirement--test-related study usually requires evaluation on semantic alignment between the given documents and the generated tests. We introduce Req2Test-Bench, a benchmark containing 5,086 execution-validated instances recovered from developer-authored behavior-driven development (BDD) artifacts in 8 open-source projects, spanning 5 programming languages and 4 BDD frameworks. Each instance pairs a natural-language requirement in Gherkin with its developer-written Test Implementation. Given the requirement, target interfaces of the required behavior, an agent must generate a complete, potentially multi-file Test Implementation. Evaluation of 8 agent--model--reasoning configurations reveals a substantial gap between execution success and behavioral adequacy, which is measured strictly as kill-completeness: a kill-complete test kills every mutant that the ground-truth test kills. The best-performing configuration, Codex with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, produces passing tests for 82.8% of instances, yet only 33.8% are behaviorally adequate. We find that (1) scaling up agents yields sharply diminishing returns in behavioral adequacy relative to generation cost; (2) under-specified requirements cause the information gap, including ambiguous setup and implicit expected outcomes; and (3) requirement-grounded harnesses that steer agent non-determinism offer a promising direction for improvement.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Behaviorally Adequate Test Generation from Software Requirements

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Azerbaijan's strategic geographical position places the country at the center of major transit routes connecting Europe and Asia. In particular, its location along the Middle Corridor (the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route) creates substantial potential for Azerbaijan to emerge as a key logistics hub within regional and global trade flows. Nevertheless, in order to fully realize this potential, systematic improvement of the country's Logistics Performance Index (LPI) indicators remains a critical requirement. The LPI serves as an important international benchmark that evaluates countries' logistics competitiveness across dimensions such as the quality of logistics infrastructure, efficiency of customs procedures, reliability of international shipments, and the quality of logistics services. This study analyzes the main determinants influencing the logistics performance of the Republic of Azerbaijan and proposes strategic approaches aimed at strengthening its position as a regional logistics hub. The research is based on a review of international best practices, an assessment of existing public policies, and an evaluation of transport corridor development strategies. Through this framework, key structural gaps and development opportunities within Azerbaijan's logistics sector are identified, providing a basis for targeted policy interventions. The findings indicate that the modernization and digitalization of customs procedures represent one of the most critical priorities for improving logistics performance. The implementation of electronic customs platforms, the expansion of risk-based inspection systems, and the simplification of documentation processes can significantly reduce transit times, enhance transparency, and optimize trade-related costs.
evidence_items.title: Azərbaycanın Logistika Performans İndeksinin (LPI) artırılması: Davamlı rəqabətqabiliyyətlilik üçün strateji yanaşmalar

evidence_items.summary: Indoor context deciphered by ambient sensing underpins many applications, from assisted living to smart buildings, yet remains weakly connected to the language-aligned paradigm of modern multimodal systems. Through billions of IoT devices, ambient WiFi Channel State Information (CSI) captures the indoor context of human activity and environmental dynamics passively via ubiquitous, always-on infrastructure. However, unlike vision or audio, CSI lacks naturally paired text like captions or transcripts, limiting its integration with language-driven AI systems. We present CSI-TextBench, a large-scale dataset and benchmark for aligning CSI data with natural language, unifying 3 sensing benchmarks into 285,790 samples across 7 tasks and pairing them with 2,291 hierarchically structured, label-derived descriptions via many-to-many assignment to construct 2.0 million CSI-text training tuples. Benchmarking 5 alignment methods from 4 paradigm families, we show that contrastive CSI-text alignment matches supervised classifiers without class labels, adapts to unseen classes with few samples, and responds to open-vocabulary natural-language prompts. A single unified model supports compositional scene understanding, answering joint queries over activity, proximity, and identity, achieving 86.9% top-1 accuracy on 140 composite scenes, outperforming task-specific classifier ensembles. CSI-TextBench enables ubiquitous ambient sensing as a language-indexed perception layer, enabling indoor contextual awareness in language-driven AI systems.
evidence_items.title: CSI-TextBench: A Dataset and Benchmark for Language-Grounded Ambient Sensing Perception

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly wired to consequential tools that send public alerts, dispatch responders, and query citizen records, where one erroneous tool call carries real-world cost. Existing agent-safety benchmarks measure generic harm or prompt-injection success and implicitly treat refusing as the safe default. In public-safety deployments that assumption breaks: an agent too cautious to dispatch help fails as surely as one that triggers a false alert. We present SentryBench, which scores agents on a two-sided, cost-sensitive frontier jointly measuring attack success, over-refusal (missing a real emergency), and over-reaction (unwarranted action) under adversarial tool use, with scenarios grounded in real emergency-call transcripts, disaster messages, and real injection/jailbreak payloads. We formalize deployment harm as an asymmetric cost functional, prove naive caution is harm-dominated whenever it refuses more genuine emergencies than the attack harm it averts, and prove a targeted trust gate adds zero over-refusal on clean input. Across 840 scored episodes over three frontier models and three defenses, refuse-more caution drives over-refusal to 100 percent on two of three models for at most a 3.7-point change in attack success and yields the worst harm everywhere, whereas our trust-gating wrapper dominates the frontier (lowest harm on every model, over-refusal at or below baseline, higher containment). Provider content filters also silently perform part of the defending and must be reported separately.
evidence_items.title: SentryBench: A Cost-Sensitive Benchmark for Adversarial Robustness of Tool-Using LLM Agents in Public-Safety Deployments

evidence_items.summary: As agents collaborate on longer tasks, responsibility may pass between models before the work is complete. The receiving model must build on prior decisions, observations, and actions while addressing the remaining requirements. Evaluating this transition requires connecting the information preserved at handoff to how the receiver continues the work, a relationship that task-success and memory-retention scores alone do not capture. We introduce the Handoff State Continuity Benchmark (HSC-Bench), comprising 1,039 tasks that evaluate two complementary aspects of task takeover: recovering relevant repository evidence and continuing from established conversational, tool, and file-work state. Comparisons across six receiving models show that structured handoff state improves repository evidence recovery for every model and continuation performance for most models. The strongest receivers differ between the two tracks, showing that evidence-recovery rankings alone do not characterize performance when continuing from inherited state. By combining these comparisons with checks of subsequent responses and actions, HSC-Bench evaluates both access to prior evidence and adherence to established commitments and completed work. This provides a basis for selecting receiving models and assessing handoff representations according to the work that must be carried forward.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Task Takeover Across Agent Handoffs
