evidence_items.summary: Production LLM agents increasingly run episodic memory pipelines and procedural skill modules (e.g., SKILL.md files) in tandem. Both are injected into the same context region with no defined precedence, so they can issue contradictory instructions that no instruction hierarchy resolves, a condition we term epistemic parity. We introduce a benchmark for measuring how LLM agents adjudicate such cross-source conflicts. We (i) develop a four-way taxonomy of memory-skill contradictions (factual, format, procedural, permission); (ii) instantiate 52 scenarios under a tripartite test-case anatomy (memory injection, skill injection, ambiguous user task), scored almost entirely by deterministic checkers over tool-call payloads and output structure; and (iii) run each scenario under three context conditions to isolate positional bias, measure the efficacy of an explicit precedence directive, and classify disclosure behavior, quantifying silent adjudication: resolving a conflict without telling the user. Across 1,383 runs on three open-weight models, neither source wins uniformly: resolution depends jointly on conflict type, model, and injection order. Moving the skill block nearer the task raises its win rate in all six factual and procedural cells (sign test, p = 0.031) but reverses for format conflicts, indicating that adjudication tracks token placement rather than source semantics. An explicit "skill takes absolute precedence" directive raises skill compliance on the two stronger models yet leaves 3-10% residual non-compliance, and moves the smallest model's factual and procedural resolution in the wrong direction. Most consequentially, in 98.8% of runs where the agent acted through a tool call it emitted no accompanying text at all, and 89% of all runs disclosed nothing about the contradiction: silent adjudication is the default. Code, scenarios, and raw outputs are public.
evidence_items.title: Navigating Epistemic Parity in LLM Agents: A Benchmark for Cross-Source Conflict Resolution Between Memory and Procedural Skills

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming language sciences. However, their widespread deployment currently suffers from methodological fragmentation and a lack of systematic soundness. This study proposes two comprehensive methodological frame works designed to guide the strategic and responsible application of LLMs inlanguage sciences. The first method-selection framework defines and systematizes three distinct, complementary approaches, each linked toa specific research goal: (1) prompt-based interaction with general-usemodels for exploratory analysis and hypothesis generation; (2) fine tuning of open-source models for confirmatory, theory-driven investigation and high-quality data generation; and (3) extraction of contextualized embeddings for further quantitative analysis and probing of model internal mechanisms. We detail the technical implementationand inherent trade-offs of each method, supported by empirical casestudies. Based on the method-selection framework, the second systematic framework proposed provides constructed configurations that guide the practical implementation of multi-stage research pipelines based on these approaches. We then conducted a series of empirical experiments to validate our proposed framework, employing retrospective analysis, prospective application, and an expert evaluation survey. By enforcing the strategic alignment of research questions with the appropriate LLM methodology, the frameworks enable a critical paradigm shift in language science research. We believe that this systemis fundamental for ensuring reproducibility, facilitating the criticalevaluation of LLM mechanisms, and providing the structure necessaryto move traditional linguistics from ad-hoc utility to verifiable, robust science.
evidence_items.title: Systematic Framework of Application Methods for Large Language Models in Language Sciences

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We present a Bayesian framework, Two-stage Inference for Light curve DEcomposition ( TILDE ), for mapping the accretion disk and the broad-line region (BLR) from active galactic nucleus (AGN) multiband light curves. By inferring delayed BLR contamination from the underlying disk variability, TILDE provides the delay measurements of the disk as well as the BLR. We validate TILDE using synthetic data, finding that TILDE recovers the known time delays of the disk and BLR. By applying TILDE to the Seoul National University AGN Monitoring Project sample, we find that the inferred BLR light curves match the observed H β emission light curves, providing consistent BLR lags compared to the reported H β lags. Using the lag spectrum, effectively corrected for the BLR contamination, we find that the disk size is broadly consistent with the standard thin-disk model, suggesting that BLR contamination can significantly bias the disk size derived from the cross-correlation analysis of the broadband photometry. These results demonstrate that the new inference method is a powerful tool for determining both disk and BLR sizes from broadband photometry in the era of time-domain surveys.
evidence_items.title: Unveiling Accretion-disk Reverberation beneath Broad-line Region Contamination with TILDE

evidence_items.summary: 30 vulnerable Python functions across 14 CWE categories, 12 adversarial comment strategies in four families (verification premise, context manipulation, credibility vocabulary, pressure and distraction), and 3,360 recorded trials from four studies run locally through Ollama at temperature 0: an attack ranking (780 trials), a comment-stripping defense (1,020), a cross-model comparison (600) and a transferability study (960), on qwen2.5-coder 7B, deepseek-coder 6.7B, codellama 7B and codegemma 7B. Includes the original harnesses and an analysis script that reproduces every headline number with Wilson 95% confidence intervals. Related work (added in v1.1.0). Moon et al. (arXiv 2505.16222, "Don't Judge Code by Its Cover") show that LLM judges of code correctness are biased by superficial variations such as comments and variable names. Alves and Henriques (SBSeg 2026, Workshop de Cibersegurança em IA, DOI 10.5753/sbseg estendido.2026.33836) test four LLMs on smart contract vulnerability detection with comments removed or identifiers renamed and report that semantically equivalent code can lead to different diagnoses. Heibel and Lowd (arXiv 2407.11072, "MaPPing Your Model") show that a small amount of added prompt text can make a programming assistant insert vulnerabilities. That is the code generation side, while CommentInject targets the review side, where the attacker controls the comments. Cihan, İçöz, Haratian and Tüzün (arXiv 2505.20206) evaluate GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash as code reviewers and report that their outputs can be faulty. Thornton (arXiv 2602.16741) tests eight models, mostly commercial, over 9,366 trials and reports small, non-significant effects of adversarial comments on detection, and that stripping comments lowers detection for weaker models. CommentInject uses four open models of about 7B parameters, so its results should not be read as holding for commercial models. v1.1.0 changes this description only. Data, harnesses and results are unchanged.

evidence_items.summary: A benchmark leaderboard reports one accuracy number, but that number is a joint product of a model and a scoring rule. We ask what changes when only the rule changes, and find that model ordering is highly sensitive to it. IndiaFinBench is a 406-item expert-annotated benchmark over SEBI and RBI regulatory text covering regulatory interpretation, numerical reasoning, contradiction detection, and temporal reasoning. We score twelve LLMs zero-shot under two primary regimes over the same predictions - strict four-stage string matching, and the verdicts of a cross-model judge sharing no model family with any evaluated system - plus one operational composite regime. The two primary regimes show no positive rank correspondence (Spearman rho = -0.273, p = 0.39, not significant), and no model holds its rank across all three regimes. Strict accuracy spans 75.12-89.66%; judge-only accuracy spans 87.19-94.83% with a different leader and trailer; the composite compresses the field to 94.1-98.0%, under which DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B ties for first despite ranking last under strict scoring, because the judge reclassifies 93.9% of its strict errors as correct. Output verbosity does not explain the reclassification once task and model composition are adjusted for, a negative result we report as such. Item-level analysis compounds the finding: 148 of 406 items (36.5%) are answered identically by all twelve models and separate no pair of systems, while a predefined higher-discrimination band captures 134 items. We also anchor the scale against one non-specialist evaluator, who scored 80.0% (48/60; 95% Wilson CI [68.2, 88.2]) on a 60-item medium/hard subset; paired bootstrap tests find no significant difference against any model after multiplicity correction. Data, harness, judge verdicts, predictions: https://github.com/Rajveer-code/IndiaFinBench
evidence_items.title: Scoring-Rule Sensitivity in LLM Evaluation: Evidence from Indian Financial Regulatory Text

evidence_items.summary: Learning controllable world dynamics from heterogeneous interaction videos is challenging because robot embodiments use incompatible action spaces, while human videos lack native control labels. We present RynnWorld-Latent, a cross-embodiment video world model that uses the 3D-grounded latent actions introduced by RynnLAM as a shared conditioning interface. This representation enables joint pretraining on human interaction videos, robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without requiring a common native action space. Built on a pretrained video transformer, RynnWorld-Latent combines global action tokens with an identity-initialized local pathway that aligns actions with future video latents. We pretrain on 23 datasets comprising approximately 553.5M frames and adapt the model to target robots through post-training. The framework supports two data-generation routes: digital teleoperation uses target robot commands to generate action-video demonstrations, while latent-action synthesis transfers source motion to an edited initial frame and pairs the resulting rollout with retargeted pseudo robot actions. Experiments show improved video prediction metrics on public benchmarks and two real-robot platforms, alongside qualitative action following when different action sequences share the same initial observation. Synthetic mid-training improves policy success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and both generation routes improve real-world policy success rates over real-demonstration-only training in the evaluated settings. These results support universal latent actions as a scalable interface for learning controllable visual dynamics across heterogeneous embodiments.
evidence_items.title: RynnWorld-Latent: A Cross-Embodiment World Model Conditioned on Universal Latent Actions

evidence_items.summary: Video stylization typically transforms entire scenes, while local artistic editing requires precise region--style association, spatial control, and temporal consistency. We introduce LociArt, a unified paradigm for free-style local video stylization that explicitly specifies where to stylize and what style to apply while preserving non-target content. At its core, GRNStyle builds on Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) and introduces a polar style-aware mask that embeds style identities as equal-norm directions within selected regions. Complementary representation--geometry conditioning combines encoded mask features with raw-mask spatial support, integrating spatiotemporal context with geometric control. To provide paired supervision, we develop an automated pipeline combining global stylization, video object removal, matting, and compositing, and construct the LociArt-100K Dataset with 100K local stylization pairs. We further establish the LociArt Benchmark, comprising 80 source videos and 84 target masks covering 168 foreground/background stylization cases, with a Style Prototype Similarity (SPS) evaluation scheme for regional style quality and complementary measures of non-target preservation and temporal consistency. Experiments show that GRNStyle outperforms existing methods in regional style quality and spatial control while maintaining strong temporal consistency. Qualitative examples further illustrate joint stylization of multiple regions with the same or different learned styles, despite training only on single-region, single-style pairs. Together, these components provide a unified foundation for learning and evaluating controllable local video stylization. Project page: https://higherhu.github.io/lociart/.
evidence_items.title: LociArt: A Unified Paradigm for Free-Style Local Video Stylization

evidence_items.summary: Preprint with the routed circuits, verifier and search code. We revisit the qubit-routing benchmark of Li, Ding and Xie (SABRE, ASPLOS 2019): 26 circuits routed onto the 43-edge IBM Q20 Tokyo coupling graph, scored by the number of added gates (three per inserted SWAP). With the same circuits, graph and metric and an exact replay verifier, our routings need 12,087 added gates in total against SABRE's published 68,559 (82% fewer). On identical inputs, Qiskit 2.4.1 SABRE gives 64,137 (default) and 53,418 (heavy trials), and pytket 2.18.5 gives 35,685. On the 15 circuits reported in common by later routing papers on this device, the best published counts (HAIL, 2025) total 13,044 against our 9,312. Our count is lower on every circuit than every method we found (SAHS, MCTS, FiDLS, ILS, TWP, HAIL), with one tie. The routings come from a level-synchronous beam search over SWAP sequences, combined with SABRE-style forward-reverse passes to refine the initial mapping. The search code was written by a language-model agent inside an autonomous discovery loop (about three hours, about 21 USD of model usage). Beam search for routing is not new. The contribution is the measured gap on this widely cited suite, the exactly verifiable routed circuits, and an account of the discovery process. Caveats: far more compute per circuit than the baselines, a metric that ignores depth and fidelity, two regenerated QFT circuits, and the design graph rather than the physical device. Files: the preprint (PDF + LaTeX source, figures, bibliography); the 26 OpenQASM benchmark circuits with the QFT generator; qmap.py (QASM parser, coupling graph, exact replay verifier, SABRE reimplementation); routings/best combined.json (initial mapping and full operation sequence per circuit) with a per-circuit source map; the baseline script and its output; every proposer run's router code, drivers and notes; SHA-256 sums. Reproduce: python qmap.py verify routings/best combined.json (prints total g add 12087).
evidence_items.title: Beam search over SWAP sequences on the SABRE benchmark: 82% fewer added gates than SABRE and 29% fewer than the best published routings for IBM Q20 Tokyo, found by an autonomous agent

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial intelligence is increasingly being applied to the assessment, monitoring and care of older adults, with potential benefits across both population health and individual clinical practice. This narrative review examines current and emerging applications of AI in common conditions and care needs associated with ageing, including hypertension, stroke, myocardial infarction, Parkinson’s disease, osteoporosis, sarcopenia and supportive care robotics. Across these domains, AI-enabled analysis of electronic health records, electrocardiograms, imaging, video, wearable-sensor data and home-monitoring measurements may support earlier disease detection, more objective functional assessment, personalised risk prediction and treatment, and greater independence. Computer-vision approaches may provide detailed measures of movement following stroke and in Parkinson’s disease, while opportunistic analysis of existing imaging may improve recognition of low bone mineral density, vertebral fractures and reduced muscle health. Care robots may additionally assist with companionship, medication management and falls detection. However, much of the evidence remains based on selected datasets, proof-of-concept studies or controlled settings. Algorithmic bias, limited representation of frail and multimorbid older adults, privacy, governance, interpretability, interoperability, user burden and workforce consequences remain important barriers. AI should therefore complement rather than replace clinical judgement. Equitable implementation will require representative datasets, rigorous external and prospective validation, transparent models, user-centred design and evaluation of clinically meaningful outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in an ageing population

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Reliable plant-disease segmentation depends on evaluation images being independent of the data used for training. We audited PlantSeg, a large in-the-wild semantic-segmentation benchmark, to determine whether visually related image families cross its released partitions and whether such exposure changes the evidence produced by standard segmentation models. The audit combined multiple similarity signals with human adjudication, followed by contamination-aware re-evaluation, class-count-matched Monte Carlo controls, a two-seed training-exposure experiment, long-tail analysis, and group-disjoint benchmark reconstruction. Verified cross-split visual families involved about 10.7% of the released images. Across four canonical architectures, released-split evaluation was consistently more favorable than contamination-aware evaluation, and the main shifts persisted after controlling for disease-class composition. The training side exposure had very limited effect in the independent clean test cases but was seen to have an estimated 11–15% advantage in related contaminated test cases in both seeds. Deletion of family ties improved independence at the cost of rare class support; while the group-disjoint reconstruction kept all 115 disease classes intact while removing known family ties. This illustrates that benchmark contamination can be overestimated and family-aware split construction is a viable solution.
evidence_items.title: Improving Reliability in Plant Disease Semantic Segmentation by Quantifying Benchmark Contamination and Duplicate Family Exposure

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Activation functions (AFs) play a pivotal role in defining the representational power and learning dynamics of deep neural networks (DNNs). However, their influence on medical image restoration (MIR) remains insufficiently explored. This empirical study presents a comprehensive, multi-phase investigation into how different AFs affect spatial and frequency characteristics across MIR tasks, such as image deblurring, image deblocking, and image super-resolution, in three medical imaging modalities: computed tomography (CT), digital mammography (DM), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The study integrates a theoretical taxonomy of AFs, a fixed-weight analysis, and a full-scale empirical evaluation involving 15 representative AFs spanning classical, rectified, exponential, and modern smooth families, benchmarked across 3,000 medical images. These functions are implemented within two widely used state-of-the-art MIR architectures: U-Net and Enhanced Deep Super-Resolution (EDSR). Model performance is evaluated using Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), Edge Preservation Index (EPI), High-Frequency Energy Ratio (HFER), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS), with statistical validation performed using Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and Tukey’s Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) tests. Results reveal that while the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) and its variants remain strong baselines due to their stability and efficiency, smoother and adaptive functions such as the Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU), Mish, and Funnel ReLU (FReLU) achieved superior performance in preserving fine spatial and frequency details.
evidence_items.title: An empirical benchmark of activation functions for medical image restoration networks

evidence_items.summary: Purpose This viewpoint examines organizational implications of agentic AI systems in planning, selecting tools, executing multistep actions, and evaluating their own outputs with limited human intervention. Design/methodology/approach This viewpoint synthesizes academic and practitioner insights to identify key organizational challenges associated with agentic AI drawing on organizational learning theory and recent research on human–AI collaboration, and propose practical directions for HR and learning and development. Findings As agentic AI becomes more autonomous, it is reshaping organizational learning, human oversight, and accountability. Organizations will need to redesign learning practices and governance mechanisms to ensure that people and AI work together effectively. Research limitations/implications This conceptual viewpoint does not include empirical validation. Future research should examine the proposed ideas across different organizational settings. Practical implications Organizations should assess workforce readiness, redesign learning around human–AI collaboration, and establish feedback mechanisms that strengthen learning, oversight, and accountability. Originality/value This viewpoint shifts the discussion from technological capabilities of agentic AI to its organizational implications, offering practical guidance for organizations adapting to increasingly autonomous forms of work.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI in organizations: reimagining learning, autonomy, and human oversight

evidence_items.summary: Objective: Agentic AI represents a paradigm shift from reactive systems to autonomous agents capable of perception, planning, reasoning, memory management, and tool usage without human intervention. This paper proposes the Healthcare Autonomous Reasoning Network (HARN), a multi-agent system designed to assist physicians with real-time diagnosis, treatment recommendations, and drug interaction detection. Methods: This paper introduces HARN’s architecture featuring a large language model (LLM) orchestrator coordinating four specialized sub-agents: radiology interpretation, electronic health record (EHR) exploration, pharmacological advice, and risk stratification. Experiments leverage the MIMIC-IV clinical dataset and curated drug interaction databases to evaluate diagnosis accuracy, decision latency, and hallucination rates. Expected results: HARN demonstrates an F1-score of 0.873 and 41% reduced clinical decision-making latency compared to baselines. Conclusions: The results validate the feasibility of agentic multi-agent systems for high-stakes healthcare applications, demonstrating better performance in autonomous clinical decision support.
evidence_items.title: Agentic intelligence: multi-agent systems for autonomous healthcare diagnostics and treatment planning

evidence_items.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence systems combine autonomous planning, memory, tool use, and multi-agent coordination, creating risks that extend beyond the behavior of an individual model to include interactions with external environments and operational workflows. Trustworthy deployment therefore requires assurance that integrates explainability, security, reliability, and governance across system layers and throughout the lifecycle. This paper proposes a unified framework that connects decision- and action-level explanations with threat modeling, bounded permissions, runtime verification, traceability, and reliability monitoring. It treats explanations as one component of assurance rather than a sufficient basis for trust, and situates them alongside calibrated human oversight and enforceable operational controls. The framework provides a structured basis for designing and evaluating agentic systems whose actions are interpretable, constrained, and auditable.
evidence_items.title: Trust by Design: A Unified Framework for Explainable, Secure, and Reliable Agentic Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: External skills provide language-model agents with reusable procedural knowledge, yet how models use such knowledge after it is supplied remains poorly understood. We identify Procedural Exposure Bias (PEB), the tendency of language models to increasingly favor an action as its associated procedural pattern is repeatedly exposed in a skill, even when the interaction state and action relevance remain unchanged. We find that PEB strongly depends on how procedural knowledge is represented: presenting the same content visually substantially attenuates exposure-induced shifts in action preference relative to textual presentation. Further analysis shows that this attenuation primarily arises from visual encoding rather than structured layout. Although repeated procedural signals remain recoverable from Visual representations, they exert a weaker influence on downstream action prediction, distinguishing signal accessibility from its use as action evidence. This effect also extends to executable action selection, where increasing exposure more strongly favors the corresponding action under Text than Visual. Layer-wise analyses show that exposure-dependent action evidence becomes more pronounced toward the model output, with stronger evidence under Text, while activation interventions reveal architecture-specific roles of internal components in transmitting or counteracting the preference shift. Complete-agent evaluations across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop further show that Visual skills achieve higher macro-average task success than Text skills for all four evaluated models. These findings establish skill representation as an important factor governing how procedural knowledge is translated into agent decisions. All code is available at https://github.com/NEUIR/Vis-Skill.
evidence_items.title: Procedural Exposure Bias in Skill-Augmented Language Model Agents

evidence_items.summary: Long-horizon agents performing multi-step Web tasks must reuse earlier page observations and interactions to support subsequent actions. However, preserving relevant history does not ensure that it exposes the relations needed for the current decision. We call this gap representation mismatch. To this end, we propose MemPrism, a task-conditioned relational memory framework that separates persistent experience storage from decision-time working memory. MemPrism records interactions as the event stream and dynamically constructs relational views according to the current task context. A lightweight view policy selects the relation structure, evidence range, outcome condition, and granularity, while a deterministic composer and renderer transform historical facts into a temporary optical working-memory view for a frozen task policy. Experiments on long-horizon embodied and web-agent benchmarks show that MemPrism consistently improves the task performance, especially as trajectories become longer, while reducing memory token consumption. Furthermore, the learned view policy transfers across different VLMs without additional adaptation, demonstrating the effectiveness of task-conditioned relational views as a general memory interface for agents.
evidence_items.title: MemPrism: Task-Conditioned Relational Memory Views for Long-Horizon Agents

evidence_items.summary: We introduce ControlAugment (Ctrl-A), an automated data augmentation algorithm for image-vision tasks, which incorporates principles from control theory for online adjustment of augmentation strength distributions during model training. Ctrl-A eliminates the need for initialization of individual augmentation strengths. Instead, augmentation strength distributions are dynamically, and individually, adapted during training based on a control-loop architecture and what we define as relative operation response curves. Using an operation-dependent update procedure provides Ctrl-A with the potential to reduce the use of augmentation operations that negatively impact model performance, alleviating the need to manually engineer augmentation policies for new image classification tasks. Experiments on the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN-core, and Tiny ImageNet benchmark datasets using WideResNet-28-10 and ResNet architectures demonstrate that Ctrl-A provides competitive performance across a range of image classification benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: Ctrl-A: Control-Driven Machine Learning using Adaptive Online Data Augmentation

evidence_items.summary: Image editing models can modify visual content through natural language, but editing dense documents requires precise local changes amid tightly coupled text, tables, and layout. We introduce VDE Bench, an evaluation resource for studying instruction-guided editing of Chinese and English document images. VDE Bench contains 3,506 instruction-guided image editing samples, including 1,578 text-region edits and 1,928 table-region edits. The benchmark pairs editing instructions and reference images with annotated editing regions and structured OCR outputs. Its evaluation protocol combines region-level and full-page measurements to assess textual correctness, structural fidelity, and visual content preservation. By focusing on the interaction between local edits and their surrounding document context, VDE Bench complements existing visual text editing benchmarks and provides a resource for diagnosing document-specific editing failures.
evidence_items.title: VDE Bench: Evaluating The Capability of Image Editing Models to Modify Visual Documents

evidence_items.summary: Existing text-to-video (T2V) evaluation benchmarks, such as VBench and EvalCrafter, predominantly contain either subject-centric prompts or static camera scenes, overlooking the importance of camera motion, essential for producing cinematic shots with realistic scenes. Due to this, the metrics developed in these works often produce incorrect results in the presence of camera motion. To fill this gap, we introduce DynamicEval, a benchmark comprising of systematically curated prompts that emphasize dynamic camera motion, paired with 45k human annotations on video pairs. DynamicEval evaluates two key dimensions of video quality: the consistency of the foreground subjects and the consistency of the background scene. To address the shortcomings of existing metrics under camera motion, we introduce two novel metrics: 1) Tracker-FG, which evaluates subject consistency by assessing the keypoint tracks of the subject. 2) Debiased Motion Smoothness, for background consistency, devoid from issues of occlusions/disocclusions arising from camera and foreground subject movements. Extensive experiments on the large-scale DynamicEval benchmark demonstrate that our proposed metrics achieve stronger correlations with human preferences at both the video level, and the model level with an increase of 0.32 in average Pearson Linear Correlation.
evidence_items.title: A Closer Look at Evaluation of Text-to-Video Models Under Camera Motion

evidence_items.summary: Unpaired image-to-image translation has seen significant progress since the introduction of CycleGAN. However, methods based on diffusion models or Schr\"odinger bridges have yet to be widely adopted in real-world applications due to their iterative sampling nature. To address this challenge, we propose Implicit Bridge Consistency Distillation (IBCD), which enables single-step bidirectional unpaired translation without using adversarial loss. IBCD reformulates consistency distillation by using a diffusion implicit bridge model that connects PF-ODE trajectories between distributions, parametrized on a signed time axis whose sign selects the target domain, so that one network translates in both directions in a single step. Additionally, we introduce two key improvements: 1) distribution matching for consistency distillation and 2) adaptive weighting method based on distillation difficulty. Experimental results demonstrate that IBCD achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets in a single generation step, and that it extends to brain MRI contrast translation.
evidence_items.title: Single-Step Bidirectional Unpaired Image Translation Using Implicit Bridge Consistency Distillation

evidence_items.summary: The rapid progress of software engineering agents drives interest in applying them to open-ended problems such as GPU kernel optimization. However, we find that existing coding agents converge to local optima on real-world, expert-written kernels (e.g., FlashInfer). We introduce Evolving Agent Teams, a multi-agent framework that escapes such local optima. It features (1) a central supervisor that diagnoses each local optimum and restructures a team of agents; and (2) a persistent file system that comprises a learning document, an evolution history, and per-team artifacts, grounding restructuring with accumulated experience. Under a matched token budget, Evolving Agent Teams consistently outperforms strong coding-agent baselines. With an extended token budget, Evolving Agent Teams generates a CUDA kernel that reaches 1.2x mean speedup over the production FlashInfer MLA paged decode kernel from scratch and wins on 36 of 47 production workloads from FlashInfer-Bench (0.86-0.99x on the remaining 11). It also demonstrates superior performance on tasks such as KDA prefill on AMD MI350X (3.01x over vLLM) and NVIDIA B200 (3.44x over FlashKDA), MoE expert-offload serving on Apple silicon (30.3 tokens/s decode for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in MLX 4-bit on a 48 GB M4 Pro), and RoboDojo robot manipulation (62.1 on held-out seeds vs. 55.3 for the best leaderboard entry). Code is available at https://github.com/caoshiyi/EAT.
evidence_items.title: Evolving Agent Teams

evidence_items.summary: We tackle the challenge of building real-time interactive video worlds with user-defined behaviors. Such worlds must track object states, apply interaction rules, and render the resulting consequences as users act. Yet existing end-to-end video world models typically learn interaction dynamics within the generator, making it difficult to specify object-level rules and reason about their consequences. In this work, we introduce BoxWorld, which separates interaction reasoning from generative rendering. Given user-specified rules, a coding agent creates a Box World Engine that determines interaction outcomes and exposes the resulting object states through a lightweight interface of layout boxes, persistent object attributes, and dynamic status variables, leaving appearance and physical effects to generative rendering. A Box-State Generative Renderer then renders this evolving state stream into video autoregressively, enabling online control over object motion, state switches, and conditional events. Rendering this state stream is non-trivial: the renderer must respond to object-level state updates in real time while remaining coherent with the generated history. To this end, we introduce a three-stage training strategy that learns object grounding from open-domain videos and state transitions from gameplay videos, both annotated automatically, and finally performs rollout distillation on self-generated histories. We further propose PairedStateBench, a paired benchmark for fine-grained interaction control. BoxWorld substantially outperforms end-to-end world models and remains competitive across multiple public benchmarks. Project page: https://boxworld-web.github.io.
evidence_items.title: BoxWorld: Let World Engines Control and Video Generators Render

evidence_items.summary: How much of zero-shot benchmark accuracy is captured by word-level alignment between a pre-training corpus and the benchmark target? We study this question through word-level unigram cross-entropy (UCE), a tokenizer-agnostic, model-free measure of lexical alignment between a reference corpus and a target benchmark. Likelihood training shapes the model's predictive distribution from the pre-training corpus, and zero-shot scores under likelihood-based evaluation depend in part on the lexical alignment between that corpus and the benchmark target. Cleanly tracing how the lexical imprint of pre-training data scales with corpus--benchmark alignment requires controlled from-scratch pre-training that varies corpus identity while holding the training recipe fixed. Across this controlled sweep, spanning 10 zero-shot benchmarks, 4 pre-training corpora, and 3 model scales, we find that corpus--benchmark lexical alignment, UCE, consistently tracks zero-shot accuracy on every benchmark, with corpora more aligned with the benchmark (lower UCE) achieving higher accuracy. The same signal extends from measurement to control at finer scopes. At the document level, strengthening the imprint by selecting training documents to maximize lexical alignment with the benchmark produces the accuracy gains predicted by the mechanism. At the prompt level, matching the imprint per prompt by routing each prompt to the drafter whose domain corpus is most lexically aligned with it produces measurable throughput gains over a generalist-drafter baseline. Taken together, pre-training corpora leave a measurable lexical imprint on base-model zero-shot behavior, and UCE provides a model-free probe of lexical alignment between reference and target data.
evidence_items.title: The Lexical Imprint of Pre-training Data

evidence_items.summary: Background The accurate detection of clinical symptoms in electronic health records (EHRs) is pivotal for advancing large-scale genetic and longitudinal studies in psychiatry. Free-text clinical notes are an essential source of symptom-level information, particularly in psychiatry; however, the automated extraction of symptoms from clinical text remains challenging. Objective We aimed to evaluate the ability of open-source generative large language models (LLMs) to detect psychiatric symptom-level concepts from clinical text in Spanish and to develop a new fine-tuned, open-source LLM that can be shared without risk of exposing patient information. Methods We tested 11 open-source generative LLMs for their ability to detect 109 psychiatric concepts from clinical text, using annotated EHR notes from a psychiatric hospital in Colombia. The LLMs were evaluated both “out-of-the-box” and after fine-tuning and compared against a traditional natural language processing (tNLP) method developed from the same data. To develop a fine-tuned LLM that can be shared without risk of exposing patient information, we created a novel synthetic dataset, leveraging real concept annotations while generating fully synthetic clinical text, and fine-tuned a top-performing LLM on these data. Fine-tuned model generalizability was assessed through cross-site evaluation using data from a second independent hospital in Colombia. Results We show that while base LLM performance was poor to moderate (zero-shot: 0.2-0.6 macro-F1; few-shot: 0.2-0.74 macro-F1), it improved significantly after fine-tuning (0.75-0.86 macro-F1), with several fine-tuned LLMs outperforming the tNLP method. In total, 100 psychiatric concepts could be reliably detected (F1>0.8) using either a fine-tuned LLM or tNLP.
evidence_items.title: Generative Large Language Models for Psychiatric Concept Detection in Spanish-Language Electronic Health Records: Development and Evaluation Study

evidence_items.summary: Proactive bug discovery is an important software-engineering problem. Even though coding agents are already widely deployed in this domain, their capabilities remain understudied. In particular, the challenging task of finding all bugs that human maintainers would repair across an entire repository has not been studied yet. To close this gap, we introduce PROBE, a benchmark consisting of all 2,457 bugs fixed over the course of 18 months across 20 diverse GitHub repositories, together with a method for matching candidate findings to this partial reference set. We evaluate coding agents across frontier models and find they all achieve a recall of below $21\%$ and a precision of less than $9\%$ with respect to the reference set. While stronger models increase recall substantially from $8\%$ to $17\%$, they do not improve precision. Surprisingly, despite the low precision, LLM and human evaluators still judge $85\%$ of findings valid. Crucially, we find that found bug distributions are similar across agents but differ substantially from those of bugs fixed by maintainers. The practical relevance of bug discovery and the low recall of frontier models make this benchmark a valuable resource for both model users and developers.
evidence_items.title: PROBE: Frontier Coding Agents Find Different Bugs Than Maintainers Fix

evidence_items.summary: Game development stresses coding agents in ways general software engineering does not: correctness depends on how engine APIs, serialized scene state, and runtime behavior interact, not on source code alone. Existing benchmarks mainly target platforms such as Godot and heavily rely on LLM judges or coarse task-level outcomes. We present UnityBench-Mini3D, a benchmark of 77 project-level Unity tasks organized around seven expert-defined skill categories rather than tutorials or genres, with three difficulty tiers. Each task pairs a complete Unity project with natural-language requirements and is evaluated using 1,178 held-out, human-authored milestone tests covering scene structure, component configuration, and runtime behavior. This in-engine evaluation provides deterministic partial credit, localizes failures, and distinguishes partial implementations from complete solutions without relying on subjective judges. Across 21 models and 9 coding harnesses, the average pass rate reaches 80.9% on easy tasks but falls to 35.2% on hard tasks, with just 57.7% overall. UnityBench-Mini3D provides a reproducible, diagnostic testbed distinguishing systems across difficulty levels.
evidence_items.title: UnityBench-Mini3D: Evaluating LLM Agents for 3D Game Development in Unity

evidence_items.summary: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) are increasingly expected to assist users while observing continuous audiovisual streams. However, existing evaluations provide limited insight into how reliably these models connect stream evidence and user needs to timely, sustained interventions. We introduce Omni-InteractScope, a benchmark of 1,479 human-annotated, cross-reviewed interactions with 1,790 temporal targets across eight task groups. It links input modalities, event triggers, intervention types, and user needs, covering event-timed tool invocation and query-free assistance alongside notifications, warnings, state tracking, and continuous responses. Our experimental results on the proposed benchmark reveal three critical limitations of current Omni-LLMs: (1) Timely tool invocation remains unreliable: all 12 evaluated models produce an on-time first response for at most 40\% of tool-invocation targets, and joint timing-and-tool accuracy reaches at most 32.0\%. (2) Query-free reminders remain poorly covered: all evaluated models achieve lower timely reference-target recall on query-free reminders than on explicit questions, measured on their respective target sets. Reminder recall never exceeds 23.0\%. (3) End-to-end guidance coverage remains limited: nine models cover none of the 26 guidance sequences in full, and the remaining three cover only one to three sequences each. Targeted controls further show that tool-invocation scores alone do not establish event grounding and that reminder coverage depends on response history and frequency. These findings motivate developing and evaluating streaming assistants for timely action, initiative under general user needs, and coverage of entire response sequences.
evidence_items.title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams

evidence_items.summary: AI agents must decide when another search is worth its cost. Answer-success probabilities capture question difficulty, while this decision requires estimating the additional benefit of search. We introduce SearchHorizonBench, a benchmark for learning and evaluating search value from execution experience. Paired continuations and repeated executions separate expected search gain from generation noise and connect prediction quality to decision utility. The resource contains 45,632 executions across 3,168 questions. On 1,632 held-out questions, historical calibration reduces Brier error by 16.2%, with the improvement concentrated in success-level information. Search gains have a standard deviation of 21.4 percentage points, and tested historical estimators explain less than 2% of this variance in point estimates. Matched-configuration learning curves probe this distinction across training scales. At the reference token price, free selection observations yield a 2.49-point utility opportunity over the best constant action, driven primarily by gain information. Reusable histories, frozen splits, strong baselines and scoring tools provide a common foundation for developing and evaluating value-aware search agents.
evidence_items.title: SearchHorizonBench: A Benchmark for Search Value in AI Agents

evidence_items.summary: An agent that truly knows and acts on behalf of its user has been a long-standing promise of AI assistants. Computer-use agents bring this promise within reach by capably executing fully specified tasks across apps. However, real-world user requests are often underspecified. To act correctly for the particular user, an agent must infer some missing information from the user's activity history and ask for other information that only the user can provide, without making unsupported assumptions or burdening the user with unnecessary questions. We present iPrefBench, a benchmark for evaluating the infer and ask capabilities of personal mobile-use agents in an executable iOS environment with an interactive simulated user. Grounded in a coherent persona with 3,051 past activity events, iPrefBench comprises 130 underspecified user tasks across 26 apps. Each omitted user-dependent requirement is, by construction, either history-inferable or ask-only. iPrefBench evaluates personalized mobile agents on both whether agents complete tasks correctly for the user (i.e., personalized task completion) and whether they seek user input when necessary (i.e., user-agent interaction). Evaluation of 7 frontier agents reveals a substantial gap between execution and personalization. Agents achieve high action completion scores (up to 91.6%) but low full task success (up to 47.7%) because personalization lags behind. They especially struggle with ask-only information, failing to request enough necessary information. Our findings highlight a challenge for personalized agents in knowing what to infer and when to ask. We hope that iPrefBench can serve as a valuable testbed for building agents that know their user and work with them.
evidence_items.title: iPrefBench: A User-Centric Benchmark for Personalized Mobile Use Agents

evidence_items.summary: Language model agents often abandon correct work when a user challenges it, yet simply telling them to stand firm makes them ignore real mistakes. Once an agent reads a complaint, it tends to discount its own earlier checks in order to agree with the user. We introduce Thinking-in-Bets, a training-free method in which an agent writes a short private record of its main claims, the checks supporting them, and its confidence before reading user feedback. When challenged, the agent consults this Claim Checklist to keep verified work intact while investigating uncertain or newly challenged parts. We evaluate five Gemini models (3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.5 Flash, 3.6 Flash, 3.8 Flash, and 4.0 Argon) across eight benchmarks: SWE-Together, SWE-Interact, and DeepSWE for software engineering, Agents' Last Exam for professional reports, Humanity's Last Exam and SycEval for academic reasoning, Vals Finance for financial analysis, and Terminal-Bench for command-line tasks. Recording claims before criticism nearly eliminates false reversals in patch review and protects passing report drafts under mistaken pushback, whereas writing the same record after reading the complaint recovers very little of the gain. In multi-turn coding, pre-reply claim records substantially reduce unnecessary file edits after mistaken complaints, and gating the record so it is written only when the agent is uncertain lowers token overhead while fixing more real bugs than the baseline. Even in non-interactive tasks without user feedback, listing the key claims in a draft and re-checking the weakest one before submission improves both answer accuracy and confidence estimates across all tested models.
evidence_items.title: Thinking-in-Bets at Test Time Reduces Sycophantic Revisions in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Embodied agents are expected to accomplish real-world goals by deciding for themselves how and when to interact with their surroundings. For many such goals, changing the physical state of the world is the means rather than the end: the agent changes the state of a system through interaction, observes the feedback, and explores until it either achieves the goal itself (e.g., discovering physical laws) or learns what the goal requires; it acts to know. Manipulation benchmarks stop at acting to change, with the target state given; scientific discovery benchmarks evaluate knowing but replace physical experimentation with symbolic actions or numerical queries. We introduce EmbodiedLab, a benchmark in which a robot must act to know. Quantitative science experiments make this setting controllable: the parameters of the system are resampled for every instance, so the result cannot be known in advance, yet it can be scored exactly. Across 30 experiments in five disciplines on 14 apparatus platforms, the agent receives an objective and the apparatus, chooses its own procedure, and operates a physics-based simulated laboratory, reading the instruments through its cameras. Evaluation checks what the agent came to know, grounded in readings recorded during the episode, as well as the physical state the task requires; every experiment is verified to be solvable. We evaluate six frontier models in their developers' coding agents with native observation and control, with added perception and motion planning, and with manipulation skills distilled from the strongest agents. With native control, even the strongest agent succeeds less than half the time; for every agent, most failures arise in interacting with the apparatus, and manipulation skills help weaker agents more than perception and planning. The benchmark and its evaluation code are available at https://github.com/HexaFuture/EmbodiedLab.
evidence_items.title: EmbodiedLab: Benchmarking Embodied Agents That Act to Know

evidence_items.summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires an agentic system to design, train, and evaluate its own successor. Data-driven post-training is a central part of that loop, yet existing evaluations measure it on a single benchmark, where an agent selects from a static pool or distills a stronger model to push one score up in one run. Real post-training is multi-domain, and a gain in one domain has to be weighed against a regression in another. We propose ParetoRSI-Gym, in which an agent searches for data, curates it, trains, reads back per-domain results, and repeats, with everything but the data held fixed: the initial LLM, the five domains (math, code, finance, medicine, science), the toolset, and the SFT pipeline. Generalization benchmarks in each domain separate capability gains from overfitting to the scores the agent optimizes against. Across three agent systems, three base models, five rounds and multiple seeds, the strongest system, Claude Code with Opus-5, raises the generalization scores of its proxy-best checkpoint by 9.2% relative to the starting model (+2.3 absolute points), averaged with equal weight over three base models and five domains, with a single-domain relative gain of up to 63% (medicine on Ministral-3-3B). Further analysis shows that the harness matters as much as the model it drives, and that each agent keeps a unique data selection strategy. We see our work as a step towards evaluation of RSI systems in real-world machine learning engineering.
evidence_items.title: ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?

evidence_items.summary: Multi-agent systems often rely on predefined collaboration structures, limiting their ability to adapt to diverse task requirements. We introduce DynaFlow, a framework that integrates free-form executable workflow synthesis into the action space of the main agent. The agent decides when collaboration is needed and generates task-specific programs that coordinate sub-agents through sequential or parallel execution, structured information exchange, and verification. Execution results and traces inform subsequent actions, enabling the agent to adapt collaboration as reasoning progresses. We train only the main agent through supervised fine-tuning on distilled trajectories, followed by refinement on examples filtered for unsupported premises, biased verification, and information-flow defects. All sub-agents remain fixed, separating orchestration learning from executor capability improvement. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and multi-hop retrieval, DynaFlow achieves 88.08% overall accuracy in Forced mode, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 10.90 percentage points with the same Qwen3.5-27B backbone. Workflow analysis finds more explicit use, verification, and refinement of upstream outputs after training, highlighting cross-stage information flow as a key dimension of multi-agent orchestration.
evidence_items.title: DynaFlow: Learning Free-Form Multi-Agent Orchestration

evidence_items.summary: In this paper, we introduce Δτ-Bench, an executable agent benchmark that models the structural evolution of large tool ecosystems. In Δτ-Bench, independently evolving services continually reshape how tasks can be accomplished: familiar tools may disappear or be replaced, while more efficient alternatives emerge amid overlapping functionality and noisy documentation. Against this moving capability frontier, we evaluate whether agents can proactively discover efficient tool-use paths and promptly revise their accumulated procedural knowledge, bringing together demands that existing benchmarks fail to examine. Δτ-Bench comprises 1,588 validated multi-turn tasks across 42 domains and six successive ecosystem states generated through capability-preserving transformations. Our evaluation shows that even the strongest evaluated model or harness achieves only 42.3% task success, while initial gains from existing skill-learning methods can not consistently translate into better adaptation as the ecosystem evolves. These findings motivate Steward, an ecosystem manager that jointly manages tools and procedural knowledge through incremental skill maintenance and dynamic provisioning during task execution. Experiments show that Steward sustains higher task success across ecosystem changes with lower skill-maintenance overhead, while improving both recovery from disrupted workflows and adoption of more efficient alternatives.
evidence_items.title: Δτ-Bench: Pushing Agents Toward a Moving Capability

evidence_items.summary: Can AI agents autonomously train useful language models and improve them using feedback from users? We introduce RSI Arena, a two-stage study of autonomous post-training as a step toward recursive self-improvement. Ten frontier models act as training agents, each starting from NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Base. During a six-day first stage, each agent has 1,000 GPU-hours and $300 in API credit on a shared 64-GPU cluster, independently selecting data, implementing training procedures, and choosing checkpoints. We evaluate their models on 20 benchmarks and through blind human evaluations. All ten agents produce working assistants, with the strongest model, trained by GPT-6 Astra, closing a median of 76% of the base-to-Instruct gap across 12 capability benchmarks. Its human-preference rating is also close to NVIDIA Instruct after statistical adjustment for answer length and formatting. In Stage 2, each agent receives the comparison records and votes involving its Stage 1 model and is given three additional days for further training. Using NVIDIA Instruct as a common reference across the two evaluation rounds, we observe an improvement from Stage 1 to Stage 2 in the style-adjusted relative rating of eight of the ten models. We show that benchmark gains were modest, with no clear link to preference gains, while some agents encouraged longer responses and one model showed increased harmful compliance on StrongREJECT. RSI Arena provides an auditable setting for studying how human feedback can guide autonomous model development. It takes a step toward recursive self-improvement with human feedback (RSIHF), in which people help define what improvement means for the AI systems they use.
evidence_items.title: RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement with Human Feedback

evidence_items.summary: Deploying language agents in real applications demands more than the right answer: an agent must execute a multi-step business process correctly, follow domain-specific rules, and interact with a user across a dialogue, where the gap between saying and doing is the gap between a satisfied customer and a real loss. We argue that a deployable-agent benchmark should jointly assess four facets: the outcome an agent reaches, the trajectory it takes, its operational viability, and its policy compliance. Customer relationship management (CRM), where mutable records meet operational rules and consequential effects, exercises all four. We introduce CRM-Agent-Bench, an execution-grounded benchmark of 555 stateful, multi-turn tasks across nine business domains and 36 capability tags. Each task supplies a task-specific executable contract drawn from checks over actions, arguments, order, response, target state, and protected state; success is the strict conjunction of the checks declared for that task. We evaluate the complete agent system through these contracts and report scored coverage, latency, and cost. Across sixteen systems evaluated on the audited final release, strict success spans 64.32% to 83.60%; the closely grouped leading systems nonetheless diverge sharply in cost and per-domain reliability. CRM-Agent-Bench offers an auditable framework for measuring contract-grounded business-transaction integrity and adherence to task-declared benchmark policies, with a portable structure designed for extension as models improve. Github repository: https://github.com/salesforce-misc/crm-agent-bench
evidence_items.title: CRM-Agent-Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Using Agents in Stateful Enterprise Environments

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents are increasingly used to solve real-world problems, and their effectiveness depends on both the underlying models and the harnesses that support their operation. However, most existing benchmarks focus on model capabilities and overall agent performance, with limited attention to the evaluation of agent harnesses. To address this gap, we introduce TraceTrial-Bench, which organizes harness reliability into seven components covering context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, and verification. We construct 95 expert-level, mechanism-oriented tasks with executable or state-based ground truth to support semantically equivalent comparisons while preserving the native behavior of each harness. We design a Trajectory Tracing (TT) module to capture agent execution traces and introduce a two-layer evaluation framework that separately assesses agent performance and harness reliability. In addition, we design a Multi-source Evidence Acquisition (MEA) module to provide evidence from the agent context, harness, and execution environment for LLM-based evaluation, and develop a Failure Attribution (FA) module that uses explicit mechanism chains to support attribution at the run level. Across 4 harnesses, 9 models, and 95 tasks, our evaluation of 3,420 runs yields macro-averaged harness scores ranging from 59.8% to 72.0%, while 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion. TraceTrial-Bench provides an auditable and reproducible foundation for comparing agent harnesses, diagnosing their failures, and studying how harness design interacts with model behavior.
evidence_items.title: Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution

evidence_items.summary: Large language models have shown outstanding performance on text-first tasks such as coding, math, and writing. Recent efforts are shifting models' training to include scientific problems that often live in highly specialized domains beyond text, such as protein structure and biological images. However, in these scenarios, their general-purpose accuracy compared with specialized algorithms remains in question. One such domain is cell tracking, which requires spatiotemporal awareness of cell dynamics. To evaluate this, we created a new benchmark, CellTrack-Bench, which assesses Vision-Language Models' (VLMs) cell-tracking-related performance against specialized trackers. The full benchmark draws from 15 standard cell-tracking datasets across four imaging modalities and comprises 1,537 problems corresponding to 9,041 cell-linking decisions. We selected a hard subset requiring greater reasoning effort by identifying failures shared across distinct algorithmic trackers. With this proposed dataset, we: (i) evaluated different environment harnesses for VLMs; (ii) benchmarked 9 frontier closed-source models and 13 open-weight models; and (iii) provided a detailed analysis of their failure modes. Code, the stored model outputs, and a pipeline that regenerates the benchmark from the source datasets are available at https://github.com/royerlab/celltrack-bench.
evidence_items.title: CellTrack-Bench: Microscopic Cell Tracking Benchmark for Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under the MIT license at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.
evidence_items.title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents

evidence_items.summary: This dataset supports the study “Oryzentra: Design and Evaluation of an Agricultural Information System for Traceable Decisions and Execution Verification.” It contains 4,494 records and 101 data fields in a single worksheet: 4,320 workflow decision evaluations covering 720 factorial scenarios across six implementation variants, 120 runtime measurements, 48 robustness probes, and six illustrative dashboard records. The workbook includes reference-policy outcomes, release and closure decisions, workflow-control configurations, trace-integrity indicators, robustness results, and serial in-process execution times. Metadata, a variable dictionary, and formula-based summaries are included in the same worksheet. Workflow scenarios use generated synthetic inputs to evaluate the reference implementation. Dashboard values are illustrative rather than field-validated observations. Runtime measurements exclude network communication, database access, interface rendering, high-performance computing workloads, and AI inference. The dataset supports examination of workflow conformance and the reported evaluation results; it does not establish production readiness or agronomic effectiveness.
evidence_items.title: Oryzentra Workflow Evaluation Dataset: Decision Conformance, Trace Integrity, Robustness, and Runtime

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Large language model (LLM) benchmarking in clinical medicine is increasingly reliant on LLM-based assessment frameworks; in these systems, one AI scores the outputs of another. This practice relies on the assumptions of evaluator neutrality and rubric consistency. These assumptions have not been empirically tested in clinical fields. Objective In this study, we aim to directly examine these assumptions by using the PARM (Planning-Action-Reflection-Memory) framework as a theoretical lens to characterize endovascular device selection and clinical reflective reasoning as a clinical field. Methods We developed a scoring rubric (C1-C6) with 40 clinical vignettes and 6 criteria across 5 endovascular fields (peripheral artery disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm, chronic venous insufficiency, coronary in-stent restenosis [ISR], and cerebrovascular/neuroendovascular; 8 vignettes per field). Four LLMs were evaluated as clinical decision support systems: GPT-4o (M1), Claude Sonnet 4.6 (M2), Gemini 1.5 Pro (M3), and Llama 3.3 70B (M4). Two LLMs served as independent raters with the same evaluation criteria: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (rater 1) and GPT-4o (rater 2). The rater identity was intentionally disclosed; the primary research question concerned rater scoring behavior rather than the absolute performance of the model. Human assessment was intentionally excluded because its inclusion would have shifted the study question from rater disagreement to rater accuracy, a distinct and secondary question. Interrater reliability was measured using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC 2,1) two-way random effects modeling. Results The combined ICC(2,1) was 0.153 (95% CI 0.007‐0.295). In this exploratory study, the low ICC was not distributed randomly: the magnitude of score differences varied across models (M2 Δ=+5, M4 Δ=+31, M1 Δ=−46, and M3 Δ=−158 points).
evidence_items.title: Systematic Scoring Differences in Large Language Model–Based Clinical Benchmarking Reveal Evaluator-Dependent Divergence: Controlled Evaluation Study

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a promising tool for automatic generation and optimization of high-performance compute kernels. This rapidly growing area spans across hardware platforms and targets programming models such as AscendC, CUDA, and Triton. However, the literature remains fragmented, with substantial variation in generation workflows, training strategies, evaluation protocols, benchmark assumptions, hardware platforms, and reported metrics. This survey provides a structured review of LLM-based automatic kernel generation. We introduce a taxonomy based on the generation-time workflow, separating direct generation, refinement via structured feedback, search-based generation, and adaptive tool-orchestrating agentic systems. We further analyze orthogonal design axes including learning strategy, input representation, output representation, and hardware platform. Beyond method classification, we examine evaluation practices, including benchmark data, harnesses, integrity policies, as well as performance metrics, and discuss why reported results are often difficult to compare. Finally, we use Ascend NPU kernel generation as a cross-platform case study, highlighting challenges introduced by AscendC, host-device co-design, toolchain constraints, and limited public data. We conclude by identifying open problems in robust evaluation, higher-level task optimization, cross-platform transfer, production deployment, and benchmark design.
evidence_items.title: Automatic Kernel Generation with Large Language Models: Taxonomies, Evaluations, and Cross-Platform Challenges

evidence_items.summary: Agricultural drought represents a devastating threat to food security and agropastoral livelihoods across Africa. While recent machine learning (ML) literature demonstrates high continuous correlation in regional drought forecasting, the overwhelming majority of existing frameworks evaluate models within the same geographical catchment using random or chronologically shuffled cross-validation. Consequently, the operational behavior of drought forecasting models under severe geographic distribution shift remains critically under-characterized. In this study, we present a reproducible, continental-scale, low-resource benchmarking framework evaluating ten forecasting architectures across six major African agricultural basins: the Nile River Basin, Sahelian Agropastoral Belt, Zambezi-Limpopo Basin, Maghreb Zone, Congo Agricultural Transition, and Horn of Africa, over a 44-year observational record (1981-2024) using 100% real CHIRPS v2.0 and ERA5-Land satellite and reanalysis data. Our key findings: (1) spatial domain shift degrades forecasting accuracy by +6.4% to +17.2% MAE; (2) uncalibrated models exhibit catastrophic event-detection failures despite high continuous correlation; (3) a modest 25% local historical calibration budget recovers over 50% of the lost transfer skill; and (4) all improvements are statistically significant (p < 0.05) while consuming less than 15 MB RAM. These results establish parsimonious, probability-calibrated ensemble architectures as a scientifically rigorous, computationally democratic foundation for regional drought early warning in resource-constrained environments.
evidence_items.title: Reliable Early Prediction of Agricultural Drought Under Geographic Shift: A Continental Low-Resource Benchmark for Data-Sparse African Basins

evidence_items.summary: Camera traps are a key tool for non-invasive wildlife monitoring, yet models trained on existing benchmarks often generalize poorly to new regions due to domain shift, class imbalance, and natural variability in illumination, season, and background. We introduce PACTraD, a benchmark of 116,973 annotated camera trap images collected in a protected area of the Baikal region across eight classes (deer, no animals, bear, boar, hare, badger, lynx, wolf), with a pronounced long-tailed distribution (deer: 73.1%; lynx and wolf: 0.3% and 0.2%) and substantial seasonal and lighting variability, including infrared night imagery. The benchmark supports three tasks under a unified, reproducible protocol: classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. We further propose a domain-specific attention mechanism augmenting self-attention with eleven learnable priors capturing contour, foreground/background separation, bilateral symmetry, discriminative part regions, texture frequency, confidence weighting, motion consistency, gradient enhancement, scale, color invariance, and shape compactness. Evaluated on six backbones for classification and detection and five for segmentation, against no-attention baselines and three generic attention modules (SE, SA, CBAM), it consistently performs best, raising weighted F1 for classification from 0.943 to 0.964 (DINOv3), AP50 for detection from 0.876 to 0.903 (InternImage-H), and mIoU for segmentation from 0.805 to 0.834 (SegMAN), with component-level ablations revealing task-specific contributions of each prior. However, performance on rare species remains limited (macro F1: 0.829 for classification), indicating that further research is needed to address long-tail recognition in camera trap data.
evidence_items.title: PACTraD: Multi-Task Benchmark and Domain-Specific Attention Mechanism for Wildlife Classification, Detection, and Segmentation in Protected Area Camera Trap Data

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Restricted access to claim-level records and confirmed fraud labels limits reproducible healthcare anti-fraud research. We present a relational, longitudinal synthetic benchmark in which “Japan-calibrated” means that selected demographic, utilization, provider, coding, and reimbursement dimensions are constrained by documented Japanese public or aggregate references; it does not imply equivalence to Japanese claim microdata. Clinical trajectories, provider identities, fraud mechanisms, event rates, and claim labels are generated by design. After removing a model-visible target-proxy channel from episode semantics, we generated a new precommitted seed-202611 scenario. Model family and hyperparameters were selected by nested temporal cross-validation on development data using injected amount recovered at a 1% review budget; Platt calibration and the operating threshold were fitted on a separate pre-final interval. The frozen LightGBM pipeline was then evaluated once on 53,609 final-period claims containing 1573 designed positives. Non-interpolated average precision was 0.8403 (95% bootstrap confidence interval 0.8266–0.8545), receiver-operating-characteristic area under the curve was 0.9764, Brier score was 0.01509, and expected calibration error was 0.03375. Reviewing the top 1% selected 537 true positives with no false positives, recall 0.3414, and JPY 128,752,597 in injected amount recovered. Corrected five-seed and designed-scenario results are reported separately as diagnostic evidence because their final partitions had prior access. This is an internal synthetic confirmation, not real-claims validation; the study does not establish Japanese fraud prevalence, claim-level realism, production performance, or deployment readiness.
evidence_items.title: A Japan-calibrated synthetic medical claims benchmark for anti-fraud machine learning
