evidence_items.summary: Polygenic risk scores (PRSs) have improved substantially in predictive performance, yet results remain difficult to compare across studies that differ in cohorts, phenotype definitions, and evaluation procedures. Comparison to machine-learning methods is harder still, since their performance depends strongly on how data are partitioned and whether related individuals leak across splits. Here, we introduce a family-aware benchmark for polygenic prediction built on version 9 of the All of Us Research Program (AoU). The benchmark assigns entire family components to fixed discovery, calibration, and test partitions, reserves first-degree relatives for within-family evaluation, and separates models trained only on AoU discovery data from those using external GWAS summary statistics. This enables direct comparison between conventional PRS pipelines and machine-learning models trained under identical data budgets. We report results for 14 binary disease traits. Our strongest scores explain 5.7-24.9% of liability-scale variance, with particularly strong prediction for Alzheimer's disease, type 2 diabetes, prostate cancer, glaucoma, and inflammatory bowel disease, and match or exceed published commercial and academic scores for most traits. Across 12 traits with interpretable within-family estimates of within-sibship-to-population effect ratio, 11 confidence intervals included a ratio of 1. Type 2 diabetes showed an attenuation ratio of 0.86 [0.76, 0.97].
evidence_items.title: A family-aware All of Us benchmark for polygenic prediction and genomic machine learning

organizations: Department of Informatics, Ionian University, Plateia Tsirigoti 7, 49100 Corfu, Greece
evidence_items.summary: Market-surveillance authorities face a growing volume of digital marketing content spanning video, social-media, influencer, and AI-generated or synthetic media, whose compliance with EU consumer and digital law cannot be assessed manually at scale. We present a deployed decision-support system that screens marketing campaigns against the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, the General Data Protection Regulation, the Digital Services Act and the AI Act using large language model agents grounded in a curated legal knowledge graph. The system enforces closed-world citation grounding: findings may reference only provisions retrieved from the graph, are validated against it, and are anchored to authentic legal text through CELLAR and ELIs. Around the engine, we build a regulator-in-the-loop calibration methodology combining a human-reviewed gold benchmark of 52 campaigns, an adversarial adjudicator for disputed citations, and a distillation step that converts confirmed errors into human-approved calibration rules. On the frozen benchmark, the deployed configuration recovered 95 of 97 must-find provisions on first-run scoring, met the minimum risk level in 51 of 52 campaigns, missed no gold-relevant routing, and produced one false positive across seven compliant controls. On a pre-designated 15-campaign holdout, calibration reduced unexpected actionable findings from 44 to 5 (11 of 15 campaigns improved, none worsened; exact Wilcoxon p < 0.001) while preserving 1.000 provision recall and 15/15 risk calibration, and improved run-to-run stability from 0.745 to 0.833. Compared to three external single-call baselines with the same closed provision vocabulary (GPT-5.4, GPT-5.6 and the open-weights gpt-oss-120b), the agentic pipeline achieved significantly higher recall (0.979 vs.
evidence_items.title: Regulator-in-the-Loop Compliance Screening: Graph-Grounded LLM Agents with a Continuously Calibrated Benchmark for EU Marketing Law

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used in manufacturing to design products, plan production, diagnose faults and operate equipment, but their designs and evaluations remain difficult to compare. We analyse 164 studies identified through Scopus, Web of Science and IEEE Xplore to examine manufacturing applications, agentic system designs and evaluation practices, and to identify where evaluation coverage falls short of the evidence that these task and design types would require. We propose taxonomies of applications, agentic designs and evaluation practices, and relate task and design characteristics to the evidence required to assess them. The findings reveal an imbalance between assessing output quality and verifying whether outputs satisfy manufacturing requirements. For planning and decision-making systems, executability and constraint compliance receive limited evaluation, while most evidence comes from offline data or simulation. Limited assessment of safety, stability across repeated runs and performance in industrial settings leaves a gap between demonstrated task performance and evidence of reliable operation under manufacturing conditions. The resulting taxonomies and evidence requirements help researchers select evaluations suited to each manufacturing use case and distinguish demonstrated task performance from evidence of reliable operation.
evidence_items.title: LLM-Based Agentic AI in Manufacturing: A Scoping Review of Applications, System Designs and Evaluation Practices

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Automated history-taking in telemedicine has to collect a structured record of a patient’s complaint over many turns while adapting to what the patient answers. MedAgent-RAG is a multi-agent system, implemented as a LangGraph state graph, which keeps an explicit clinical state the slots gathered so far, a ranked differential diagnosis, the questions already asked, the red flags detected, and the current questioning phase, and selects every question as a function of that state, before grounding its final assessment in clinical guidelines retrieved by a parent–child retrieval-augmented pipeline. Evaluated on the MediTOD corpus with a language-model patient simulator, the system raises BERTScore F1 from 0.68 to 0.84 over a single-shot baseline. Beyond that system description, we study history-taking itself as a network problem. From 231 annotated interviews, we build a bipartite network of symptoms and differential diagnoses whose links are statistically validated against a hypergeometric null model, its one-mode projections, and questioning-flow networks over the topics physicians ask about. The knowledge network separates into 8 syndromic modules (bipartite modularity 0.70, z = 5.4) and is less nested than a degree-preserving null model (z = −6.4): the knowledge an interview must cover is compartmentalised rather than hierarchical. Frequent symptoms such as cough and dyspnoea bridge those modules and carry little information about the differential, whereas rarer findings such as haemoptysis, dysphagia and weight loss carry most of it. Physician questioning separates into two phases: a clinical history followed by a social, family, and exposure history, and a first-order Markov model over topics is the most parsimonious description of how physicians move between them. We discuss what these results imply for the design of language-model interviewers.
evidence_items.title: MedAgent-RAG: an agentic retrieval-augmented system for adaptive clinical history-taking, with a network analysis of medical interviews

evidence_items.summary: Advanced monitoring technologies provide increasingly detailed information about the condition of cultural heritage assets. However, their practical value depends on how effectively this information can be interpreted and used by heritage managers and authorities, who may lack specialised expertise in the underlying technologies. Moving beyond data collection and technical analysis towards accessible information and informed decision-making is therefore a key challenge in digital cultural heritage management. This work presents the ARGUS Intelligence Platform, developed within the Horizon Europe ARGUS project, as a human-centric digital environment designed to bridge the gap between advanced monitoring technologies and the needs of cultural heritage decision-makers. The platform integrates interactive 3D representations of monuments and their surrounding terrain with sensor observations, diagnostic results, Earth Observation products, expert knowledge, and integrated risk assessments. Rather than exposing users to fragmented technical outputs, ARGUS brings heterogeneous information together within a unified visual environment, supporting the exploration and interpretation of monument conditions and potential risks. Particular emphasis is placed on communicating risk assessments alongside the information, assumptions, and uncertainties underlying them, allowing users to examine how different sources contribute to the overall assessment without requiring detailed knowledge of the computational methods involved. By connecting monitoring data, analytical results, and expert knowledge with the practical information needs of heritage managers, ARGUS extends the role of digital twins beyond asset representation and monitoring towards human-centric decision support.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Monitoring: Human-Centric Intelligence for Cultural Heritage Management

evidence_items.summary: This record contains the protocol, search strategies and full review dataset of a scoping review that maps which machine learning models, wearable sensors, reference measures of fatigue and model validation methods have been used to detect fatigue in athletes, physically active people and healthy adults performing exercise, and in which sports. The review follows the JBI methodology for scoping reviews and is reported according to PRISMA-ScR. Elicit, PubMed, IEEE Xplore (searched 21 October 2026), Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection (searched 28 October 2026) were searched for open-access studies published from 2010 onwards. Of 2776 records, 78 studies were included. Retrospective registration. The protocol was drafted on 21 October 2026, before screening, and is deposited after screening, data charting and synthesis. All changes made after the first draft are listed with dates in the change log of the protocol file. Files 00 README.md – description of the record and files 01 protocol and change log.pdf – review protocol with the dated change log 02 TableS2 search strategies.pdf – full search strategies, dates, limits and record counts for all five sources (Supplementary Table S2) 03 review dataset.xlsx – all screening decisions (AI first pass and human verification), full-text decisions with reasons, charted data for the 78 included studies, synthesis coding and summary counts 04 TableS3 included studies.xlsx – characteristics of the 78 included studies (Supplementary Table S3) 05 PRISMA flow diagram.png – PRISMA-ScR flow diagram Use of AI tools. Elicit (Elicit Research PBC) was used for searching, AI-assisted screening and initial data extraction. Claude (Anthropic) was used for first-pass screening of the Scopus and Web of Science records, data extraction for studies Elicit could not retrieve, a consistency check of the charted data and coding of synthesis categories.

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains questionnaire responses collected for a research study entitled “Examining Operations Strategy Adaptation: The Mediating Role of Supply Chain Disruption and the Moderating Role of Organizational Adaptability in the Logistics and Distribution Industry.” The study investigates the relationships between geopolitical risk intensity, cost volatility, logistics disruption, supply chain disruption, and operations strategy adaptation, with organizational adaptability examined as a moderating variable. The data were collected through a structured questionnaire designed to capture respondents’ perceptions and experiences regarding supply chain challenges, operational disruptions, and organizational responses within the logistics and distribution context. The dataset includes recorded survey submission timestamps and responses to the questionnaire items. This dataset is intended to support academic research, statistical analysis, and further investigation into supply chain disruption and operations strategy adaptation. It may be used for examining relationships among the study variables and supporting empirical analysis related to supply chain resilience and organizational adaptability. The dataset is shared to promote research transparency and facilitate the reproducibility of relevant analyses. Users should consider the scope of the questionnaire, the characteristics of the respondents, and the limitations of self-reported survey data when interpreting the results.

evidence_items.summary: Diffuse soil contamination represents a widespread environmental issue, resulting from multiple low-intensity and spatially dispersed sources, including atmospheric deposition, agricultural practices, traffic emissions, and legacy industrial activities. Unlike point source pollution, diffuse contamination lacks a clear spatial origin, requiring methodologies that can integrate measured data with environmental processes. In this case, concentration-based mapping alone is often insufficient to support risk-informed management decisions. This study presents a regional-scale environmental risk assessment framework for diffuse soil contamination, building on the methodological advances introduced in the companion article (Part I) and extending them to spatially distributed pressures. The assessment is expanded to a multicontaminant context, including inorganic and organic compounds, and contaminant concentrations are evaluated against land use–specific regulatory threshold values. Hazard maps are normalized according to the established criterion whereby soils are considered hazardous when concentrations exceed threshold values by one order of magnitude, enabling consistent comparison and aggregation across contaminants. Exposure is modeled through four exposure pathways (groundwater, surface water, direct contact, and air dispersion), and receptor vulnerability is further articulated for groundwater resources, surface waters, protected areas, and human health.
evidence_items.title: Regional risk assessment, Part II: Identification of diffuse soil contamination hotspots

evidence_items.summary: This paper investigates the impact of transmit-to-receive interference leakage on monostatic millimeter-wave sensing, comparing Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) and Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) modulations under practical hardware constraints typical of compact implementations, such as laptops. Transmit-receive leakage fundamentally limits monostatic radar performance when hardware isolation is constrained by physical design. Through comprehensive numerical evaluation with realistic system parameters, we demonstrate that FMCW maintains consistent centimeter-level accuracy across varying isolation levels, while OFDM exhibits strong isolation-dependent degradation at lower isolation values. The performance gap arises from fundamental differences in interference handling: frequency-modulated (e.g., FMCW) approaches exploit beat frequency separation to isolate leakage in a different frequency domain from target echoes, while orthogonal multiplexing (e.g., OFDM) processes both in the same baseband, requiring substantially higher hardware isolation. Systematic validation across a wide isolation range reveals three distinct performance zones and establishes quantitative thresholds for practical system design. The key finding is that interference suppression architecture, rather than signal-to-noise ratio alone, determines monostatic sensing viability in compact implementations. These results provide practical design guidelines for integrated sensing and communication systems (ISAC) operating at millimeter-wave frequencies.
evidence_items.title: Interference Leakage Impact on Monostatic mmWave Sensing: OFDM vs FMCW Performance with Practical Passive Isolation

evidence_items.summary: The deliverable D10.4 presents a comprehensive technical concept for implementing eLTER Data Products within the European Long-Term Ecosystem Research Infrastructure (eLTER RI), developed under the eLTER PLUS project (EU Horizon 2020, Grant No. 871128). It synthesizes workflows from Research Challenges (RCs) in biodiversity loss, biogeochemical cycles, climate-water-food interactions, and socio-ecological systems, drawing on prior deliverables (e.g., D10.2, D10.3) and aligning with the Whole Systems Approach to ensure FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) compliance and interoperability with European data spaces like EOSC and the Green Deal Data Space. The document outlines a Reference Architecture based on Open Groups Architecture Framework TOGAF standard (10 th edition) 1 for modelling end-to-end data lifecycles from raw to FAIR data sources, emphasizing metadata management, persistent identifiers (PIDs), provenance tracking, and governance for reproducibility. Data products are defined as bundled, machine-readable resources following the Data Space Support Centre (DSSC) definition (blueprint draft) 2 , progressing through five processing levels (0-4: raw to modelled outputs). A review of related Research Infrastructures (e.g., ICOS, NEON, EMODnet) highlights multi-level categorizations, FAIR practices, and integration of external data. Stakeholder needs stress harmonized time-series, multi-scale datasets covering climate, soils, hydrology, biodiversity, and socio-economic variables to support integrated analyses and policymaking. eLTER data origins (standard, legacy, third-party) and types (continuous, sample-based, inventory-based, retrieval-based) are detailed, with governance frameworks ensuring quality, transparency, and reusability via ISO 19131-aligned documentation.
evidence_items.title: Technical Concept for Implementation of eLTER Standard Data Products

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Timestral, a family of four time series foundation models for probabilistic forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters. Timestral sets a new state of the art on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, where Timestral-209M and Timestral-123M take the top two places on every metric. We achieve this with three ingredients: Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF), which separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that longer horizons are trained without masking context and each observed value is both a forecast target and context for later forecasts; a covariate framework that natively supports known-future covariates within a causal architecture; and a two-stage pipeline that pretrains exclusively on a diverse, large-scale synthetic corpus before post-training on a mix of real and synthetic data with extended context. This report describes the model design and its benchmark results. Weights for all four models are available on Hugging Face and inference code on GitHub.
evidence_items.title: Timestral

evidence_items.summary: Reliable, high-resolution operational data from com munity mini-grids remain limited, constraining empirical analysis of electricity demand, customer behaviour and system performance in energy-access settings. We present a multi-source operational dataset from 2 4 com munity solar mini-grids in Kenya and Nigeria. The dataset int egrates project and infrastructure characteristics, records for 11,942 customer connections, approximately 471 million smart-meter observations at 15-min resolution, customer payment and financial transactions, historical electricity tariffs, and approximately 2.89 million remote-monitoring observations describing generation, battery storage and other system operating conditions. We also provide a derived 15-min electricity-consumption product that reconstructs consumption across com munication gaps while retaining information on whether individual int er vals were directly observed or reconstructed. We removed direct personal identifiers and pseudonymised customer identifiers to preserve permitted longitudinal linkages across data products. The resulting relational dataset enables analyses of electricity demand, load profiles, payment behaviour, tariff effects, customer characteristics and the int er action between electricity consumption and mini-grid system operation across diverse com munity settings.
evidence_items.title: High-Frequency, Multi-Domain Operational Dataset for Community Solar Mini-Grids in Kenya and Nigeria

evidence_items.summary: Description SynThermFace-Digi2Real is a synthetic heterogeneous face recognition dataset consisting of paired visible (VIS) and synthetic thermal face images for 1000 synthetic identities. For each selected visible image from the Digi2Real dataset, a corresponding synthetic thermal image is generated using the SynThermFace VIS-to-thermal synthesis pipeline. The thermal generation model is based on Qwen-Image-Edit and is adapted using paired real VIS–thermal face images from the MCXFace dataset. The dataset is intended primarily for training and adapting heterogeneous face recognition models across the visible and thermal domains. The SynThermFace-Digi2Real dataset is derived from the Digi2Real synthetic face dataset, which provides photorealistic synthetic visible-spectrum face images with identity labels. A subset of 1000 Digi2Real identities is selected, and the corresponding visible images are used as inputs to the thermal generation pipeline introduced in SynThermFace. The generation model is based on Qwen-Image-Edit and is adapted for VIS-to-thermal face translation using paired visible and thermal images from MCXFace. MCXFace provides spatially and temporally registered real RGB and thermal face images and is introduced in the Prepended Domain Transformer work for heterogeneous face recognition. For every generated thermal image, the corresponding Digi2Real visible image is also included in the dataset, resulting in explicitly paired VIS–thermal samples. The two modalities are stored in separate VIS and THERMAL directories, with one subdirectory per synthetic identity. The filenames preserve the correspondence between modalities. For example, the visible image 1 image 1.jpg corresponds to the synthetic thermal image 1 image 1 nir.jpg . Thus, the corresponding visible image can be obtained by removing the nir suffix from the thermal filename. All samples are stored as .jpg images.
evidence_items.title: SynThermFace

evidence_items.summary: Abstract: Climate change poses increasing risks to agricultural systems in semi-arid regions through rising temperatures, changing rainfall variability, increasing crop-water requirements and growing pressure on groundwater resources. This study assesses potential future climate-related risks to agricultural sustainability in Hisar district, Haryana, using a scenario-based framework that combines the historical climatic context of 1990– 2025 with published CMIP6-informed scenario information under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5. We consider representative future periods to examine how climate-related agricultural risks progress. We translate scenario-based temperature changes into indicative crop-productivity responses using previously established Hisar-specific crop-temperature elasticities for wheat, mustard, cotton, and bajra. The assessment further examines the potential implications of warming and rainfall variability for agricultural water requirements and groundwater stress. Results indicate that wheat exhibits the greatest temperature-related sensitivity among the crops considered, followed by mustard, while cotton and bajra show comparatively lower direct temperature sensitivity. The findings also indicate that rising temperatures may increase evapotranspiration and irrigation needs, potentially intensifying groundwater extraction pressure in areas already experiencing groundwater stress. The study highlights the interconnected nature of climate, crop productivity, and agricultural water security in Hisar. It emphasises the need for heat-resilient crop planning, efficient irrigation, groundwater conservation, and integrated climate– water management. The study provides a district-level scenariobased assessment that can support future climate-resilient agricultural planning and more detailed modelling using highresolution climate, crop-water and groundwater datasets.
evidence_items.title: CMIP6-Informed Climate Change Projections and Their Implications for Agricultural Sustainability in Hisar District, Haryana

evidence_items.summary: PERSEPHONE-WORLDS is a set of Gazebo (Ignition Fortress) simulation worlds of deep and abandoned underground mines, for testing robots and autonomy software without access to a real mine. It runs with ROS 2 Humble on Ubuntu 22.04. The main environment is a textured mesh model of the abandoned Koutzi magnesite mine in Greece, built from structural data and operational input provided by Grecian Magnesite. Five variants are included: the full-scale baseline, a rescaled version with a roughly 2 m by 2 m cross-section for narrow-corridor tests, a version with tunnel deformation, a version with rockfall debris, and one that combines deformation and rockfall. The release also contains a generic mine tunnel, a generic mine with embedded magnesite deposit geometry, and maze, depot and warehouse worlds. The worlds were built to benchmark autonomous navigation in GPS-denied tunnels, multi-robot exploration, risk-aware path planning and traversability analysis, autonomous drilling, and localization and mapping. This archive is a snapshot of the GitHub repository at commit e19f36f; the repository will receive further environments over the course of the project. Developed within the PERSEPHONE project, funded by the European Union's Horizon Europe research and innovation programme under Grant Agreement No. 101138451.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objectives Child-bicyclist crash-severity data are strongly imbalanced, making ordinary accuracy potentially misleading. This study compared three tabular deep-learning models with machine learning and statistical reference models under a train–validation–test design. Methods The analysis used 2394 Texas child-bicyclist crashes from 2017 to 2022 classified as killed or incapacitating injury (KA), possible or non-incapacitating injury (BC), or other/no injury (O). The original records were partitioned before feature selection, preprocessing, and imbalance treatment into training ( n = 1454), validation ( n = 475), and untouched test ( n = 465) sets. Random Forest and XGBoost rankings were calculated using the training partition only, yielding a common 10-predictor input. Validation performance was used to select class weighting for XGBoost and training-only Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTEN) for the three deep-learning models. The final primary-model estimates were averaged across five seeds. Results Adaptive Relation-Modeling (ARM)-Net had the highest primary-model accuracy (0.662 ± 0.020) and macro-F1 (0.335 ± 0.011); XGBoost had the highest primary-model balanced accuracy (0.340 ± 0.008); and FT-Transformer had the highest primary-model macro-ROC-AUC (0.540 ± 0.006). However, the dummy-majority accuracy was 0.787 because BC dominated the test set and multinomial logistic regression exceeded all four primary models in balanced accuracy (0.378), macro ROC−AUC (0.561), and macro average precision (0.361). Minority-class discrimination was weak, bootstrap intervals overlapped substantially, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) rankings showed limited stability relative to cross-seed permutation importance. Conclusions Class-balanced performance was limited across all models.
evidence_items.title: Predicting Child-Bicyclist Crash Severity Under Severe Class Imbalance: A Benchmark of XGBoost and Tabular Deep Learning

evidence_items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. Experiments often see only a coarse two-level signal (a channel open or shut, a motor bound or unbound) produced by a hidden Markov network of unknown size. One model-based way to bound the network's dissipation is to fit the smallest hidden model that reproduces the signal and minimise entropy production over it. This paper shows, with an exact example, that the smallest model can overstate the least possible dissipation even when the signal is known perfectly. For a binary alternating-renewal family P q (0<q<1), three hidden states are the fewest that reproduce the signal, and the exact three-state entropy minimum is (1−q)log(1/q), attained uniquely by the homogeneous driven ring. For every q an explicit finite four-state model reproduces the same complete stationary observed law and dissipates strictly less. At q=1/20 exact rational four- and five-state models have certified costs 2.7730766578…, 2.7659977105… and 2.7469854029…, all below the three-state minimum 2.8459456598…. Over all finite hidden architectures matching only the entrance intensity r, mean complete dwell m and initial dwell density f 0 , the exact entropy infimum is 4r√(1−mf 0 ) artanh√(1−mf 0 ) when 0<mf 0 <1; no finite model attains it. For the benchmark this gives a floor about 108 times the one certified in an earlier Evidence Press candidate. The exact four-state and unrestricted minima remain open. The archive contains the 20-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX source), standard-library exact certificates, supporting checks, numerical discovery records, a bounded prior-art audit, the public review record, a replay driver, semantic negative controls, CI and SHA-256 sums.
evidence_items.title: Hidden architecture and the thermodynamic cost of an exact stochastic signal

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal perception forms the foundation of multimodal intelligence. In particular, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding are two pivotal tasks that underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents. However, synthesizing targeted, high-quality training data for these tasks remains difficult and costly. Our key insight is that these tasks share an underlying capability, which we call connecting evidence: identifying relevant visual facts, binding them to the correct entities, recovering their relations, and composing them into an answer. Crucially, targeted training data are far easier to synthesize for this capability than for these tasks themselves. To strengthen this capability, we propose EvidenceConnect, an easy-to-implement data synthesis framework that uses zoomed views of related regions within a single image to generate questions requiring comparison, aggregation, or chaining of visual evidence. To ensure quality, a reference answer is retained only when independent VLMs agree on it, and region-ablation tests discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions. We then train base VLMs on the resulting data with RLVR, obtaining Zooming without Zooming v2 (ZwZ2). Although the synthesized data are not tailored to any downstream benchmark, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with further gains on embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning. These results establish EvidenceConnect as an effective framework for supervising evidence connection and suggest that strengthening this shared capability leads to more generalizable multimodal perception.
evidence_items.title: Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception

evidence_items.summary: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited. Video world models can capture scene dynamics, yet generating future videos introduces high latency into the control loop. We introduce PDRVLA, whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts physical tokens from vision--language features to condition action generation without online video generation. The module learns through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision through a frozen pretrained video world model. Training relies entirely on publicly available data, expanded through human-to-robot synthesis, subtask annotation, and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotation. Across four simulation benchmarks, PDRVLA achieves success rates of 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin~2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv. Ablations show improved future prediction with world-model supervision and evaluate how subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT training affect action success.
evidence_items.title: PDRVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Physical Dynamics Representations

evidence_items.summary: AI research agents can propose, execute, and improve programs that solve machine learning tasks. However, executing each candidate program requires training and evaluating ML models, limiting how many candidates an agent can explore at each step. We introduce MLE-World, a world model finetuned from Qwen3.5-4B that predicts a program's terminal output (error traces, training logs, and validation scores) from its code and data description without executing it, together with a confidence score estimating the prediction's correctness. Because a prediction costs one inference call rather than a training run, MLE-World makes test time scaling (TTS) affordable for these agents. We build five TTS policies, guided by MLE-World, that compare several candidates per step by their predicted outputs: Sequential revision, Best-of-N, Pairwise judging, Fusion, and a UCB style rule that also adds an exploration bonus from this confidence score. Since predictions can be wrong, we run a candidate for real only when its confidence score is low. On 17 MLE-bench Lite tasks, MLE-World matches the real terminal output on 77.9% of held out programs, versus 41.1% for much larger prompted models. MLE-World guided TTS achieves up to 22.1% higher observed mean performance than the agent without a world model, with less real execution. Project webpage: https://mle-world.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: MLE-World: Predicting Machine Learning Experiment Outcomes with a Learned World Model

evidence_items.summary: Interactive world generation requires models to follow successive commands while preserving relevant history and action consequences. We present Hy-Nomas, a video world model with an 8B diffusion backbone that supports free-form text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple interaction turns. It generates variable-length segments conditioned on current inputs and cached history. Our central design aligns structured video captions with action-aware causal attention: descriptive context remains accessible across segments, while action instructions are restricted to their intended temporal windows. A vision-language Prompt Enhancer (PE) translates user requests and multimodal interaction histories into structured conditions for the next segment. A multi-stage curriculum progressively introduces causal generation, text interaction, camera control, and training on model-generated histories, followed by diffusion distillation. In human evaluation, Hy-Nomas shows superior performance over existing world models. We release model weights, code and benchmarks, together with a lightweight adaptation workflow, to support reproducible research on interactive world generation.
evidence_items.title: Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation

evidence_items.summary: Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question. In a world with altered physical laws, can large language models (LLMs) notice unexpected behavior, such as heavier objects falling more slowly, and discover the law through experiments without being told what to investigate? To evaluate this ability, we introduce LongChang, an automated framework that creates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics. The evaluated LLMs act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to investigate their own questions without research tasks or hints about these laws. Separate LLM agents generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and evaluate reports for correctness and experimental support using the altered physical laws and exploration records. These records guide scene evolution for further exploration, allowing the full cycle to run without human intervention. Among 12 LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7%, while the other 11 score 0%. The exploration records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.
evidence_items.title: Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration?

evidence_items.summary: Objective: To evaluate the triage accuracy, response quality, safety, and repeatability of widely used large language models (LLMs) in urologic emergencies and to examine their potential clinical utility and risks. Methods: We developed 50 standardized clinical vignettes covering 10 categories of urologic emergencies, including testicular torsion, acute urinary retention, and Fournier gangrene. The set comprised high-risk vignettes requiring immediate emergency care, borderline vignettes, and atypical vignettes containing misleading cues. Six commercially available LLMs—Kimi 3.0, DeepSeek V4, Qwen 3.8-MAX, GPT-5.6 Sol (ChatGPT), Claude Opus 4.8, and Ant Afu (AQ)—were evaluated in Chinese-language interactions. Each vignette was submitted three times in independent conversations. Two urologists with more than 10 years of clinical experience assessed triage accuracy using a three-level reference standard (immediate emergency department [ED] evaluation, routine outpatient evaluation, or home observation). They also rated response quality across eight dimensions using a 5-point Likert scale and evaluated medical-error severity (0–3), response stability, and Chinese readability. Overall differences were assessed using the Friedman test, followed by pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm adjustment. Results: A total of 900 responses were generated. Overall three-class accuracy was 89.11%, and the macro-averaged F1 score was 85.73%. Qwen achieved the highest accuracy (94.00%), whereas Claude achieved the lowest (80.67%). However, none of the pairwise comparisons between models reached statistical significance after Holm adjustment. All models generally recognized scenarios requiring immediate ED evaluation, but their ability to distinguish routine outpatient evaluation from home observation varied substantially.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Large Language Models for Emergency Triage in Urology: A Multi-Model Study
Domain Adaptation of a Large Language Model for Radiology Impression Generation – Multi-Reader Evaluation

organizations: Rush University Medical Center, Chicago, IL, USA
evidence_items.summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Mistral are increasingly used to obtain medical information, but their accuracy in carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) management is uncertain. This study evaluated whether LLM-generated recommendations align with American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) clinical practice guidelines (CPGs). Methods: Four LLMs (ChatGPT-4, Gemini, Claude-3, Mistral-7B) were queried with standardized prompts derived from AAOS CTS CPGs. Each prompt was asked 3 times per model, and responses were synthesized. Two blinded reviewers graded outputs as concordant, discordant, or indeterminate, with disagreements resolved by consensus. Concordance distributions were compared using χ 2 testing with Bonferroni correction. Inter-rater reliability was measured with Cohen’s κ. Results: Across 252 recommendations, 72.6% were concordant, 11.5% discordant, and 15.9% indeterminate. ChatGPT achieved the highest concordance (92.1%) and lowest discordance (1.6%), while Mistral performed poorest (52.4% concordance, 17.5% discordance). Reviewer agreement was excellent (κ = 0.91). Conclusions: Over 1 in 4 LLM-generated CTS recommendations were not concordant with AAOS CPGs. ChatGPT outperformed other models, though variable performance underscores the need for clinician oversight and careful validation before clinical use.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Large Language Model Concordance With AAOS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

evidence_items.summary: Background The Functional Independence Measure (FIM) is a standard functional assessment tool in rehabilitation medicine; however, formal assessments are often conducted only at limited intervals. Free-text clinical notes contain more frequent observations of patients’ functional status and may complement these assessments. Objective This study aimed to estimate item-level FIM scores from Japanese free-text rehabilitation notes using a locally deployed large language model (LLM) and to evaluate estimation performance; item-level estimability; and differences across diseases, therapy types, and admission FIM severity groups. Methods We retrospectively analyzed free-text notes from physical therapy (PT), occupational therapy (OT), and speech-language pathology (SLP) for patients hospitalized with cerebral infarction (CeI), hip fracture (HF), or vertebral fracture (VBF) at Saiseikai Moriyama Municipal Hospital between October 2019 and September 2024. Using zero-shot prompting, an LLM estimated all FIM items from each note. Estimated scores were matched to reference FIM scores recorded for the same patient on the same calendar date. Performance was evaluated using the mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error, and quadratic weighted kappa. Estimation rates and comparisons with modal-score and last-observation-carried-forward (LOCF) baselines were also examined. Results Among 2,952,702 eligible note-item pairs from 164,039 retained rehabilitation-note-level outputs, the model produced 980,000 valid estimates, corresponding to an overall estimation rate of 33.2%. Among 170,744 note-item opportunities with an available same-day reference score, 57,246 (33.5%) were estimable, of which 77.7% (44,481/57,246) were within 1 point of the reference score. Estimates derived from OT notes had a lower MAE than those derived from PT notes in CeI and HF, whereas the difference was not significant in VBF.
evidence_items.title: Estimating Functional Independence Measure Scores From Japanese Rehabilitation Notes Using a Large Language Model: Retrospective Study

evidence_items.summary: Masked diffusion language models repeatedly compute representations for unresolved tokens, but conventional denoisers do not explicitly retain these representations for reuse across steps. We introduce Temporal Self-Conditioning Diffusion Language Model (TDLM), which lets each unresolved position attend to its own history of hidden representations within a frozen denoiser. This gives later predictions access to computation already performed. Training uses self-generated trajectories and a simple cross-entropy objective for tokens revealed between consecutively sampled decoding steps, while causal temporal attention permits parallel evaluation during training. On LLaDA, the temporal modules add only approximately 0.84% trainable parameters. Across LLaDA and Dream, the main comparison shows up to 7.15× faster generation than the corresponding original diffusion language model, with competitive answer quality on the evaluated tasks. These results motivate temporal memory as a practical way to make more effective use of repeated denoising computation.
evidence_items.title: TDLM: Temporal Self-Conditioning Diffusion Language Model

organizations: Liaquat National Hospital and Medical College, Karachi, Pakistan
New Jersey Institute of Technology, USA
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objective To evaluate the extent to which large language models (LLMs) reproduce human assessments of the quality of stroke-related information on social media. Background Social media is a major source of health information, yet content quality varies. The reliability of LLMs in evaluating stroke-related social media content against human assessments remains uncertain. Methods This cross-sectional study evaluated 50 TikTok and Instagram videos using human reference scores and three AI models: ChatGPT, Microsoft 365 Copilot, and Claude. Publicly unavailable videos and those featuring songs or lacking transcribable speech were excluded. Spoken audio was transcribed using a free tool, and transcripts were submitted to all three models with an identical standardized prompt. Scores were compared using Mann–Whitney U tests; Spearman’s correlation assessed associations with human ratings, and linear regression quantified explained variance. Results The median human reference score was 37.00 (IQR, 35.00–45.00). All AI models scored significantly lower: ChatGPT, 34.50 (p = 0.001); Microsoft Copilot, 33.50 (p < 0.001); and Claude, 26.00 (p < 0.001). All models correlated significantly with human ratings, with the strongest association for Claude (ρ = 0.593; p < 0.001), followed by ChatGPT (ρ = 0.550; p < 0.001) and Copilot (ρ = 0.396; p = 0.004). Claude explained 32.1% of the variance in human scores (R² = 0.321), compared with 31.4% for ChatGPT and 14.8% for Copilot. Inter-model correlation was strongest between ChatGPT and Copilot (ρ = 0.862; p < 0.001). Conclusions All three LLMs showed significant positive correlations with human ratings but systematically assigned lower scores. Claude showed the strongest correlation, whereas Microsoft Copilot showed the weakest. These findings highlight the limitations of LLMs in reproducing human judgments and the need for further validation before their use as standalone evaluators of social media content.
evidence_items.title: Can Large Language Models Judge Stroke Information on Social Media? A Cross-Sectional Comparison of Large Language Models Against Human Ratings of Health-Related Videos

evidence_items.summary: Background Shared decision-making (SDM) is a core competency in patient-centered care, yet it is challenging for physicians. Simulation-based education with standardized patients (SPs) offers valuable practice opportunities for undergraduate medical education (UME), but is limited by cost, scalability, and variable feedback quality. Advances in large language model (LLM) technology and virtual patient (VP) design present a promising pathway toward accessible, realistic, and high-quality SDM skill training. Objective This study aimed to develop LLM-powered, real-time interactive 3D avatars for SDM training in UME and to evaluate their acceptance among undergraduate medical students. Methods We conducted a descriptive, cross-sectional mixed methods study at KU Leuven, Belgium (November-December 2025). The avatar system was developed through an iterative, interdisciplinary collaboration between medical educators, SDM experts, software developers, user experience designers, and AI engineers, grounded in prior work on physicians’ educational needs and SDM learning mechanisms. Development comprised prototype case authoring, usability testing with medical students, and iterative refinement. The final system is a web-based platform featuring real-time, LLM-powered spoken dialogue with diverse, photorealistic 3D patient avatars; layered prompts configuring avatar personality, clinical scenario, and difficulty; an educator panel for case authoring; and automated AI-generated formative feedback structured around 6 phases of SDM. After using the system for 1 month, a convenience sample of UME students completed a 9-item, 5-point Likert scale questionnaire grounded in the technology acceptance model (TAM), assessing perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and intention to use. Optional open-text responses were narratively analyzed to triangulate these findings. Results Of 25 recruited participants, 24 were included in the analysis.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model–Powered 3D Avatars to Train Shared Decision-Making in Undergraduate Medical Students: Design and Mixed Methods Acceptance Study

evidence_items.summary: Formal mathematics has a data problem, and large language models have become one of the tools applied to it. LeanConjecturer mined 40 seed files from Mathlib and produced 12,289 candidate statements, of which 3,776 resisted the automated tactic used as a filter. AlphaGeometry solved 25 of 30 olympiad geometry problems by letting a language model propose auxiliary constructions whenever symbolic deduction stalled. FunSearch improved on earlier results for the cap set problem by having an evaluator score programs written by a model. Evidence of this kind still supports a narrower claim than mathematical discovery. Five studies are compared in this review: LeanConjecturer, the Conjecturing-Proving Loop, AlphaGeometry, FunSearch, and Unlearning as Ablation. Using literature analysis and comparative case analysis, task objectives, generation mechanisms, verification procedures, and evidential limits are examined side by side. Two findings stand out. External verification is what makes candidate selection and iterative repair function in each system, and each system demonstrates a different slice of the work: conjecture supply, proof repair, geometric construction, program optimization, and, in the case of Unlearning as Ablation, a proposal for auditing knowledge provenance. Correctness, novelty, and independence from previously acquired target knowledge remain three separate questions that require three separate kinds of evidence. A more reliable evaluation framework would combine auditable knowledge boundaries, dependency checking, and expert assessment of mathematical significance.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models for Mathematical Discovery: Generation, Verification, and Knowledge Provenance

organizations: Mayo Clinic Alix School of Medicine, Scottsdale, AZ, USA
George Washington University, Washington, DC, USA
evidence_items.summary: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been utilized as a supplemental tool by patients and providers in the evaluation of common hand pathology. This study evaluated the ability of 3 large language model (LLM)-based AI systems (ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude) to characterize Dupuytren’s contracture involvement and recommend treatment based solely on patient images. Methods: A heterogeneous set of publicly available images was obtained from open-access databases and literature sources. Images were evaluated by LLMs in independent stateless sessions using a standardized prompt to identify contracture characteristics and recommend treatment. Artificial intelligence outputs were compared with consensus assessments from 3 board-certified hand surgeons. Results: Large language models demonstrated limited accuracy in characterizing Dupuytren’s contracture involvement from patient images. Treatment recommendations were often within 1 ordinal tier of surgeon consensus; however, agreement with surgeons was no greater than chance. No consistent differences in performance were observed among the models. Conclusions: Large language model-based AI systems demonstrated limited capability in the image-based assessment and treatment recommendation of Dupuytren’s contracture. These findings highlight a gap between current LLM performance and surgeon consensus when evaluating Dupuytren’s contracture from single-patient-submitted images. Further research is needed to determine whether the incorporation of standardized clinical information can improve the reliability of AI-assisted treatment recommendations.
evidence_items.title: Performance of Large Language Models in Image-Based Evaluation of Dupuytren Contracture

organizations: Guangdong University of Science and Technology
Zhuhai College of Science and Technology
evidence_items.summary: Background Increasing use of large language models in nursing education has raised questions about the association between reliance on these tools and academic distress. This study examined direct and specific indirect associations between large language model dependence (LMD) and academic anxiety (AA) through artificial intelligence addiction (AIA) and academic burnout (AB). Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted from March to April 2026 among 473 nursing students in Guangdong Province, China, including students undertaking clinical placements. The four constructs were assessed using items selected from published self-report instruments. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was performed with age and sex included as covariates. Direct and specific indirect associations were evaluated using bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples. Results Cronbach’s α ranged from 0.914 to 0.944, composite reliability from 0.935 to 0.954, and average variance extracted from 0.560 to 0.721. Heterotrait–monotrait ratios ranged from 0.485 to 0.733, supporting discriminant validity. Model fit evidence was mixed: SRMR was 0.068, whereas NFI was 0.812, below the 0.90 reference value. The model explained 49.2% of the variance in academic anxiety. Large language model dependence showed a small positive direct association with academic anxiety ( β = 0.138, 95% CI [0.006, 0.278], p = 0.048). Significant specific indirect associations were identified through academic burnout ( β = 0.205, 95% CI [0.123, 0.303]) and through artificial intelligence addiction followed by academic burnout ( β = 0.098, 95% CI [0.049, 0.147]); both p &lt; 0.001. Conclusion Large language model dependence was positively associated with academic anxiety among nursing students, with specific indirect associations through academic burnout and through artificial intelligence addiction followed by academic burnout.
evidence_items.title: The association between large language model dependence and academic anxiety among nursing students: statistical indirect associations through artificial intelligence addiction and academic burnout

organizations: Facultad de Salud Pública, Escuela Superior Politécnica de Chimborazo (ESPOCH)
evidence_items.summary: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored in dental education as a tool to support teaching, learning, assessment, and clinical decision-making. This systematic review synthesized current evidence on the implementation and educational impact of AI technologies in undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing dental education. Methodology A PRISMA-guided systematic review was conducted using Scopus, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore. Studies published between 2020 and 2025 evaluating AI applications in dental education were identified using predefined PICO criteria. Educational outcomes included knowledge acquisition, diagnostic accuracy, clinical reasoning, procedural skills, learner engagement, and perceptions of AI-assisted learning. Results The included literature reflects an expansion from machine learning, deep learning, and computer vision systems primarily evaluated for diagnostic support toward generative AI platforms, including large language models and retrieval-augmented generation systems. Across the included studies, AI applications were frequently associated with favorable diagnostic and examination performance and, in selected educational contexts, with supportive findings related to clinical reasoning, technical competency, feedback, and self-directed learning. However, the evidence was predominantly based on technical performance assessments and observational or cross-sectional designs. Discussion AI is increasingly being explored as a potential complementary educational resource, with applications including interactive tutoring, adaptive learning, and support for clinical reasoning. Nevertheless, heterogeneous methodologies and limited longitudinal evidence indicate the need for standardized educational evaluation and responsible curricular integration. Conclusion AI shows potential as a complementary resource in dental education.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in odontology education

organizations: Department of Organization and Management, Faculty of Economics and Business, University of Zagreb, Trg J. F. Kennedyja 6, 10000 Zagreb, Croatia
evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence in corporate boards refers to the use of data-driven computational systems, including machine learning, predictive analytics, natural language processing and generative models, to support the work of boards of directors in one-tier systems and supervisory boards in two-tier systems. Executive management, including management boards in two-tier systems, is considered insofar as it supplies information to or is overseen by these bodies. Such systems are applied to the established functions of the board: monitoring and control, strategic direction, advice and counsel to executive management, and the provision of information, expertise and external linkages. Applications range from anomaly and compliance monitoring to environmental scanning, scenario modeling and the synthesis of board materials. A distinction is essential between decision support, in which systems supply information and analysis; decision augmentation, in which board members and systems jointly shape an evaluation; and autonomous decision-making, in which a system determines an outcome without human deliberation; board-level use is discussed in the literature almost entirely in the first two modes. The central governance tension is that capabilities which expand the information-processing capacity of a body constrained by limited meeting time and by dependence on management-supplied reporting also introduce opacity, vendor dependence and new difficulty in attributing responsibility. Under prevailing corporate governance arrangements, formal responsibility for board decisions remains with the human members of the relevant governing body. Responsible use therefore rests on explicit governance arrangements: defined human oversight, documentation, verification, data governance and board-level competence.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Corporate Boards

evidence_items.summary: Objective Traditional ultrasonic detection for kidney stones is prone to variability due to the experience and skill of the operating physician, leading to inconsistent diagnostic outcomes. Factors such as stone size, location, and surrounding tissues can further compromise accuracy. Artificial intelligence (AI), with its advanced data processing and deep learning capabilities, offers a solution by automating the analysis of medical images to improve diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted at our hospital between 01/06/2022 and 03/07/2024. After excluding 50 poor-quality ultrasound images, the final dataset included 1,130 images: 918 stone images and 212 non-stone images. At the patient level, 791 stone images were used for training/validation, and 127 stone images plus 212 non-stone images ( n = 339) were held out as an independent test cohort. The High-Resolution Network (HRNet) was employed for model training to detect kidney stones in ultrasound images. Detailed image annotations were created using the labelme tool and converted to COCO format for compatibility with AI algorithms. Results In the independent test cohort ( n = 339), the confusion matrix was: TN = 200, FP = 12, FN = 34, and TP = 93, corresponding to 212 actual negatives and 127 actual positives. The HRNet model achieved an accuracy of 86.4% (95% CI 82.4–89.7%), sensitivity of 73.2% (95% CI 64.9–82.2%), specificity of 94.3% (95% CI 90.4–96.7%), positive predictive value (PPV) of 88.6% (95% CI 81.1–93.3%), and negative predictive value (NPV) of 85.5% (95% CI 80.4–89.4%). The model showed high specificity but moderate sensitivity, missing approximately 26.8% of renal stones in the test cohort. Conclusions HRNet-based AI may improve specificity and reduce false-positive findings in ultrasound-based renal stone detection.
evidence_items.title: Enhancing renal stone detection through artificial intelligence models

organizations: Old Dominion University (ODU) Virginia Modeling, Analysis, and Simulation Center (VMASC)
School of Mines in Alès (IMT Mines Alès)
evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly support time-consuming conceptual modeling tasks such as building or combining models from text. In this context, causal maps are labeled, directed graphs that represent causal relationships (edges) between selected factors (nodes) in a problem domain. Modelers control the output through the LLM’s prompt and decoding parameters such as temperature, and recent studies either use a default temperature or minimize it by expecting that it supports replicability. However, evidence about this expectation remains limited, as does our understanding of how different LLMs and decoding or prompting strategies shape results. We assess the extent to which findings are an artifact of the LLM or its variability rather than a reflection of the modeler’s controls. We focus on the common conceptual modeling task of combining models, exemplified through three algorithms that reflect a variety of prompting techniques. We use five LLMs (DeepSeek, Gemini, GPT, Qwen, Ministral) and different versions to account for the potential impact of the architectures. Using the Design of Experiments approach of factorial analyses (supplemented by paired tests and confidence interval checks), our results show that outcomes differ significantly across LLMs and versions. Depending on the algorithm, randomness from the LLM can be the dominating factor, responsible for up to 96% of the variation in results. This happens even if we directly control the decoding, as evidenced by our comparison of greedy, beam-search, and contrastive decoding. We find that prompt effects are systematic but metric-dependent, while decoding affects performance but there is no universally best strategy. Since our findings suggest that replicability of conceptual modeling studies using LLMs may be limited, future studies may report the distribution of performance measures alongside exact model, decoding, replication, and baseline-normalization settings.
evidence_items.title: On the variability of generative artificial intelligence methods in conceptual modeling: an experimental evaluation on combining causal maps

organizations: University of Birmingham, School of Computer Science, University of Birmingham, Birmingham, United Kingdom
evidence_items.summary: Learning paths personalized by behavior have become common among personalized learning systems. However, the traditional methods are usually inefficient at building coherent paths as the learner's knowledge state changes dynamically, and the prerequisite structure exists. In light of this problem, we present a generative learning-path optimization framework based on EdNet-KT1 interaction dataset, Transformer knowledge tracing model, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct candidate generator, and constraint-aware reranking. Mastery profiles of learners are extracted, and then five ten-resource candidate paths are generated and sorted according to learning gain, prerequisites, difficulty deviation, and repetition. We compare our method to collaborative filtering, GRU4Rec, and knowledge-tracing greedy recommendation on offline experiments. The generative optimizer gets NDCG@10 of 0.589, future-concept coverage of 0.721, and prerequisite violation rate of 0.031, and thus outperforms the best baseline on all three metrics. Ablation analysis shows that the prerequisite violation rate rises to 0.091 without constraints, and the learning gain drops to 0.104 without the learning gain term, respectively. Moreover, the full model still achieves better NDCG@10 performance on all learner history categories than other baselines, costing 0.84 s per learner with the memory peak of 13.6 GB. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of combining the generation of learning paths with pedagogical constraints.
evidence_items.title: Personalized Learning Path Optimization Based on Generative Artificial Intelligence

organizations: Department of Pharmacy, The Fourth Hospital of Changsha (Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine Hospital of Changsha)
International Advanced Technology Application Promotion Center (Hefei)
evidence_items.summary: Objective Clarify the effects of large-language-model types and health-education content categories on generated-text quality (patient-education suitability, overall quality) and readability, so as to provide empirical evidence for standardized AI-assisted health-communication applications. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted between July 10 and July 15, 2026. Twenty herpes zoster-related questions were developed by a dermatologist and a pharmacist and categorized into five themes. The questions were then entered into five mainstream large language models (GPT-5, Doubao, DeepSeek, Qianwen, and Gemini), generating 100 textual responses. Response quality was assessed using the Chinese version of the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials (C-PEMAT-P) and Global Quality Score (GQS). Readability was evaluated via seven indices including the Automated Readability Index (ARI) and Flesch Reading Ease Score (FRES). Readability outcomes were compared using one-way repeated-measures analysis of variance with Greenhouse–Geisser correction. C-PEMAT-P raw totals and ordinal GQS scores were compared using Friedman tests. Post-hoc comparisons were adjusted using the Holm method. Category-level comparisons were performed using linear mixed-effects models with likelihood-ratio χ 2 tests for continuous outcomes and an ordinal generalized estimating equation with a Wald χ 2 test for GQS. Results Significant overall differences among models were observed for all seven readability indices and both assessment scores (all p &lt; 0.001). Median C-PEMAT-P raw total scores were 12.50, 11.00, 10.00, 9.00 and 9.00 for GPT-5, Doubao, DeepSeek, Qianwen and Gemini, respectively; corresponding median GQS scores were 5.00, 4.00, 4.00, 3.00, and 3.00. After Holm correction, GPT-5 achieved higher scores than each of the other models on both assessment measures.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence chatbots as information sources for herpes zoster: an evaluation of patient-education suitability, overall quality, and readability

organizations: Drs. Kiran & Pallavi Patel Global University (KPGU), Vadodara, Gujarat, India
evidence_items.summary: The transition from academic education to professional employment requires students to communicate technical skills, projects, certifications, education, and experience in a form that is relevant to a specific job. This paper presents an AI-based resume analysis and job-matching approach designed to provide understandable, job-specific feedback to engineering students. The system accepts a PDF resume and a target job description, extracts resume text using pdfplumber with pypdf as a fallback, and submits the normalized information to an AI analysis component. The revised methodology makes the compatibility score more transparent by interpreting it through three dimensions: required-skill coverage, semantic relevance between resume evidence and job requirements, and evidence strength from projects, education, and experience. The system returns four structured outputs: an ATS-style compatibility score, matched skills, missing or insufficiently represented skills, and actionable recommendations. Unlike a commercial Applicant Tracking System, the score is explicitly positioned as a decision-support estimate rather than an employer-generated recruitment score. Implementation-level testing on three sample technical cases produced compatibility scores of 78%, 64%, and 71%, with a mean of 71.0%. These values demonstrate functional variation across job-specific inputs but are not treated as predictive accuracy because the current study does not use a sufficiently large labeled benchmark. A literature-grounded comparison further shows that existing approaches emphasize resume information extraction, skill taxonomy alignment, deep-learning recommendation, or job recommendation, whereas the proposed system integrates these ideas into a student-facing feedback workflow.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Based Resume Analysis and Job Matching

organizations: Dazhou Vocational College of Chinese Medicine
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background As AI becomes integrated into nursing education and clinical practice, students must develop the competence to use, evaluate, and ethically govern AI-generated information. However, the psychological mechanisms linking students’ emotional responses to AI and their AI literacy remain underexplored in vocational nursing contexts. This study aimed to examine the mediating role of artificial intelligence (AI) self-efficacy in the relationship between AI anxiety and AI literacy among higher vocational nursing students. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted using a convenience sample of 921 nursing students from five higher vocational colleges in Sichuan, China. Participants completed the Chinese Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale, the revised Chinese Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale, and the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale. Structural equation modeling was used to test the mediating hypothesis. Results AI anxiety was negatively correlated with AI self-efficacy (r = − 0.470) and AI literacy (r = − 0.370), while AI self-efficacy was positively correlated with AI literacy (r = 0.392). AI self-efficacy partially mediated the association between AI anxiety and AI literacy, accounting for 42.22% of the total effect (indirect effect β = −0.171, 95% BC CI [− 0.255, − 0.100]). After adjustment for covariates, attitude toward nursing and residence remained independently associated with AI literacy. Conclusions AI literacy among higher vocational nursing students is shaped by psychological (AI anxiety, AI self-efficacy), professional (attitude toward nursing), and educational (residence) factors. AI education should be embedded in competency-based nursing preparation with emphasis on critical evaluation, safe application, professional accountability, and equitable access to structured learning opportunities.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence anxiety and literacy among higher vocational nursing students: the mediating role of artificial intelligence self-efficacy in a cross-sectional study

organizations: Department of Sociology, Faculty of the Social Sciences, University of Ibadan
Department of Sociology, Faculty of Humanities University of Johannesburg
Department of Sociology, Ladoke Akintola University of Technology, Ogbomoso
evidence_items.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is impacting societies’ social relations, institutions and social structures in definitive ways. Not many innovations have impacted human behaviours as significantly as AI. Deviating from the previous studies on AI that focuses on the potential implications of AI for everyday human society, this paper adopted secondary method of data collection, decolonial theory, and case study analysis to examine the sociological utilisation of AI in Africa. It provided answers to the fundamental sociological question of—why sociology of AI is needed in Africa? What forms of historical and social context shape AI’s incursion into Africa? Findings from this study revealed that while AI in Africa is driving positive innovations like financial inclusion, climate resilience, agriculture and food security, rapid diagnosis, education and language inclusion and job creation, it is also exacerbating technological asymmetry, expanding existing inequalities, strengthening unequal geopolitical power relations and perpetuating historical institutional dynamics on the continent.
evidence_items.title: The sociology of artificial intelligence development and utilisation in Africa

organizations: KCG College of Technology, Chennai, India
Hindustan Institute of Technology and Science, Chennai, India
evidence_items.summary: The incorporation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the design and analysis of renewable energy systems has become a revolutionary method for enhancing efficiency, reliability and sustainability. AI-driven models provide intelligent forecasting, optimization, and regulation of renewable energy sources, including solar, wind, hydro and biofuels. Utilizing techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, and evolutionary algorithms, AI enables precise forecasting of energy production, dynamic load regulation and fault identification. This chapter examines the approaches and frameworks for integrating AI into the design and performance evaluation of renewable energy systems. Focus is directed towards data-driven enhancement of system components, energy storage administration, and smart grid incorporation. The results indicate that AI integration improves energy conversion efficiency and operational stability while facilitating the shift to cleaner, more adaptable energy systems.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract. We study revenue maximization in the unit-demand single-buyer setting. Our main result is that Uniform-Ironed-Virtual-Value Item Pricing guarantees a tight 3-approximation to Duality Relaxation Benchmark (Chawla, Malec, and Sivan, EC’10 and GEB’15; Cai, Devanur, and Weinberg, STOC’16 and [ SIAM J. Comput., 50 (2021), pp. STOC16-160–STOC16-200]), breaking the barrier of 4 since Chawla et al. [ Proceedings of STOC’10, 2010, pp. 311–320] and Chawla, Malec, and Sivan (EC’10 and GEB’15). To our knowledge, this is the first benchmark-tight revenue guarantee of any simple multi-item mechanism. Technically, all previous work employs Myerson Auction as an intermediary. The barrier of 4 follows as Uniform-Ironed-Virtual-Value Item Pricing achieves a tight 2-approximation to Myerson Auction , which then achieves a tight 2-approximation to Duality Relaxation Benchmark . Instead, our new approach avoids Myerson Auction , thus enabling the improvement. Central to our work are a benchmark-based 3-competitive prophet inequality and its fully constructive proof. Such prophet inequality variants will likely find applications in, e.g., multi-item mechanism design, when the optimal revenue objective is relaxed to various more accessible benchmarks. We complement our benchmark-tight ratio with an impossibility result. All previous works, including ours, follow the single-dimensional representative approach introduced by Chawla, Hartline, and Kleinberg [ Proceedings of EC’07, 2007, pp. 243–251]. Against Duality Relaxation Benchmark , it turns out that this approach cannot beat our bound of 3 for a large class of Item Pricing .
evidence_items.title: Benchmark-Tight Approximation Ratio of Simple Mechanism for a Unit-Demand Buyer
