evidence_items.summary: Introduction Assessing residual contamination in coastal wetland soils after oil-well retirement requires comparisons with both active oil-well sites and natural reference wetlands. Methods We analyzed a September 2022 soil survey from the Liao River estuary wetlands in northeastern China, comprising five active oil-well plots, five retired oil-well plots, and three reference wetland plots. Three separately collected surface soil samples were averaged per plot, giving 13 independent analytical units. Soil properties, total petroleum hydrocarbons (TPHs), and five trace metals were compared among well-status groups. Results Mean TPH concentrations were 35.71 g/kg in active plots, 12.95 g/kg in retired plots, and 1.20 g/kg in reference plots (exact Kruskal–Wallis P &lt; 0.001; false-discovery-rate-adjusted q = 0.0015). Total organic carbon (TOC) followed the same ordering (43.15, 29.76, and 18.99 g/kg, respectively; P &lt; 0.001; q &lt; 0.001) and was positively associated with TPHs (Spearman rho = 0.76, P = 0.003). No overall group differences were detected for As, Cd, Cr, Cu, or Pb after multiple-testing correction, although one active plot showed locally elevated As, Cd, and Cr benchmark ratios. Discussion Retired plots had lower mean TPH concentrations than active plots, but all retired-plot values exceeded the reference range. These findings support monitoring residual petroleum contamination after oil-well retirement and targeted assessment of local metal enrichment.
evidence_items.title: Contrasting petroleum hydrocarbon contamination across active, retired and reference wetlands in the Liao River estuary

evidence_items.summary: Which computational features can predict the functional consequences of kinase mutations, and where do they stop working? We benchmark five feature families spanning physics-based, docking and learned paradigms — FoldX folding stability, AutoDock Vina docking perturbation, FoldX interaction energy, AlphaMissense and ThermoMPNN-D — against deep mutational scanning of FGFR1–4 kinase domains under pemigatinib and futibatinib selection (7,522 unique variants; Tangermann et al. 2026), adding an erdafitinib-specific docking dimension the screen did not cover. The capability map is non-uniform in three ways. Classical features stay below 0.74 across the panorama but transmit strong signal inside annotated hotspots (0.65–0.88, region-level q ≤ 4.5 × 10⁻⁶). ThermoMPNN-D crosses the conventional 0.7 line where classical FoldX does too: FGFR3 activation reaches 0.877 (95% CI 0.798–0.938, q = 5.1 × 10⁻⁶) and resistance 0.702 — distributed across the domain, not hotspot-driven. Resistance to erdafitinib specifically never exceeds 0.63 on the experimental structure (0.663 on one modelled pose). We trace this staircase to the mechanistic homogeneity of each phenotype and document three distinct failure modes: drug-resistant variants are enriched among those AlphaMissense calls benign; docking features degrade whenever the ligand pose is modelled rather than experimental; classical FoldX has an isoform-specific blind spot on FGFR1. The map converts into 30 falsifiable predictions absent from the screen and from clinical databases. Mechanistic homogeneity, not model sophistication, sets the ceiling for mutation-effect prediction.
evidence_items.title: Mechanistic homogeneity, not model sophistication, sets the ceiling for mutation-effect prediction: a five-family FGFR benchmark against deep mutational scanning

evidence_items.summary: Embodied foundation models now allow robots to act on open-ended instructions, yet success on long-horizon physical tasks also depends on the runtime around the model, which organizes the task, invokes skills, guards execution, and retains experience. Digital agent research treats this runtime, known as the harness, as a first-class design object that can be engineered and even improved from experience, since the same model can perform very differently under different harnesses. Such harness designs do not carry over directly, because physical execution is embodiment-specific, partially observed, time-constrained, and often irreversible, which also makes experience costly to learn from. Embodied AI systems increasingly build similar runtimes, yet the field still lacks a unified view of them. This survey treats the physical agentic harness as a research object in its own right. We define it as the runtime system that maintains task and execution state for an embodied foundation model and mediates the model’s interaction with the physical world through one or more physical bodies. We then review over 200 works and organize them by six functional responsibilities: task orchestration, digital resources, embodied capabilities, execution governance, digital-physical interaction, and persistent evolution. This organization offers a common lens for comparing methods across communities, making explicit how model decisions reach physical execution and how grounded evidence flows back. The reviewed benchmarks and applications provide limited evidence of individual runtime contributions, particularly the effects of execution governance and sustained gains from persistent evolution. We close with open problems in model-harness co-design, capability composition, real-time decision making, distributed execution, and continual improvement from physical experience.
evidence_items.title: Where the Harness Meets the Physical World: A Survey of the Physical Agentic Harness

evidence_items.summary: The convergence of large language models (LLMs), federated learning (FL), and edge computing offers a pathway to autonomous decision systems that can reason near data sources while limiting reliance on centralized infrastructure. Edge-deployed LLMs can support latency-sensitive and privacy-conscious applications, although their computational demands challenge resource-constrained devices. FL enables collaborative adaptation without directly pooling private data, but heterogeneous devices, non-identically distributed data, and communication constraints complicate training. This paper proposes an agentic edge-intelligence framework that combines local LLM inference, federated model adaptation, and multi-agent coordination for sensing, planning, and decision execution. The framework identifies interfaces among reasoning, learning, and edge-resource management, and articulates design considerations for privacy, communication efficiency, and device heterogeneity. It provides a systems-oriented basis for developing and evaluating autonomous edge applications under practical network and resource constraints.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Edge Intelligence: Integrating Large Language Models, Federated Learning, and Edge Computing for Autonomous Decision Systems

evidence_items.summary:
Energy-based models have shown promising properties for domain-specific tasks but remain challenging in modeling general-purpose scenarios. To bridge this gap, we design energy-steered models (ESMs) for foundational language modeling. ESMs integrate energy steering and token generation within a single architecture to leverage the energy-guided search to refine token generation. Specifically, ESMs first optimize a latent state over the energy landscape, then leverages the refined latent state for token generation. By performing such energy-guided pre-training on large-scale corpora, ESMs learn generally effective energy landscape where favorable tokens correspond to lower energy values. To explore the scaling behavior of ESMs, we pre-train ESMs on three large-scale corpora, then evaluate across 26 downstream tasks spanning a broad range of domains. Our results demonstrate that ESMs have promising scaling behaviors with increasing model size and training data, and outperform GPTs on most downstream tasks. These findings highlight ESMs as a promising architecture for large-scale pre-training and general purpose problem solving. We fully release the model weights and training infrastructure to enable the community to completely reproduce and extend our results.
  GitHub: https://github.com/datamllab/openesm HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/collections/guan-wang/openesm
evidence_items.title: OpenESM: Energy-Steered Models Are Scalable Foundation Learners

evidence_items.summary: AI agents no longer act alone: they cooperate, coordinate and compete within and between groups, increasingly alongside humans who are in, on or out of the loop''. Whether such mixed groups can govern themselves is an open question about machine behaviour and human-computer interaction that needs a testbed for hybrid institutions. We present Megabike, a multi-agent simulator and serious game with interdependent arenas for common-pool resource management, cooperative survival and constitutional choice. Riders sharing a megabike must agree their arrangements for steering, pedalling and distributing resources, and their political regime, while negotiating with rival bikes and avoiding an existential threat. Every rule is enforced by the simulator, every action is logged, and any seat can be taken by a human or a machine, so governance can be studied under well-defined metrics. We demonstrate Megabike with forty sessions in which language-model riders with cooperative, lazy, subversive or opposing dispositions chose regimes, elected leaders and expelled one another. The results show that different combinations of agent archetypes could produce unexpected and counterproductive outcomes. We conclude with extensions for systematic experiments mixing human and computational agents.
evidence_items.title: A Serious-Game Testbed for Self-Governing Human-Machine Institutions

evidence_items.summary: Safe household navigation requires robots to regulate clearance and speed according to what an obstacle is and how close it is, without unnecessary conservatism. Yet existing evaluations do not test whether semantic safety distinctions are reflected in continuous motion. To that end, we introduce OSMA-Bench, an Obstacle-Conditioned Safe Motion Adaptation Benchmark built on spatially matched scenario sets that differ only in obstacle type. We also propose the Semantic Sensitivity Index (SSI), which measures whether clearance and distance-dependent speed and smoothness follow the caution ordering of obstacles. Evaluating VLM-based and vision-language-action (VLA) policies on the benchmark, we find that neither consistently adapts its motion to obstacle safety, even with explicit safety prompts. Our analysis shows that the policies can correctly distinguish obstacles by safety relevance but fail to reflect this distinction in the motion parameters or actions they produce. For VLM-based policies, which recognize the obstacle and then generate a navigation program, adding an explicit parameter-inference step between these two stages improves adaptation. These findings expose a gap in semantic-to-motion grounding, highlighting the need to translate semantic caution into appropriately safe motion.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Obstacle-Conditioned Safety in Household Robot Navigation

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.
evidence_items.title: The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents

evidence_items.summary: Despite rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), their deployment in the sports and health domain remains high-risk due to the absence of domain-specific evaluation benchmarks. Existing general-purpose benchmarks (e.g., MMLU and HELM) primarily assess broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but fail to capture critical domain requirements such as exercise safety, physiological appropriateness, personalization, and actionable coaching quality. This gap is particularly concerning in fitness and health applications, where incorrect or unsafe recommendations can lead to physical harm. To address this limitation, we introduce MoveBench, the first comprehensive benchmarking framework specifically designed for evaluating LLMs in sports and health coaching. The proposed benchmark integrates heterogeneous task formats, including multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and open-ended question answering (OpenQA), grounded in real-world user scenarios and paired with structured rubrics emphasizing safety compliance, scientific validity, and training logic. Through large-scale evaluation of 15 diverse LLMs on 809 questions with 5,012 rubric-level criteria, our results reveal substantial performance variability, particularly in safety awareness, structured program design, and personalization capability, highlighting a critical gap between knowing and doing. Our work establishes a foundational evaluation standard for sports and health LLM applications and provides a reproducible framework for advancing safe, reliable, and context-aware AI-driven coaching systems. Open resources are available at https://github.com/SatoSakula/MoveBench.
evidence_items.title: MoveBench: A Rubric-Based Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Sports and Health Coaching

evidence_items.summary: As foundation models evolve from information generation to digital work execution, agents are increasingly capable of completing complex tasks across tools, applications, and workflows. However, existing research lacks a unified perspective on how agents reliably accomplish delegated work. To address this gap, we present a work-centric, system-level perspective that views work agents as systems combining foundation models and runtime harnesses to execute tasks in stateful workspaces and deliver verifiable outcomes. We introduce two complementary dimensions, work persistence and work openness, to characterize working conditions, and classify digital work into five forms according to task scope and organization. Building on this framework, we identify five core capability families required for reliable work execution and examine approaches to model optimization, harness optimization, and their joint optimization. We further analyze existing evaluation methods and metrics from the perspective of work outcomes. Finally, we discuss future research directions, including sustained work delegation, adaptation to open environments, and the interaction between work execution and capability improvement. This paper provides a unified framework for understanding, optimizing, and evaluating work agents, supporting the development of systems capable of delivering reliable, verifiable, and practically valuable work outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models are shifting from offline passive understanding toward online proactive interaction. However, prevailing methods largely rely on explicit requests while miss the implicit user intent (e.g., "where should I click next?" while a user navigate a website), meanwhile fail to update the state simultaneously as user requests might update continuously. These limitations make them less suited to intent-aware interaction in practical. To address these challenges, we introduce StreamVibe-Bench, a new benchmark serving as testbed for user intent interaction, with 4.1K evaluation samples and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents. Building on this benchmark, we develop StreamVibe-VL, a streaming proactive model that infers implicit user intents from continuous observations and dynamically tailors its interactions as these intents evolve. We further introduce StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains user intents as persistent states with a fleixble lifecycles via a hierarchical memory to track the latest user intent and environmental state. Our experiments reveal three key findings: (i) StreamVibe-VL preserves strong general video understanding while improving response timing and answer quality by 10.7% over other baselines; (ii) existing proactive models remain limited in understanding user intent and deciding when to respond, especially under implicit and dynamic intents; and (iii) StreamVibe-Harness further improves response consistency and adaptation over sustained interaction, resulting in a 12.3% gain in proactive interaction.
evidence_items.title: StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent

evidence_items.summary: Memory is increasingly used in long-horizon agents, yet the net value of building memory over direct retrieval from raw history remains largely unclear. Through a large-scale evaluation across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, we find many dedicated memory systems underperform naive RAG in many cases, indicating a negative net value. Taking RAG as a reference, we dissect the net value of memory into the gains and losses over direct retrieval, termed memory benefit and memory tax. These gains and losses arise because memory process changes how the raw information is organized and accessed. We view such changes as the double-edged deviations from the raw history. They are originally designed and introduced to benefit the task, for example by reorganizing facts or distilling preferences, but some may also remove or obscure evidence, giving rise to memory tax. Since memory benefit reflects the expected gains of its design, we then focus more on the overlooked memory tax, study how it arises from the system and evaluation side, and generalize the concept to more application scenarios of memory. We hope the notion of memory tax can provide a new lens and shift more attention from standalone performance to the net value of memory, informing more reliable memory designs and evaluations. We will open-source the code and results to the community. Project Page: https://hexuan21.github.io/MemoryTax/
evidence_items.title: Memory Tax: Dissecting the Net Value of Agent Memory

evidence_items.summary: Generative models increasingly expose a reasoning effort setting that lets users scale inference-time compute, trading higher cost for potentially improved performance. Users must choose an effort level before knowing whether extra reasoning will help, and even a successful run does not reveal whether the effort purchased was necessary. Reasoning effort is therefore a credence good: buyers observe the outcome but cannot assess the marginal value of the computation they paid for. In this work, we measure the counterfactual effect of effort levels on both proprietary and open-weight models on four benchmarks, spanning single-call reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks. Effort, it turns out, does not consistently preserve tasks that lower effort solves, can overspend, and can change trajectory behavior. First, we find that although higher effort can raise accuracy in aggregate, it frequently fails on tasks that lower effort solved. Second, on the subset of easy tasks that every effort level solves, higher effort is generally more costly, with the highest effort level costing up to 42x as much as the lowest. Lastly, effort changes not only how many tokens are used, but also how agents solve tasks: at higher effort, agents verify their own work more heavily and more often search for solutions than work through problems directly, both of which lengthen trajectories without necessarily altering the outcome. These findings show that naively choosing the highest level is not only cost-inefficient but also offers no guarantee of the best instance-level performance. A simple alternative, starting at the lowest effort and escalating only after a verified failure, matches or improves on fixed top effort across all models and benchmarks at lower cost for most proprietary models.
evidence_items.title: What Effort Level Should I Choose? On the Economics of Reasoning Effort in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Agent harnesses enable large language models to act through tools, observe the results, and iteratively work toward a task goal. Verification checks and revises agents' work to improve output quality. Yet there is limited guidance on how harnesses should organize this effort. We study verification as an axis of test-time scaling by examining when to intervene, who checks the work, and how checking leads to revision. Our framework spans four layers of the agent lifecycle: initial instructions, mid-turn reminders, completion gates, and independent review. We compare 17 designs across seven frontier coding models on Terminal-Bench (TB) and SWE-bench Verified (SWE), and introduce VisualBench for expert evaluation of visual and interactive artifacts. Initial instructions and execution-time reminders yield modest, model-dependent average gains on the coding benchmarks, without substantially increasing average output token use. Completion gates can yield larger gains but may substantially increase cost. Independent review by a critic offers a more favorable accuracy-cost tradeoff, improving average accuracy by 5.9-9.5 percentage points on TB and 3.9-6.6 on SWE at 1.13-1.25 and 1.00-1.04 times baseline cost, respectively. On VisualBench, independent review achieves net preferences of 13.2-23.8 points over the baseline across its four designs, exceeding the evaluated L0-L2 designs. Additional review rounds or independent critics further improve average TB accuracy by up to 3.5 percentage points. Together, these results provide empirical guidance for verification design in agent harnesses and support independent review as a practical axis of test-time scaling.
evidence_items.title: Rethinking Verification in Agent Harnesses

evidence_items.summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel at zero-shot reasoning, their spatial capabilities are primarily evaluated through static, passive observation. In complex, human-centric scenes, occlusion often hides crucial geometric evidence, and passive benchmarks force models to guess rather than recognize their own visual uncertainty. To bridge this gap, we introduce SATE-Bench, a novel interactive benchmark comprising 316 real-world scenes and 2,525 multi-turn QA pairs to evaluate visual self-awareness and active exocentric view-exploration. It combines a Passive multi-view control with an Active exploration setting, where models start from a severely occluded view and must iteratively query adjacent viewpoints until they gather enough evidence to fully ``sate'' the question, scored by a step-penalized efficiency reward. Evaluating state-of-the-art MLLMs reveals that they terminate exploration prematurely while reporting high confidence, and struggle with fine-grained 3D geometric tasks; matched-view controls further attribute the Active--Passive gap primarily to insufficient evidence acquisition. Moreover, fine-tuning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) shows that rewarding view-seeking increases active exploration but lowers overall accuracy, as models over-explore and fail to fuse expanding multi-view contexts across turns. These findings indicate that scaling passive multi-view perception does not intrinsically yield active spatial reasoning, highlighting the need for models that know where to look, how to integrate what they see, and when to stop. Code and data are available at https://gtc-gh.github.io/SATE-Bench/
evidence_items.title: Humans in Space: Can MLLMs Construct Human-Centric Spatial Understanding via Active Exocentric Exploration?

evidence_items.summary: Reusable Web-agent verification requires a rule to follow changing requirements and support subsequent execution. We introduce AgentProofBench, which connects paired tests of a frozen acceptance rule to execution from identical saved openings. The resource spans 97 tasks, 79 families, and four Web services. Experiments with DeepSeek Flash/Pro establish two linked measurements. Across 48 families, complete-panel and decision-replay tests retain 82/96 Flash and 79/96 Pro source programs; paired reuse-rebuild BA intervals are [-5.47, 1.57] and [-10.16, 0.00] percentage points. Across 22 execution families, deployment-state panel correctness separates program assignments whose two saved openings are both delivered correctly: 32/33 assignments with error-free panels, versus 1/11 with panel errors. All reference-defined program-gate regressions and withheld deliveries occur in the latter group. Neutral continuation attains the highest correct delivery under the tested generic feedback, providing a concrete baseline for measuring the value added by a gate. Released instructions, states, programs, reference rules, and trajectories connect each test failure to its execution consequences. AgentProofBench makes reusable verification assessable at both the requirement and policy levels.
evidence_items.title: AgentProofBench: Benchmarking Reusable Verifiers for Web Agents

evidence_items.summary: People have long dreamed of an assistant that is always there to guide them and remind what they forget, from new dishes to lost keys. Powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), egocentric AI assistants on wearable devices are bringing this dream within reach: they see what the user sees and give instructions for user's physical work when necessary. However, testing such assistance is challenging and usually requires real people. The expensive and rare real interaction data leaves a key question unanswered: Can today's MLLMs truly help people in physical world? To answer this question, we propose InteractiveWorld, the first verifiable environment for closed-loop interaction between human and AI assistant. Unlike existing robot-centric simulators, InteractiveWorld lets the assistant guide a human agent who observes the scene, understands instructions, and acts independently. It thus realistically simulates how AI assistant collaborates with human: the assistant instructs, the human acts, and the environment executes actions and updates what they see next. Building on it, we introduce InteractiveBench, the first dynamic benchmark for egocentric AI assistants, with 120 multi-turn tasks across six categories. In each task, the assistant guides the human in real time, and every instruction shapes the outcome, which is scored by verifiable, state-based rewards. Experiments with 12 frontier MLLMs show they are still far from reliable assistants. Even the strongest model, Claude Fable 5.1, achieves at most 20% and 25% on long-horizon Guidance and Planning tasks, respectively. Overall, our work offers a verifiable platform and a rigorous evaluation set, laying a solid foundation for research on interactive MLLM assistants that truly help people in the physical world.
evidence_items.title: InteractiveWorld: A Verifiable Human-Centric Environment for Building Better Interactive MLLM Assistants

evidence_items.summary: Catastrophic forgetting in continual learning (CL) manifests not only as accuracy degradation but also as explanation drift: models maintain predictive accuracy while silently shifting attention from diagnostic features to spurious correlations. This work identifies and resolves a previously overlooked structural flaw in explanation-aware CL: pixel-level saliency regularization derives supervision targets from the model's own frozen saliency maps, creating a self-referential drift loop that actively reinforces spurious attention across tasks. We introduce C^3L (Concept-Consistent Continual Learning), which breaks this loop by anchoring regularization to class-consistent semantic concepts (e.g., ``curved beak'', ``striped pattern'') discovered offline, independent of model state, providing (i) target independence from model drift, and (ii) cross-instance semantic consistency across every instance of a class. We identify that our concept-based objective, combined with approximate LRP relevance conservation, induces a crowding-out effect: since concept and background regions compete for the relevance of the same prediction, enforcing high relevance within concept regions implicitly suppresses spurious background correlations without explicit penalization. \method does not require human-annotated concept sets, as it employs a fully automated concept discovery and spatial grounding. Extensive evaluation across five benchmarks and over 20 baselines demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in accuracy, forgetting, explanation quality, spurious correlation mitigation, and out-of-distribution robustness.
evidence_items.title: Semantic Concept Steering Breaks the Explanation Drift Loop in Continual Learning

evidence_items.summary: Many robot manipulation videos do not indicate whether the task was successfully completed. RoboJev-27B is an open-weight vision-language model that takes a task instruction, 10 frames of a manipulation attempt, and (if available) final frames from auxiliary cameras and predicts whether the robot accomplished the task. RoboJev-27B is a variant of JEV-27B-VL, trained with a rank-32 LoRA adapter on the language model only (keeping the vision encoder frozen) using 52,598 episode records. It also uses a source-specific KL penalty that applies only to research data, anchoring predictions closer to the original model on those sources. It uses a calibrated two-token readout that outputs success/failure probabilities in a single forward pass. On 268 held-out episodes of the same robot model (SO-101), RoboJev-27B attains 95.2% balanced accuracy and 0.993 AUROC. It also generalises to episodes collected by unseen labs/robots (AUROC = 0.890 over 459 episodes) as well as to clearly labelled community-collected episodes (accuracy = 93.3% over 135 episodes), where the base model attains an AUROC = 0.900 on the unseen-lab/robot subset with the same inputs. It takes 0.26 seconds per episode (median, serial) to infer on a single H100, which is about \0.19 per 1,000 success predictions at 2.69 per GPU-hour (not including media processing and serving costs). RoboJev-27B is released together with its inference code, along with a transparent evaluation: 20,628 predictions organized into 29 model/protocol entries are made available to facilitate browsing and to enable reproducible benchmarking of success detection. We also compare against strong API-based frontier VLMs, which take in fewer input frames (4 images from the primary camera only); note that this comparison is not strictly like-for-like because RoboJev-27B is given more frames at inference.
evidence_items.title: RoboJev: An Open Vision-Language Judge for Robot Success Detection

evidence_items.summary: Localized AI manipulations in long-form videos often affect brief events within otherwise authentic content, making video-level classification insufficient for forensic analysis. Existing audio-visual deepfake benchmarks largely focus on short talking-head clips, while long-form temporal forensics remains predominantly visual. We introduce AV-FABLE, a dual-timeline benchmark for sparse manipulations in open-scene long-form audio-visual videos. AV-FABLE contains 16,650 pristine--manipulated twin pairs (998 hours) created with 27 editing configurations, with separate audio and visual timelines that enable modality-specific temporal localization and expose errors hidden by joint-timeline evaluation. On AV-FABLE, zero-shot prompting of audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) yields near-chance detection and poor temporal localization. In contrast, supervised readouts of their frozen perception features recover strong forensic signals, suggesting manipulation evidence is encoded in these representations but not effectively exposed through language outputs. Motivated by this observation, we propose NFSR(Native Forensics via Separated Readouts), which reads frozen AV-LLM features with separate audio and visual temporal decoders. NFSR achieves the best audio-visual localization performance in-domain and across all three out-of-distribution settings, including transfer to held-out videos from an external long-video forensic benchmark. AV-FABLE, code, and model weights will be publicly released.
evidence_items.title: AV-FABLE: Audio-Visual Manipulation Forensics in Long-Form Videos

evidence_items.summary: Hallucination detection is increasingly important for evaluating and deploying large language models. However, existing methods are often compared across benchmarks that define and measure hallucination in substantially different ways, making reported scores difficult to interpret across settings. We study hallucination detection as a benchmark-conditioned measurement problem and organize existing benchmarks along three axes: provenance, which describes how model outputs and evidence conditions are obtained; typology, which captures the factuality and faithfulness failures represented by benchmark labels; and granularity, which specifies the unit at which hallucinations are annotated, predicted, and evaluated. Using this framework, we analyze how benchmark construction, annotation, and evaluation choices shape the underlying prediction task, and relate detector mechanisms and assumptions to the settings in which their performance is measured. We also examine span-level evaluation, where variation in annotation boundaries can substantially affect reported results, and propose Span Coverage F1 as a complementary containment-based metric. Our analysis clarifies what detector scores capture, highlights limitations of cross-benchmark comparisons, and motivates more explicit evaluation of generalization across benchmark conditions.
evidence_items.title: Mycelium: A Meta-Study of Hallucination Detection Across Provenance, Typology, and Granularities

evidence_items.summary: Learning visual design is essential for prompt enhancement (PE) to turn underspecified user requests into coherent visual specifications for text-to-image (T2I) generation. Existing methods preserve user intent and improve overall visual appeal, with less explicit emphasis on fine-grained design dimensions. To address this gap, we introduce Qwen-Image-PE, which learns visual design through two-stage training. Supervised fine-tuning with Caption-Based Reverse Distillation (CRD) uses dense captions of well-designed images as design supervision. Reinforcement learning with Groupwise Design Reward (GDR) jointly compares all candidate images for the same request to refine lighting, composition, layout, and detail. On Qwen-Image-Bench with Qwen-Image-2.1, Qwen-Image-PE-397B improves over original requests by 7.81 points, while Qwen-Image-PE-9B outperforms all evaluated PE baselines. Further evaluations show gains in visual design, aesthetics, image quality, and human preference. We find that PE scales along three axes: training data, model size, and information density, with sufficient information density as a prerequisite for effective enhancement. Moreover, we demonstrate that Qwen-Image-PE generalizes to four additional T2I backbones, even surpassing native prompt enhancers on HunyuanImage-2.1 and FLUX 3 Image Klein. We release Qwen-Image-PE-9B at https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1-PE-T2I.
evidence_items.title: Qwen-Image-PE: Learning Visual Design for Text-to-Image Prompt Enhancement

evidence_items.summary: We introduce OvisOCR3, a 0.8B model for a broad range of OCR-related tasks. OvisOCR3 unifies document parsing, general OCR, key information extraction (KIE), document figure captioning, and cross-page table reconstruction in a single model. We train the model on real and synthetic data through continued pretraining and use domain-balanced mid-training to balance supervision across tasks with different data volumes and response lengths. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation transfers expertise from five domain-specific 4B teachers into the shared model, followed by mixed-task reinforcement learning with domain-specific rewards. We compare OvisOCR3 with general-purpose vision-language models and specialized OCR models on public and in-house benchmarks covering all five task families. In these comparisons, it achieves an overall score of 96.74 on OmniDocBench v1.6 and the highest overall scores on PureDocBench, Real5-OmniDocBench, and MDPBench. On OCRBench v2, it ranks first, scoring 65.9 and 61.3 on the English and Chinese splits, respectively. It also outperforms the baselines on OCRBench and all four KIE benchmarks. On DocFigCapBench, it achieves the highest localization F1 and a caption score close to that of Qwen3.8-Max. For cross-page tables, it leads in Relation F1 on CrossTabBench and truncated-table TEDS on MPDocBench-Parse. These results demonstrate that a compact 0.8B model can achieve strong performance across diverse OCR-related tasks. OvisOCR3 is available at https://huggingface.co/ATH-MaaS/OvisOCR3.
evidence_items.title: OvisOCR3 Technical Report

evidence_items.summary: In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions. These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies. Retaining past interactions alone does not ensure that agents can infer habits and apply them appropriately. We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate how well agent memory systems infer habits from weak evidence and apply them to later requests. We construct synthetic user histories from task-oriented dialogue data and controlled habit graphs. The histories span hundreds of sessions across food, finance, software, and travel. Four-choice tasks assess agents' ability to infer user habits and apply them appropriately. They include temporary exceptions, changes in habits, and suggestions that users have not accepted. Sampled tasks undergo independent human review. We evaluate eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash. The best-performing memory method achieves 33.61\% macro accuracy across the four domains. Performance remains limited even when annotated evidence is supplied directly. These results expose a persistent gap between access to past interactions and the ability to infer and appropriately use user habits.
evidence_items.title: HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory

evidence_items.summary: Modern image generation largely relies on specialized generative models that leave the process of image construction implicit in learned parameters. We explore an alternative: general-purpose coding agents that construct images through executable programs. Our study of zero-shot drawing on AgentDrawBench, a 200-prompt benchmark, reveals a distinctive capability profile. Agents excel at preserving structure and satisfying precise visual constraints, achieving competitive results in domains where compositional accuracy matters more than photorealistic appearance, while remaining limited in perceptual richness. Their visual expressiveness varies with the drawing interface, and a qualitative study on reconstruction shows how procedural skills extracted from human demonstrations support different artistic media. We then examine code as an external visual language of thought: a structured, executable representation that agents can construct and inspect. We test it in visual question answering task and find reconstructed visual code retains substantial information for question answering and, in some domains, supports higher accuracy than the original image. These abilities raise a further question: do agents draw on a shared internal representation of scene content beyond a particular drawing program? We explore an internal visual language-of-thought hypothesis, in which a shared, compositionally structured representation supports visual operations across drawing languages. Cross-harness drawings and images assembled from independent single-pixel queries exhibit related layouts and tones. Agents also maintain self-generated room arrangements across viewpoints after visible drawings are removed. These results demonstrate that the coding agent would maintain a consistent and coherent world inside its imagine even before the harness gets involved and the generation starts.
evidence_items.title: How Far Can Coding Agents Go in Visual Generation?

evidence_items.summary: Harness self-evolution offers a practical route for LLM agents to improve from execution experience without updating model parameters. Its effectiveness depends on whether models can successfully act on the guidance provided by their harnesses. However, we find that harness benefits are not uniform across model capabilities: skills that improve stronger models can provide little benefit or even degrade performance for weaker ones. Across seven models and three benchmarks, we identify 103 task-skill pairs where skills improve GPT-5.6-luna by 31.1 points but degrade Gemma-4-E4B by 8.8 points. In 86% of failed weak-model runs, the violated requirement is already stated in the skill. This motivates skill adaptation: reformulating existing skills to match the executor's capabilities and make their guidance easier to execute. To achieve this, we diagnose failures in tool execution, context management, instruction following, and verification, and distill these diagnoses into a fixed meta-skill that guides adaptation during harness self-evolution. Guided by the meta-skill, a capable external rewriter, Kimi-K3, adapts skills without execution evidence, improving the three weak executors by 5.1-14.1 points over the original skills. We then incorporate this adaptation into a five-round self-evolution loop, where each model revises its own skill from execution trajectories and verifier feedback. Across seven executors, from Gemma-4-E4B to Kimi-K2.5, the meta-skill consistently improves final scores by 2.0-5.1 points over the same loop without the meta-skill. Our findings provide practical design guidance for developing more effective harness self-evolution methods.
evidence_items.title: Evolving to Match Capabilities: Improving Harness Self-Evolution via Skill Adaptation

evidence_items.summary: Native NVFP4 promises to accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs), but achieving stable learning across separate training and sampling engines remains challenging. We show that matching model weights and numerical formats is insufficient to ensure consistent policy evaluation, highlighting the importance of cross-engine numerical execution. We introduce miniTE, a lightweight framework that combines execution diagnostics, cross-engine numerical alignment, and efficient native W4A4 (4-bit weights and activations) GEMM computation for LLM RL. It improves numerical execution consistency without modifying the RL objective, while reducing implementation overhead to realize the benefits of native low-bit computation. Long-horizon RL experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate stable training and benchmark performance close to BF16, outperforming naive Transformer Engine (TE) NVFP4 in evaluation quality. On single NVIDIA B300 GPU node, the optimized learner reaches 33,540 tokens/s, yielding 1.39x and 1.47x the throughput of BF16 and TE NVFP4, respectively, for complete learner updates. We released the framework, kernels, diagnostics, and training configurations to make native low-bit RL easier.
evidence_items.title: miniTE: Diagnosing and Bridging the Execution Gap in Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Benchmark scenarios, system prompts, generated LLM responses, human ratings, and analysis code for a study of a prompt-layer response policy that keeps an AI from handing high-school students a ready-to-use research theme, while still giving useful support. All ratings are human; no LLM judging was used. Scenario texts, responses, and rubrics are in Japanese; the README and all data field names are in English. The associated paper is under review; the citation will be added upon publication. Version 3 adds files for the post-hoc C11/C13 rating batch (360 responses): the first rater's initial ratings, before re-rating (8 H3 in 360); the 92 responses re-rated under a selection rule fixed in advance, with the initial and final value of each (56 raised, 6 lowered, 30 unchanged); a script that recomputes these counts. Nothing in version 2 was changed or removed. The procedure is described in README.md, "Blinding and amendment record". License: data CC BY 4.0; code MIT.
evidence_items.title: Withholding Ready-to-Use Research Themes in AI-Supported Inquiry Learning: Benchmark, LLM Responses, and Human Ratings

evidence_items.summary: Background. Clinicians score the NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) at the bedside, often under time pressure, and ambient AI tools that listen to clinical encounters are now entering practice. It is not known whether software can score the NIHSS from the exam conversation itself, rather than extract a score that has already been written in a note. Methods. We created 112 synthetic code-stroke cases. One hundred were allocated in proportion to real code-stroke presentations, and 12 stress cases tested special scoring rules. For each case, a large language model (Claude Opus 5.5) wrote a reference score form (the answer key) and a speech-to-text-style exam transcript, with main-set transcripts split evenly between a narrated and a telegraphic examiner style. A second model (Claude Fable 5.1), blind to the key, scored every transcript and agreed with the key on 99.2% of items. Each transcript was then scored by Jev, a decision model, and by gpt-6-luna, a general large language model (LLM). The primary outcome was item-level accuracy against the key. Results. The LLM scored 99.0% of items correctly (95% CI 98.4-99.4) and Jev 94.4% (93.2-95.4; McNemar p < 0.001), with exact totals in 101 and 63 of 112 cases. Jev was faster (median 0.15 vs 5.78 s per exam) and cheaper (USD 0.23 vs 0.67 per 1,000 exams). With telegraphic examiners, accuracy fell from 98.0% to 90.9% for Jev and from 100% to 97.7% for the LLM. In a post-hoc analysis that kept only the examiner's words, accuracy stayed high when the examiner narrated (Jev 96.9%, LLM 98.8%) but dropped to about 80% when the examiner used shorthand. Most of Jev's errors fell on four items (language, extinction and neglect, LOC questions and visual fields), and on each it tended to repeat the same mistake, for example scoring slurred speech as aphasia. Its confidence flagged most of these errors. Re-checking the 14.8% of items with confidence below 0.70 would have caught 86% of them, and a simulated hybrid reached 98.8% accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Scoring the NIH Stroke Scale from bedside exam transcripts: a synthetic benchmark of a decision model and a large language model

organizations: Hongik University Research Institute of Science and Technology (HIRIST), Hongik University, Seoul, Republic of Korea

evidence_items.summary: This study proposes a methodological framework for analyzing public transit user satisfaction by processing unstructured, voice-derived trip chain data. Traditional survey methods often do not capture the contextual and real time aspects of user experience. To address this limitation, this study employs large language models and natural language processing techniques to analyze trip-related feedback collected from 5,000 public transit users. Sentiment scores were extracted from a station-labeled subset of the data set and applied to a broader corpus to assess satisfaction levels across subway stations in the Seoul Metropolitan Area. Using a combination of sentiment analysis and K-means clustering, this study categorized 102 subway stations into three groups: (1) High Satisfaction Station Group; (2) Low Satisfaction Station Group; and (3) Moderate Satisfaction Station Group. These clusters were the basis for grouping stations, and user feedback on transit experiences was summarized for each station within its respective cluster. This approach enables the identification of low-satisfaction transit stations requiring immediate attention, as well as moderate-satisfaction transit stations where service equity must be addressed. The proposed methodology offers a practical alternative to traditional survey-based assessments by leveraging unstructured public transit users’ data. With further refinement and institutional support, this approach can enhance data-driven, user-centered transit planning and contribute to broader improvements in urban mobility.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model-Based Sentiment Analysis for Public Transit Satisfaction Using Trip Chain Data

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Patients increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for health information, yet the evaluation of the quality of fecal incontinence (FI) content from these models is limited. We aimed to evaluate the quality, understandability, and actionability of LLM responses to FI queries. We hypothesized that LLMs would provide variable quality responses with variable understandability and actionability. Methods Search data was extracted from Google Trends’ top five search queries related to FI to create identical prompts used to generate responses from four LLMs: ChatGPT version 4o mini (OpenAI), Perplexity version sonar (Perplexity AI), LLaMA version 3.2 (Meta AI), and Gemini version 2.0 flash (Google). Responses were assessed using DISCERN, Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT), and the Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL). Statistical analysis was performed using R version 4.4.2 (R Core Team, 2025). Results Response quality was moderate (median DISCERN 44 out of 80), nominal understandability was median 77% ([7/9] PEMAT) although inter-rater agreement was poor, and actionability was poor (median 40% [2/5] PEMAT). DISCERN scores varied significantly ( p = 0.033). The responses were at the high school to college level using the FKGL score. Readability differed significantly ( p = 0.022). Conclusions LLM responses demonstrated structural clarity using PEMAT criteria but lacked actionability and were above the recommended reading level for consumer health information. Continued evaluation of artificial intelligence is essential before LLMs can be recommended for patient education.
evidence_items.title: Quality, understandability, and actionability of large language model responses to fecal incontinence: a cross-sectional study

organizations: Department of Neurology, Bern University Hospital (Inselspital) and University of Bern, 3010, Bern, Switzerland;

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Large language models (LLMs) may enable the extraction of clinically relevant information from unstructured electronic health records, but most previous work focused on identifying diagnoses without preserving their temporal context. We evaluated the ability of an LLM to extract diagnoses and associated dates from longitudinal clinical reports. Methods In an observational study using the Bern Sleep-Wake Registry, diagnostic annotations from 248 patients comprising 2343 clinical entries were analyzed. Six common comorbidity groups, subdivided into 32 hierarchical diagnostic categories, were evaluated. Using gpt-oss-20b, we extracted diagnosis presence, the number of diagnostic instances, and dates per instance. A reference standard was established through independent review by two physicians, with disagreements adjudicated by a third physician. LLM performance was assessed using diagnostic classification and temporal agreement. Direct annotation costs were compared. Results At the patient level, the LLM achieved an overall F1 score of 0.88 for diagnosis presence and 0.96 for the presence of a reported date. For the earliest reported diagnosis date, agreement with the reference standard was 86.73% at the day level. When considering the cumulative set of dates for each diagnosis, date recall was 87.63%, the extra-date rate was 20.88%, and full agreement was achieved in 58.19% of cases. Human annotators showed substantial disagreement in temporal annotation, with a date recall of 75.49%, an extra-date rate of 17.89%, and full agreement in 58.64% of cases. LLM-based extraction reduced direct annotation costs by 94.65%. Conclusions LLMs can extract diagnoses and their dates from heterogeneous clinical text with high agreement with an adjudicated reference standard. These findings support the scalable use of LLMs for longitudinal clinical registries.
evidence_items.title: Bern Sleep-Wake Registry: temporal extraction of comorbidities from unstructured clinical text using a large language model

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Mentalization - the ability to infer others’ beliefs and intentions to guide one’s own choices - is a key cognitive function underlying human social interactions. Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate behaviour consistent with humans on theory-of-mind tasks, yet whether these models can guide adaptive behaviour through mentalization is unknown. Here we use two economic games with cognitive computational modeling to uncover the latent strategies underlying mentalization in LLMs. We tested individual LLM agents across four model families, DeepSeek, GPT-4.1, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.0 Flash (N = 2,099), against opponents of varying sophistication and examined whether a prompting strategy designed to elicit strategic reasoning improved performance. We benchmarked results against human participants (N = 251) as a comparative measure. Across both games, LLMs showed clear behavioural and computational signatures of mentalizing that differed markedly by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance by inducing more sophisticated reasoning, yet the extent of the benefit differed across the two tasks. Last, GPT-5 agents flexibly adapted their recursive depth of reasoning to increasingly sophisticated opponents, demonstrating superior performance to human participants. Collectively, we demonstrate different capacities for mentalization across LLMs, and highlight cognitive computational modeling as a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence across humans and machines.
evidence_items.title: Assessing mentalization in humans and large language models

organizations: Institute of Space and Earth Information Science The Chinese University of Hong Kong  Hong Kong SAR China

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Simulating human mobility is crucial for urban planning, environmental exposure assessment, and social behavior studies. However, existing methods often rely on rules and assumptions, making it difficult to provide robust results and explicit decision‐making processes when generating plausible daily activity trajectories from sparse location records such as check‐ins. To bridge these gaps, we propose a large language model (LLM)‐based agent framework that innovatively incorporates the Chain‐of‐Thought (CoT) approach and Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF) mechanisms, namely Daily mobility LLM (DaiLLM). This framework consists of three modules: the Profiler derives user characteristics from historical trajectory data; the Generator simulates movement through the CoT process, which integrates constraints from Profiler outputs; and the Discriminator employs RLAIF to evaluate the similarity between generated results and real data, providing feedback to optimize the results. Experiments demonstrate that: (1) our method improves accuracy by 34.2% compared to traditional approaches in daily activity trajectory generation; (2) the CoT approach enhances activity logic and results in a 26.1% increase through task decomposition and constraint integration; (3) the RLAIF mechanism explicitly provides an optimization process through Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) analysis; and (4) our method excels in transfer learning and long‐term generation across different city contexts. This study provides a robust, transparent, and cost‐effective solution for plausible daily activity trajectory generation from sparse check‐in data, which will establish a new paradigm for mobility behavior analysis in data‐scarce scenarios.
evidence_items.title: DaiLLM: An Agent Framework Based on a Large Language Model and Reinforced by AI to Generate Daily Activity Trajectories

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) show promise in supporting drug recommendations both within and outside clinical settings, but they may also amplify systematic biases affecting equity and cost. We examined the commercial neutrality of LLM-generated product name recommendations among US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved products containing the same active ingredient. We evaluated product name recommendations from five LLMs using 177,120 synthetic clinical vignettes spanning 123 disease–drug pairs and 1,440 sociodemographic profiles. Each vignette specified a disease and an active ingredient and asked the model to recommend FDA-approved products. Across disease–drug pairs and models, the most frequently recommended product accounted for a mean of 97.5% of first-choice recommendations, and the models showed almost perfect agreement on which products to recommend. LLM-recommended product distributions differed from real-world prescribing patterns and often yielded higher projected acquisition costs. Recommendations inconsistent with regulatory information varied across LLMs and sociodemographic factors. Models more often recommended products with greater online visibility (Google search counts, odds ratio (OR) 1.70; a dedicated Wikipedia page, OR 3.00) and favoured originator products (OR 20.5), whereas products with later FDA approval and those more commonly prescribed in practice were recommended less often (ORs 0.76 and 0.87, respectively). Although modified prompts shifted recommendations in the intended direction, LLMs still favoured a narrow set of products, which could have potential implications for drug costs and pharmaceutical markets. Rigorous evaluation and targeted mitigation are needed before widespread use.
evidence_items.title: Large language models show product name convergence in drug recommendations

evidence_items.summary: Abstract In the legal domain, judgement prediction is an important and challenging problem. In real-life proceedings, judicial decisions depend on the precise presentation of complex case information and, above all, on the argumentative interplay among petitioners, respondents, and judges. However, most existing research work on this judgment prediction primarily focuses on case facts, rather than on argumentative legal reasoning. Furthermore, many such approaches rely on single-agent Large Language Models (LLMs), which are not analogous to the real-life courtroom. To address this limitation, simulating a courtroom conversation becomes essential. Some prior studies explored multiple LLMs (multi-agent) based courtroom simulations, with limited investigation on the quality of argumentation. Motivated by this crucial gap, in this work, we propose simulating courtroom arguments employing a multi-agent conversational system, termed as \naam, specifically tailored to crime-related cases. We consider solely legal cases from the U.S. Supreme Court, evaluating the ability of LLMs in generating courtroom arguments using different in-context learning approaches, including zero-shot, and the variant of few-shot techniques, within a multi-agent setup. Empirically, we find that the quality of arguments improves significantly when using local precedent retrieval based approach employing GPT-4o models. This strategy yields 12$%$ improvement over the zero-shot (baseline) setup. Subsequently, to measure the quality of LLM-based arguments, we propose a new algorithm -- coined as ArguEval. Eventually, to showcase the efficacy of generated arguments, we utilize them in a downstream \texttt{judgment prediction} task, which results in a 14$\%$ performance gain over the zero-shot baseline.
evidence_items.title: ArguGenCourt: Courtroom Argument Generation using Judicial Multi-agent Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We present an automated framework employing large language models to categorize atomic spectroscopy literature for NIST bibliographic databases. The system processes native PDFs and supplementary materials via instruction-driven reasoning agents to assign structured search keywords encompassing target species, subject codes, and experimental methodologies. Validation against human-curated datasets demonstrates high precision in elemental species identification, while establishing that granular subject code assignment remains the primary source of categorization error.
evidence_items.title: Categorization of scientific publications using large language models as applied to atomic spectroscopy

evidence_items.summary: Physical exercise lowers blood pressure, but guidelines address broad populations and rarely consider age, comorbidities, medications or baseline severity. No structured, queryable database of exercise interventions for hypertension exists, and manual curation is not scalable. We present PAHD (Physical Activity for Hypertension Database), built with large language models (LLMs). An LLM screened 2,548 PubMed records by title and abstract, then full text, selecting 255 studies. LLMs extracted each study's groups, exercise protocols, patient characteristics and results; two LLMs cross-checked the study structure, and every value carries a verbatim quote. Code standardized and joined the extractions into 17,312 records from 254 studies, one per reported comparison. Against adjudicated benchmarks, screening reached 86.3% recall and 80.6% precision, and extraction recovered 90.1% of blood pressure values with 90.5% precision. A web portal matches patients' hypertension stage and comorbidities to studies. PAHD provides a structured evidence base for personalized exercise interventions on hypertension management.
evidence_items.title: A Knowledge Database of Physical Activity Interventions for Hypertension using Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal entity alignment identifies equivalent entities referring to the same real-world object across heterogeneous multimodal knowledge graphs and is essential for multi-source knowledge integration. Existing methods often rely on manually labeled seed alignments and multimodal feature similarity, limiting their ability to capture implicit semantic equivalence under heterogeneous attribute and relation expressions. Large language models (LLMs) offer strong semantic understanding and reasoning capabilities for unsupervised alignment, but their direct application remains challenging because of the large entity search space, redundant knowledge graph information, and the stochasticity of LLM inference. To address these challenges, we propose MEA-LLM, an LLM-based fully unsupervised multimodal semantic-enhanced entity alignment method. MEA-LLM first pre-screens candidate entities by jointly exploiting multimodal similarities derived from visual, attribute, and relational information. It then selects discriminative attributes and relations based on degree of freedom, candidate frequency, and discriminability for LLM reasoning. Multiple inference and result aggregation are further employed to improve robustness. Experiments on FB-DB15K and FB-YAGO15K show that MEA-LLM outperforms existing methods across multiple evaluation metrics. Further ablation studies, hyperparameter analyses, experiments with different model-scales, and efficiency evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of the core components and indicate that MEA-LLM achieves a favorable trade-off between entity alignment performance and inference cost.
evidence_items.title: An Unsupervised Multimodal Semantic-Enhanced Entity Alignment Method Based on Large Language Models

authors: Marc J. C. van den Homberg
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming disaster risk reduction and management by enhancing prediction, preparedness, response, and recovery. Leveraging techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, and foundation models, AI can analyse diverse datasets, including satellite imagery, sensor networks, social media, and historical disaster records, to improve early warning systems and risk assessments. AI applications range from predictive modelling of floods, earthquakes, landslides, and tropical cyclones to real-time damage assessment using computer vision and drones, and optimised emergency response planning. Additionally, AI supports post-disaster reconstruction and long-term recovery through economic modelling, infrastructure planning, and psychological support. Despite these benefits, challenges such as data scarcity, algorithmic bias, privacy concerns, and infrastructure requirements must be addressed to ensure equitable and effective deployment. Incorporating ethical frameworks, community engagement, and transparency is essential for maximising AI’s potential in building resilient communities and mitigating the social, economical, and environmental impacts of disasters.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Disaster Risk Management

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The environmental comparison of artificial intelligence (AI) systems is context-dependent regarding lifecycle boundaries, the sharing and allocation of infrastructure, the accounting of electricity use and the accounting of water use. A low operational carbon value can coexist with substantial upstream water consumption or a large unallocated hardware burden. This paper develops a lifecycle framework in which primitive resource events are assigned once to workload stages and translated into energy, greenhouse-gas, and water inventories through explicit, versioned factors. The framework separates physical water consumption from scarcity characterization, operational electricity from upstream energy carriers, and attributional reporting from consequential scheduling. We derive conservation under allocation, an exact temporal aggregation bias identity, an identifiability condition for incomplete inventories, a shared-infrastructure allocation model, and a service-volume break-even condition. A constrained minimax routing extension evaluates conflicting operational objectives without collapsing physical units into an unexplained score. A fully specified synthetic study covers three hypothetical regions, 168 hourly intervals, 24 demand profiles, four routing policies, and 10,000 uncertainty draws. For the base case of 3.36 million requests, carbon-only routing reduces serving carbon by approximately 50.5% relative to the reference, but increases serving water consumption by approximately 124.3%. Once fixed lifecycle burdens are included, the corresponding changes are approximately − 4.2% and + 9.6%. Through this specific situation, the minimax policy is redefined, so no enhancement over the minimax reference is claimed. This study does not exhibit accounting accuracy but rather accounting consistency and conditional decision behavior.
evidence_items.title: Lifecycle Intelligence for Carbon Energy Water Footprint Optimization in Artificial Intelligence Systems

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT The translation of nanomedicines is frequently bottlenecked by trial‐and‐error optimization. Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) transforms this process into a closed‐loop, experimentally grounded discovery ecosystem. This Review provides a roadmap for this paradigm, demonstrating how AI, high‐throughput testing, and nanoscale design converge to generate clinically translatable nanotherapeutics. We emphasize the necessity of standardized multimodal data—spanning pharmacokinetic, biodistribution, and drug‐release profiles—anchored strictly to validated biological phenomena. Furthermore, we evaluate an algorithmic spectrum, ranging from classical machine learning to physics‐informed neural networks (PINNs) and reinforcement learning (RL), to align models with specific formulation objectives. To bridge computational design and empirical reality, we examine how high‐throughput technologies, such as robotic laboratories and in vivo DNA‐barcoding multiplexing, operationalize the “Design‐Make‐Test‐Analyze” (DMTA) cycle for dynamic model recalibration. Ultimately, this review demonstrates how integrating AI, physical constraints, and automated validation accelerates the rational design of next‐generation nanomedicines.
evidence_items.title: An Integrated Artificial Intelligence Framework for Nanomedicine Engineering

organizations: İZMİR KATİP ÇELEBİ ÜNİVERSİTESİ, TIP FAKÜLTESİ
evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into modern healthcare, supporting diagnostic interpretation, clinical decision-making, workflow optimization, documentation, patient communication, medical education, and outcome prediction. This narrative review examines the current clinical applications and future directions of healthcare AI, with radiology presented as a model specialty because of its standardized workflows, large datasets, and measurable outputs. It discusses the growing roles of generative AI, large language models, multimodal foundation models, patient-facing applications, and AI-assisted medical education, while emphasizing persistent limitations such as hallucinations, bias, limited generalizability, inadequate reporting, and insufficient prospective clinical evidence. Emerging approaches, including digital twins and agentic AI systems, may enable patient-specific simulation, longitudinal monitoring, and multi-step workflow automation; however, their clinical use remains at an early stage. Successful implementation will require external validation, transparent reporting, continuous performance monitoring, institutional governance, and clearly defined human oversight. The future value of AI will therefore depend not on complete autonomy, but on its ability to improve healthcare safely, effectively, equitably, and responsibly within human-supervised clinical systems.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Modern Healthcare: Present and Future

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now embedded in higher education. Yet educators often adopt it more slowly and cautiously than students, and generic guidance rarely translates into changes in teaching or assessment practice. We designed a short, hands‐on, pedagogy‐first workshop in which life‐science educators work with their own course materials, intended to increase confidence in pedagogically informed AI use and prompt concrete changes to course design, teaching and assessment. However, this is an exploratory feasibility and specification report; therefore, the evaluation was not designed to test that intention. Here we describe the design of a transferable three‐session FEBS Education and Training Academy module, organised around the PICRAT (Passive‐Interactive‐Creative/Replace‐Amplify‐Transform) framework, a four‐element prompt structure and studio‐style application to participants' own teaching artefacts, and evaluate it using matched pre/post surveys, anonymous after‐session feedback and an online follow‐up meeting. Thirty‐four educators from 14 countries attended; 21 completed the pre‐workshop and 13 the post‐workshop survey (12 matched). Among the 12 respondents who completed both surveys, the proportion reporting high confidence rose by the same margin, 4 of 12, in each of the five practical domains. Ten of 13 follow‐up respondents reported implementing at least one idea and while views of AI as beneficial were already positive and changed little, agreement that AI poses significant risks to academic integrity fell. These participant‐reported, uncontrolled findings should be read as evidence of feasibility and perceived usefulness rather than causal impact.
evidence_items.title: Design and evaluation of FEBS Education and Training Academy module – Integrating generative artificial intelligence into life‐science education

evidence_items.summary: Background. Pulmonary embolism (PE) phenotyping aims to stratify patients according to clinical, radiological, and prognostic features to guide management. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly applied to PE for risk stratification and outcome prediction, yet the scope, methodological quality, and clinical applicability of these approaches remain unclear.Aims. To systematically map the existing literature on the application of AI in PE phenotyping, describe methodological characteristics and performance metrics, and identify gaps in current evidence.Methods. A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the JBI methodology and the PRISMA-ScR checklist. Eligible studies included adult patients with imaging-confirmed or administratively coded PE and applied AI methods for phenotyping.Results. After screening 2,074 records, 22 studies met inclusion criteria. Publications increased markedly in recent years, with 17 of the 22 studies published between 2023 and 2025. Reported sample sizes varied widely, ranging from 70 to 6,853. All studies were retrospective, with most conducted at a single center. Traditional machine learning models were used in 14 studies, deep learning approaches in 3, combined deep learning and traditional machine learning in 2, commercial imaging AI in 2, and quantitative imaging plus traditional machine learning in 1; radiomics-based features were used in 4 studies. Imaging-only inputs were most common, followed by clinical/laboratory data and multimodal models. Mortality prediction was the most frequent clinical task, followed by PE risk stratification or severity classification, composite adverse outcome prediction, functional marker assessment, and clot-burden evaluation. AI-derived model performance was most frequently reported using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with values ranging from 0.63 to 0.97; 6 of 20 studies with reported AUCs achieved an AUC ≥0.90.
evidence_items.title: PO094 |  ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN PULMONARY EMBOLISM PHENOTYPING: A SCOPING REVIEW

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Benchmarks – shared prediction tasks with fixed data and a common metric – have driven cumulative progress in many fields but remain rare in the social sciences. We document PreFer (Predicting Fertility in the Netherlands), a data challenge in which participants predicted whether Dutch residents aged 18–45 in 2020 would have a child in 2021–2023, using longitudinal LISS panel surveys or full-population administrative registers. About 150 researchers made 69 valid survey-based and 11 register-based submissions. We describe the challenge design and review how teams handled thousands of features, a small and imbalanced survey sample, missing values and longitudinal data. We then analyse the reproducibility of submissions two years after the challenge. Requiring code and trained models rather than predictions in the survey phase made most submissions reproducible: 67 of 69 saved models reproduced their original scores, while retraining from code reproduced the original F1 score to within 0.03 for 52 submissions. Finally, using feature importance and ablation experiments, we identify which topics contributed to predictive performance. The predictive signal was highly concentrated: in the survey data, fertility intentions with partnership and household information came close to full-model performance; the remaining demographic, economic and attitudinal variables added little. In the register data, which lack intentions, partnership and household characteristics each recovered most of the attainable performance. These analyses inform other data challenges in the social sciences and establish PreFer as a reusable benchmark for cumulative fertility research by providing a reference point against which new predictors, data, and methods can be tested.
evidence_items.title: Building a reusable benchmark for life-outcome prediction: design, modelling approaches, predictors, and reproducibility of the PreFer data challenge

evidence_items.summary: Scientific priors speed up Bayesian optimisation in materials discovery, but a prior that steers a small budget toward the materials it favours may miss those it disfavours. We measured this in a benchmark with a registered analysis plan: 7,020 searches (3,000 of them over 3,550 metallic multielement Materials Project structures), for the shear modulus and the specific Young’s modulus, with a historical prior and a composition-only elemental-modulus heuristic, each mixed into expected improvement search with a fixed weight β. Coverage was the recall of the half of the top-5% materials that the prior itself scores lowest. Coverage loss at moderate weight was detected in 4 of 6 prior–objective settings. The elemental heuristic reduced the restricted mean number of acquisitions to a top-1% shear-modulus material by 13.9 at β = 0.25 with no detected loss of coverage, but its shear-modulus form, applied to the specific modulus, lost 44.0% or more of the baseline coverage at every nonzero weight. A weight both beneficial and safe under the registered criterion existed in 3 of 6 settings (2 under a post hoc joint error control), never above β = 0.25, and depended on the safety margin and on curation. At β = 0.5, in 5 of 6 settings the weighted search found more top-5% materials in total but, by its estimates, fewer of those its prior disfavours (a loss detected in 3): the prior redirected the search rather than reducing its yield. Faster discovery alone therefore does not show that a search keeps what its prior disfavours.
evidence_items.title: The efficiency–coverage trade-off of scientific priors in Bayesian search: a registered benchmark on metallic multi-element elasticity data
